National has released a new small-business plan, which includes establishing a fast-track for minor employment disputes and a central service so businesses only need to tell government once about changes.

The party’s small-business spokesperson Cameron Brewer said the policy package was intended to simplify employment rules “so it is easier to take on new staff and create more opportunities”.

“The First Employee Support Package will deliver practical, dedicated advice for new employers through first year of their first hire – employment agreement tools, payroll guidance, and tax and ACC reminders,” he said.

“Small businesses don’t have teams of people to deal with government paperwork. Often it is the owner doing everything themselves late at night after the kids are in bed.

“That is why this plan is focused on practical changes that give them time back, whether that is helping them through their first hire, resolving employment disputes faster, or letting them update core business information once instead of repeating it across government.”

National would progress MP Dan Bidois’ Member’s Bill to give independent mechanics better access to car-makers’ information – something Labour earlier this week pledged to do.

Elsewhere in the plan is a promise to review the compulsory GST registration threshold, which National says has remained at $60,000 since 2009.

The party would develop a fast-track process for minor employment disputes through a simplified Employment Relations Authority (ERA) pathway, make better use of mediation to resolve disputes, require ERA determinations within a month of the investigation meeting or final submissions, and review the authority’s enforcement powers.

It would require a minimum level of employee support before new collective bargaining can begin, proposing a threshold of the lesser of 10 employees or 20% of those proposed to be covered, with a minimum of two employees.

A “Tell Government Once” Service would be centred around the New Zealand Business Number so business information can be updated once and then shared across agencies and councils.

“Unjustified” paper-retention requirements would be removed and new guidance would be published on accepting lawful electronic records and evidence.

The party would replace “unnecessary compulsory newspaper notices with searchable online publication and appropriate community notification”.

Similarly, “obsolete fax, telex, and paper requirements that impose a real compliance burden” would be removed.

Raul was born in Santa Catarina, Brazil, and started playing football when he was still a preschooler, influenced by his father, who played semi-professionally in Brazil when he was younger, and his grandfather, who was “football-mad”.

When the family decided to move to New Zealand in 2018, Raul was about 9, and he had one condition.

“I’ll only go if there’s football. If there’s no football, I’m not going,” Rubia recalled him saying.

The family settled in Hawke’s Bay, where Raul played football and futsal for several teams before successfully trialling for the Christchurch United academy in 2023.

At 15, he moved to Christchurch alone to join the club’s residential programme.

He lived with other young players and attended St Thomas of Canterbury College, representing the school in both football and futsal.

After two years, his family followed him south.

Rubia said supporting the ambitions of her two sons – her older son, Ruben, competes professionally in Brazilian jiu-jitsu – had meant travelling, moving cities and finding ways to meet the costs that came with elite sport.

Contact our Christchurch newsroom.

His routine now revolves almost entirely around football.

“Most of my days are basically gym, eating, recovering and training,” he said.

But Raul was used to the discipline.

In Christchurch, he trained before and after school and played at weekends.

He said missing parties and nights out had never felt like much of a sacrifice.

For Raul, coming back is not the plan. Yet.

His goal is to keep progressing in European football, and, one day, he hopes to play internationally for the All Whites.

“It’s always a dream playing for your country,” he said.

“I lived most of my life in New Zealand, so I would choose them.”

Fears copper thieves targeting pivot irrigators could end up being killed

New Zealand Herald October 06, 2026

Thieves have targeted farms across Canterbury with pivot irrigators, stripping copper wire from the expensive equipment to sell. Photo / RNZ, Nate McKinnon

By Gianina Schwanecke of RNZ

A Canterbury irrigation specialist fears thieves targeting large pivot irrigators for their copper wiring may end up being killed.

Farms with pivot irrigators across Canterbury have been targeted by thieves stripping copper wire from the expensive equipment to sell.

The large irrigators, worth thousands of dollars, run on three-phase 400 volt power, with the cables targeted by thieves found on the tallest part of the machine, about 3 to 4m above the air.

Irrigation specialist Waterforce’s Rangiora branch manager, Andrew Panasiuk, said the thefts were a relatively new development but had been happening on and off since December last year and that police were aware and looking into it.

He said many of the irrigators are operated remotely or on automatic timers, meaning there’s no warning before they turn on or move.

“We’re now entering a phase where the machines are running, and if these thieves continue, they’re going to get a shock - literally - and you know someone could get killed.

“They’re taking their lives into their own hands.

“They’re walking out on these machines 3 or 4 metres above the air - presumably in the dark.

“It’s very dangerous, the work that they’re doing.

“Like I say, it’s very easy for someone to get killed with this voltage that we’re talking.”

One farmer RNZ spoke to, who didn’t want to be named, said he felt “anxious” and “angry” over the thefts.

Having been targeted himself, he said it was frustrating.

He was still working on making an insurance claim so didn’t know the final cost of the repairs.

“They’re integral to what we do,” he said.

“The inconvenience is one factor; the cost of replacing the cable is another.

“But the real problem for us looms in the fact that here in Canterbury we simply can’t grow grass through summer if these irrigators aren’t running every day.”

The farmer said other input costs for fuel and fertiliser had already increased, and feed was also likely to, with El Niño conditions looming.

He said this put margins under further pressure.

He’d increased security measures on-farm and was talking to other neighbours as well as police about the incident.

“We’re just going to have to make it as hard as possible.”

Panasiuk said it was an expensive process repairing the damage – not just for the replacement costs, but also labour and downtime while the irrigator was out of action.

For farmers, he said it was worth checking irrigators they haven’t used in a while, and they should consider having an anti-theft system turned on.

“A lot of these sites are quite remote. We have seen a good number of these sites accessible from public land – so roads that back onto farms.”

He urged farmers to stay vigilant and report any thefts to police.

“These lowlifes are around, and they are targeting these machines.”

The Crown has announced this morning that it won’t be seeking a re-trial for David Tamihere, who until recently was one of the nation’s highest-profile double-murder convicts.

The decision, announced by prosecutor Claire Paterson during a brief administrative hearing in the High Court at Auckland, comes just over six months after the Supreme Court quashed the now 73-year-old’s 1990 convictions.

“A criminal trial is about what can be proved with admissable evidence,” Paterson said. “... There is no longer sufficient evidence to support Mr Tamihere being re-tried.”

That trial was unfair and based partly on evidence that was “concocted to secure convictions”, New Zealand’s highest court announced in March. But the court did not allow a full exoneration, leaving it to the Crown to decide if it would be feasible for a new trial nearly four decades later.

At the conclusion of today’s brief hearing, attended by media and documentary filmmakers from New Zealand and abroad, Justice Simon Mount told Tamihere he was allowed to leave the dock, a free man.

Tamihere first returned to court at the end of July expecting a decision, but the Crown announced at that time that more time was needed to assess the case.

Tamihere served 20 years in prison following his convictions for the murders of Swedish tourists Sven Urban Hoglin, 23, and Heidi Birgitta Paakkonen, 21, who were last seen alive together in 1989 on the Coromandel Peninsula.

The former defendant admitted before his trial that he stole the couple’s car and sold or dumped their possessions. But he insisted he had never met the backpackers.

His convictions were based in part on evidence from a fellow remand prisoner who, many years later, was discredited and prosecuted for perjury.

Hoglin’s remains were found in the bush by pig-hunters in 1991, many kilometres away from where they should have been if the prosecution’s theories were correct. Paakkonen’s remains have never been found.

Tamihere has always maintained his innocence, even after his release from prison in 2010. The case was reviewed twice by the Court of Appeal before the Supreme Court decision.

The Supreme Court justices found that the Crown’s later case theories, after the witness was discredited, had never been tested in front of a jury.

The last confirmed sighting of Höglin, 23, and fiancée, Paakkonen, 21, was in Thames on April 7, 1989. But some witnesses said they believed they saw the couple in the northern part of the Coromandel Peninsula the following day.

Their distinctive white Subaru four-wheel-drive station wagon with a bull bar was seen at Tararu Creek Rd, on the western side of the Coromandel Peninsula, north of Thames, on April 9.

Tamihere was already convicted and serving a life sentence when Höglin’s remains were found in 1991, in the bush many kilometres away from where they should have been if the prosecution’s theories were correct.

Paakkonen’s remains have never been discovered, although her jacket and wallet were found near Crosbies Clearing.

In 2024, the Court of Appeal found there had been a miscarriage of justice because of the evidence the discredited prison informant, Roberto Conchie Harris, gave at the original High Court trial. But the Court of Appeal also determined that new evidence in the case trumped that and “for that reason, the miscarriage does not justify setting the convictions aside”.

The Supreme Court disagreed.

“Were there a retrial, the Crown case would be a circumstantial one…” Paterson told the court in a prepared statement.

“That evidence has always been, and would be, strongly disputed, by Mr Tamihere. Some of that evidence is no longer available to the Crown. These witnesses who would give it are no longer available. Other evidence would not be admissible in a retrial, following amendments to evidential admissibility rules since the first trial.

”Additional forensic testing has been carried out but the results were inconclusive," she told the court.

“As a result of the passage of time, some 36 years, significant pieces of evidence that the Crown introduced in the 1990 trial are no longer available. Or, if available, will likely be subject to reliability challenge.

“The conclusion is, therefore, that… the evidential test for prosecution is not met.”

She emphasised, however, that prosecutors first met with the victims’ families to gather their views.

Craig Kapitan is an Auckland-based journalist covering courts and justice. He joined the Herald in 2021 and has reported on courts since 2002 in three newsrooms in the US and New Zealand.

Fire crews return to large Walter Peak wildfire as strong winds forecast

New Zealand Herald October 06, 2026

Smoke from the Walter Peak fire rises behind the Homestead Restaurant on the shores of Lake Wakatipu on Tuesday afternoon.

Air and ground operations have resumed fighting an out-of-control vegetation fire at Walter Peak which threatens to continue growing.

Four helicopters with monsoon buckets are cooling hotspots and dampening the fire perimeter, with a fifth helicopter directing the air attack.

The fire had reignited from a controlled scrub burn, and had doubled to about 390ha when firefighting efforts stopped last night.

Just before 7am, Fire and Emergency said conditions were “relatively calm ... but we expect things to get more challenging when the wind gets up this morning”.

There are 11 firefighters on the ground, with extra crews arriving swelling numbers up to 25.

Send us your photos, videos and news updates

Assistant district commander Nic McQuillan said the protection of Walter Peak Station homestead and farm stock was the priority.

“While overnight conditions were relatively favourable, the fire has continued to grow and is now estimated at approximately 1,200 hectares.”

He said the fire could grow if weather conditions.

“Members of the public on the lake are reminded to stay at least 500 metres offshore to keep clear of where our helicopters are operating.

“This exclusion zone will be monitored by the Harbourmaster and Coastguard throughout the day to ensure public and firefighter safety.”

MetService meteorologist Sophie Huntington said strong winds had been recorded before dawn, with some gusts in the area approaching gale-force.

Windy conditions this morning were expected to ease by the afternoon.

Locals were warned to keep doors and windows shut to avoid smoke exposure.

RealNZ, owners and operators of Walter Peak station, said the area was south of the Walter Peak Homestead.

“Following a controlled scrub burn last week, the site has reignited this afternoon,” a spokesperson said yesterday.

The homestead and nearby treeline were not affected but guests and staff had been evacuated to an amphitheatre as a precaution.

Tour guide Kevin Pilbrow told the Herald the blaze was the biggest he had seen in 26 years of taking groups around the South Island.

Pilbrow arrived by boat about 11.45am with American tourists for lunch at the Colonel’s Homestead Restaurant. He said the group noticed a “little bit of smoke” while they were on the water.

“Then, in the course of us having lunch, I popped out a couple of times just to keep an eye on it and it had spread quite rapidly,” he said.

By the time they finished eating, he said there was a “tremendous amount of smoke” sweeping along the mountainside towards Queenstown.

Pilbrow estimated the fire was about 200m from the restaurant but said he did not believe the group was in danger.

“Even the smoke never came because there was a very, very strong southerly wind and it was blowing away from the restaurant itself and all the way up the hill. So we never even got a smell of the smoke.”

GDT: Dairy prices rise 1.2% as skim milk powder jumps 4.3%

New Zealand Herald October 06, 2026

The GDT index rose 1.2%, reversing a 1.1% decline at the previous auction. Photo / Christine Cornege

The Global Dairy Trade price index rose 1.2% at the latest auction held overnight.

This follows a 1.1% dip at the previous auction three weeks ago.

Whole milk powder, which has the biggest influence on Fonterra’s farmgate milk price, rose 1.2% to an average of US$3605/MT.

Skim milk powder, Fonterra’s second-biggest reference product, was up 4.3% to an average of US$3847/MT.

Butter milk powder also posted a gain, rising 0.7% to an average of US$4123/MT.

On the negative side, cheddar dropped 3.7% to an average of US$3925/MT, and butter dipped 0.3% to an average of US$4740/MT.

Anhydrous milk fat was down 1.1% to an average of US$5683/MT, and mozzarella fell 3.9% to an average of US$3833/MT.

Lactose recorded the largest decline, falling 6.9% to an average of US$1677/MT.

A total of 41,692MT of product was sold to 124 winning bidders across 18 bidding rounds, with 165 participants, compared with 42,444MT sold to 126 winning bidders and 155 participants at the previous event.

On July 13, Fonterra revised its 2026/27 farmgate milk price forecast to $9.25 per kgMS, within a range of $8.00-$10.50, down from the opening forecast of $9.75 per kgMS and a range of $8.00-$11.00 announced in May.

On September 21, the co-op lifted its forecast midpoint to $9.50 per kgMS and narrowed the forecast range to $8.50-$10.50.

For the 2025/26 season, which ended on May 31, the co-op narrowed its forecast range to $9.60-$9.80 per kgMS, from $9.40-$10.00, with the midpoint unchanged at $9.70.

The forecast compares with the record $10.16 per kgMS paid for the 2024/25 season.

Sumner cyclist fatal incident: Learner driver going at ‘excessive speed’ and drove away after fatal collision

New Zealand Herald October 06, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

A learner driver travelling at an “excessive speed” in a 50 km/h area honked his horn at a cyclist before knocking him off his bike and killing him, a court has heard.

Tyson Delaney Stechman, who was 20 at the time, then accelerated to about 100km/h while driving away from Christchurch man Ian Huntsman, later denying to police that he had hit the 60-year-old multisport athlete.

Members of the public found Huntsman unconscious on the roadway, and he was taken to hospital, where he died 10 days later.

The agreed summary of facts released to the Herald detailed the events before and after the fatal crash on the evening of February 22 this year.

Huntsman was travelling down Evans Pass Rd towards Sumner about 5.30pm that evening.

Evans Pass Rd is a sealed two-lane road running between Summit Rd and Sumner.

Huntsman was wearing a highly visible bright orange top, a helmet and had a bicycle with GPS tracking.

He was also an experienced cyclist, familiar with the road, and had been riding with a friend.

About the same time, Stechman, who held a learner driver licence, drove his 2002 Holden Commodore with a passenger down the road towards Sumner, the summary of facts says.

Contact our South Island newsroom

In the direction travelled, the road descends downhill and contains bends.

The speed limit in the area drops from 60km/h to 50km/h before the intersection with Ocean View Terrace, with limited shoulder space and no dedicated cycling infrastructure.

Huntsman was travelling at approximately 58 km/h when Stechman drove from behind and " into proximity to the victim", sounding his horn, according to the court summary.

Stechman overtook Huntsman, “driving at an excessive speed of between approximately 79 km/h and 96 km/h and in dangerous proximity to him”.

Stechman’s vehicle made contact with Huntsman’s bicycle, causing him to lose control and be thrown onto the roadway.

Seconds later, Stechman reached speeds of between 96km/h and 112km/h, while still travelling within the 50km/h speed zone.

He subsequently drove past the person Huntsman was cycling with at “excessive speed”.

He also discussed what had occurred with his passenger as he drove away from the area.

However, Stechman did not stop to ascertain whether Huntsman had been injured or to render assistance and did not attempt to call emergency services.

Shortly after, members of the public found Huntsman lying unconscious on the road.

He was transported to Christchurch Hospital in a critical condition and put on life support.

After 10 days, life support was withdrawn on March 3, and he died on March 4, 2026.

After the crash, Stechman admitted to police he was driving on Evans Pass Rd at the relevant time and sounding his horn at a cyclist before overtaking.

However, he “denied making contact with the cyclist and denied seeing the cyclist fall”.

In July, Stechman pleaded guilty to dangerous driving and failing to stop today after a fatal collision.

At the time of Huntsman’s death, people shared condolences online to his partner.

“Ian was an amazing guy and will be missed by many,” one friend said.

Another said they were “heartbroken” and “in shock”.

One friend described Huntsman as a “great teammate and fierce competitor”, and another said he was “a champion man” and “a powerhouse”.

Others spoke of him as a respected friend and “amazing outdoor enthusiast”.

In 2021, Huntsman survived a terrifying ordeal after falling on Aoraki Mt Cook.

Stechman will be sentenced on October 23.

Pat Spellman joined Moana Radio in 2010 and hosted its Drive Show. Photo / Ruth Kerber

Originally published by Māori Television

Community stalwart and former iwi radio broadcaster Pat Spellman (Ngāti Maruwharanui, Mangaia) has died, with Māori Touch NZ confirming his death on social media on Monday.

Spellman is being remembered as someone who worked tirelessly to create opportunities for whānau to thrive in both local and international sport.

Māori Touch NZ described Spellman as a treasured and much-loved member of the touch community.

“A trusted friend and mentor, and a tireless advocate for the touch community – his mahi will leave an everlasting legacy in Aotearoa and across the Pacific. An irreplaceable figure who will be dearly missed.”

Spellman spent years working in media, where he amplified the voices of his community. The Moana Radio whānau paid tribute to him, describing him as funny, cheeky and warm.

“Pat joined the Moana Radio whānau in 2010 and over the next five years became a familiar voice across Tauranga Moana. He spent much of his time behind the mic hosting our Drive Show.

“But many will remember Pat best from his time on the Moana Radio Breakfast Show alongside Takiri — and later with his good friend Harley Wall joining the pair, creating an unforgettable trio on the morning airwaves. Pat brought an energy that was uniquely his.”

Sport was another major part of Spellman’s life.

As a trustee and partnerships director with Māori Touch NZ, helping grow the Māori Touch Nationals and develop international opportunities, including a Māori Touch tour to New South Wales in 2025.

He also co-founded Pacific Cup Sports Trust in 2019 and served as its chair until June 2026.

Spellman was also a familiar voice at Touch New Zealand events, commentating for nine seasons.

In 2026, he was appointed Touch NZ’s community engagement and partnerships manager.

His immense contribution to community sport was recognised with a Kiwibank New Zealander of the Year Local Hero Medal in 2026.

“As the founder of the Pacific Cup Touch Tournament, Pat Spellman has pioneered a space where Pacific peoples can celebrate their identity and heritage through sport – welcoming everyone from rangatahi to kaumātua in an environment that is inclusive, culturally affirming, and community-driven.”

Funeral and tangihanga arrangements are still being finalised with whānau requesting privacy at this time.

National’s proposed foreign aid cut could make NZ ‘invisible’ on world stage, expert says

New Zealand Herald October 06, 2026

Christopher Luxon has proposed a $431 million cut to New Zealand's foreign aid budget. Photo / RNZ, Nick Monro

By Lucy Xia of RNZ

An international aid and development expert says National’s proposed $431 million cut to the foreign aid budget could see New Zealand becoming “invisible” on the international stage and cut off from important global conversations.

The National Party wants to redirect foreign aid money into funding for new medicines if it leads the new government; aid to the Pacific would be protected.

This week, Christopher Luxon said National believed that “we should put our country and our people first” and used the example of indigenous farmer workshops in Patagonia as the kind of foreign aid that would be cut.

Massey University’s associate professor Gerard Prinsen said the move would be a bad idea in terms of geopolitical and business interests, and that New Zealand could be retreating into a corner of the world only looking at the Pacific.

“[The Pacific] are indeed our neighbours, but the world is bigger than the Pacific,” he said.

Currently, nearly 60% of New Zealand’s Official Development Assistance funding goes to the Pacific, in an aid budget of about $1.2 billion in the 2025/2026 fiscal year.

Prinsen said New Zealand may lose personal networks and business networks with countries in Africa and Latin American, and possibly compromise its voice at the United Nations (UN) level if the cut went ahead.

“We contribute to quite a lot of UN bodies, if we cut back our contribution then we are no longer at the table, so people will forget what NZ thinks, what NZ has to offer, we become invisible at the international stage,” he said.

He said this could mean not being invited to certain UN conferences and losing touch with the latest developments on important issues – such as the impact of artificial intelligence on education, which would be discussed at Unesco forums.

Not attending these events meant New Zealand would be relying on papers to be published by the agencies, which could mean being six months or a year behind the international debate on these issues, said Prinsen.

He said New Zealand currently contributed to more than 40 UN bodies, and that he’d be interested to see how the aid budget could be reduced without affecting those contributions.

RNZ has approached National Party leader Christopher Luxon and health spokesperson Simeon Brown for comment.

Regarding international aid to Africa, Prinsen said New Zealand’s contribution was already “miniscule” – amounting to less than 1% of its aid budget – and that further reducing it would lead to New Zealand disappearing from the view of African nations.

“I think it’s important to realise that the African population will grow to be the third largest in 10 years’ time, so that’s a huge market, and nobody would’ve heard of New Zealand.

“New Zealand will not be participating, will have no personal networks, we will be a small island in the Pacific that maybe looks good on the tourist folder, but that’s about it,” he said.

Prinsen said decision-makers should also keep in mind the importance of bilateral relations between New Zealand and major African nations such as Nigeria, Kenya and South Africa.

He said it’s “silly” for the Prime Minister to use Patagonia as an example, as a place where many people would not have heard of.

Prinsen said aid programmes helped New Zealand to build relationships with other nations, and he couldn’t see how cutting hundreds of millions of dollars in foreign aid could be worth losing contacts with the world.

Foreign Minister Winston Peters called National’s foreign aid cut campaign promise dangerous and desperate, particularly during one of the most uncertain global times in history.

“It is irresponsible for National to jeopardise the relationships we have in the very markets we need to grow our economy,” he said.

Act leader David Seymour, the minister responsible for Pharmac, welcomed the policy, saying it was a great sign for the next coalition.

Australia sells itself as ‘a reef, a rock and a harbour’. Melbourne wants to be its new face

Sydney Morning Herald October 07, 2026

Victoria boasts about being home to Australia’s sports and arts capital. We explore what it needs to do to retain this status and attract more international visitors.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

When the NFL made landfall at the MCG, it catapulted Melbourne into global focus.

Thousands of Americans came here unaware of the Yarra River or the city’s laneway culture, instead equating Australia with images pushed in advertising – the outback, kangaroos and Uluru.

Most knew the Sydney Harbour Bridge and the Opera House – but little of Australia’s second-largest city, whose cultural assets and imagery are, as research has repeatedly attested, consistently absent from the country’s most internationally recognised emblems.

Tourism Australia’s latest major ad campaign, fronted by Robert Irwin and an animated toy kangaroo, snubbed the city for sweeping shots of the Eyre Peninsula, Great Barrier Reef, a Margaret River winery, and, of course, Sydney Harbour. Victoria was granted a few seconds, with a view of the Great Ocean Road.

So, when Americans drawn to Melbourne for the NFL stumbled off their long-haul flights, they were pleasantly surprised, says sports magnate Eddie McGuire.

“Australia’s tourism has been 30 years out of date when they continue to say, ‘Go to the outback’, and, ‘See a shark’, or ‘See a kangaroo’,” McGuire told The Age, sitting in his Toorak office, surrounded by mementoes from four decades in Melbourne’s sports industry.

“The Americans came here [for the NFL] and said, ‘Wow, Melbourne’s a gun city … The MCG, how long’s this been going on? What is this game?’ One of the blokes was saying he discovered John Farnham.”

Committee for Melbourne acting chief executive Agostino Giramondo said this was exactly the kind of experience national advertising campaigns should be capitalising on.

He was in Italy last year visiting family, and all they knew of Australia was “a reef, a rock and a harbour”, Giramondo said.

“I couldn’t believe how none of my relatives knew much about Melbourne,” he said.

“It’s a great shame because when you talk about Melbourne, you talk about the great vibrant melting pot of cultures, the food scene, the coffee scene, our laneways. That’s really difficult to talk about if there isn’t any imagery … so I do feel that we’re at a disadvantage.”

Giramondo wants Tourism Australia to showcase more of the city. He envisions an ad campaign trailing the path of an average visitor to the Australian Open – following the easy walk from their hotel, to a world-class precinct, and back to the bustling CBD.

A Tourism Australia spokesperson said it worked closely with its state and territory tourism partners “to promote the breadth and depth of visitor experiences” in Australia. While Melbourne “is already the first stop” for millions of visitors, the agency is also keen to drive them beyond the big cities and into the regions, the spokesperson said.

The Victorian government often cites Melbourne as the sports and arts capital of Australia.

What needs to be done to retain this status, and remain internationally competitive, will be discussed later this month at Melbourne Assembly, a civic forum The Age is hosting, bringing together industry leaders, key decision-makers and the community to shape the city’s future.

With a new sense of freedom and a longing for community, travellers came out of the COVID-19 pandemic hungrier for experiences such as live sport and music, according to research including from Tourism Australia.

Last year, Sydney embraced this shift towards experience-based travel, rolling out its “Live Like A Local” campaign. But Victorian Tourism Industry Council (VTIC) chief executive Lisa Patroni said Melbourne should be owning this identity.

“[Melbourne is] where you experience the Australian lifestyle that Australians genuinely live today ... It is less about one single monument and more about a way of experiencing the full city, with each visit,” Patroni said.

“The opportunity here is to make Melbourne and regional Victoria more than just a place visitors add to an Australian itinerary, but an essential part of the Australian story – a city of moments, experiences and connections that could only happen here.”

According to the state government, Victoria’s visitor economy reached record highs this year, with spending up by 6.6 per cent in the 12 months to June. In 2025, it led all Australian states in total attendance, drawing almost 9 million spectators across 442 events, according to crowd data platform Austadium.

And while NSW reaped a higher direct gross value add than any other state for every category of tourism goods and services in the 2024-25 financial year, there was one exception. Victoria matched it on arts and recreation, reaping a gross value add of $1 billion.

Other states have been increasingly agitating for the title of Australia’s sports and arts capital. The Age asked every Australian sports minister which city was the country’s sports capital. Seven ministers – from Victoria, NSW, Queensland, Tasmania, Western Australia, the ACT and the NT– named their own capital city.

The Victorian government has laughed off other states’ claims, but with the high-profile loss of the Commonwealth Games and Brisbane’s successful bid to host the Olympics, industry leaders have warned against taking Melbourne’s status at the forefront of events and entertainment for granted.

As the state government regularly boasts in press releases and on social media, Victoria is now the only place in the world with a tennis grand slam, a Formula One Grand Prix and an NFL regular season game.

And that’s not to mention the Melbourne Cup, the Boxing Day Test and the AFL grand final, which recently led to a huge influx of visitors from Perth and Brisbane.

However, several contracts are due to run out in the next few decades, and there is no certainty whether they will be renewed. The AFL grand final is locked in at the MCG until 2059, the Australian Open until 2046, the Australian Grand Prix until 2037, and the NFL until just next year.

While both the F1 and Australian Open attracted record crowds in Melbourne this year, the organisers of both events have threatened several times to move them interstate or overseas. The company that owns Formula 1, Liberty Media, recently followed through with pulling the MotoGP out of Phillip Island and giving it to Adelaide after three decades in Victoria.

Retaining key existing events without becoming overdependent on them, and working out how to use the spaces they occupy for the remainder of the year, will pose both a challenge and an opportunity for Melbourne in the years ahead.

John Harnden, chief executive of the state government-owned Melbourne Park, said continuing to expand the city’s events remit – and tap into new, diverse audiences – was essential.

To demonstrate his point, on a tour through the precinct, Harnden stopped at John Cain Arena, where staff were preparing to host a bull-riding event the following day. Outside of an already expansive tennis, basketball and netball roster, he said the venue had hosted sporting events as diverse as ice hockey and Indian contact sport kabaddi, and everyone from The Wiggles to Kesha.

At Margaret Court Arena, Harnden pointed out the curtain that could be drawn across the back half of the stands to give the audience a more intimate live concert atmosphere. He said a smaller stage could also be rolled out to simulate what he called “band-room mode” – one of many ways the precinct is adapting to meet the needs of its expanded music offering.

At Flemington Racecourse, Victoria Racing Club (VRC) has been moving in a similar direction – increasingly using music and entertainment to activate its 127-hectare precinct year-round, diversify its income, and engage more young people in racing.

In 2023, it welcomed the Laneway Festival, which was forced to find a new home in Melbourne, as its previous site in Footscray was redeveloped.

VRC chief executive Kylie Rogers said it was incumbent upon all racing administrators on large parcels of land to ensure they opened up their spaces to the community. Flemington Racecourse is Crown land, leased by the state government to the VRC.

“If we’re going to drive more fandom and more understanding of racing and bring different audiences in, how do I have a conversation with the 50,000 18-to-35-year-olds who go to the Laneway Festival? How do we introduce them into racing?” Rogers said.

“Let’s give them a discount pass or free entry into our next race day so they can get a taste of it, and they can learn about it.”

Looking at the big picture of arts events, Frontier Touring chief executive Dion Brant told The Age more investment needed to be made in permanent infrastructure throughout Melbourne to make sure it continued to attract a range of overseas artists, saying several venues were beginning to look “tired and old” compared to those interstate.

Live Nation Australia and New Zealand President Alex Klos said Melbourne is also now competing with other cities around the world. Pre-pandemic, he said Australia was generally considered a top-five international touring destination, but in recent years, emerging markets such as South America, the Middle East, Asia, India, and Eastern Europe had invested heavily in infrastructure, giving artists more choice, often closer to home.

“We can’t just assume that Australia is still going to be number five or even top five destinations [artists] will tour,” Klos said.

“The artist will make a decision on where they can get the best return in the shortest possible timeframe. The challenge for us is – how do we keep Australia really competitive and relevant in that global conversation?”

VTIC’s Lisa Patroni said visitors needed to be able to get here first, backing in the long-awaited Melbourne Airport rail link as a priority project. Alluding to Melbourne Airport’s incoming third runway, Patroni said infrastructure should match aviation capacity to help people travel from the airport to the city, and then into regional Victoria.

“If we want Melbourne to claim a larger share of the Australian tourism story, we need a 10-year vision for the Victorian visitor economy that positions tourism at the centre of our economic future,” Patroni said.

A state government spokesperson said its investments supported more than 322,000 jobs and generated almost $50 billion annually in tourism spending across the state.

“We’ve invested over $2.4 billion in community sport infrastructure since 2014, giving Victorians world-class facilities to play, train and compete,” the spokesperson said.

“With nearly 800,000 volunteers and more than 12,000 community clubs, Labor backs sport in every corner of the state, not just the big events.”

According to University of Melbourne pro vice-chancellor Tiriki Onus, however, major events are only one piece of the puzzle. In his eyes, the most important thing the government can do to preserve the city’s cultural identity is to invest more in the local industries that have built and sustained its reputation as a place where people want to perform or play.

In particular, Onus, a Melbourne Assembly panellist, said there needed to be more support for “mid-tier” projects – somewhere between the local pub gig or junior footy game, and the major stadium event – because that was where the innovations that would take us into the future lived.

”The arts and performance and indeed sport have been used as these great moments of identity-making that’s happened throughout generations … It’s all well and good to go to that one show or to go that one football event, but it’s the way we keep engaging and keep coming back together that means that our arts organisations, our festivals, our artists survive and flourish,” he said.

“We also need to make it easier for us to move between the sporting field and the theatre, to normalise that type of engagement … because if there’s one thing that all these spaces have in common, it’s the beautiful way that they draw us all together … So how do we create more of those spaces that draw us in? How do we break down the elitist nature of these institutions and these spaces so they are accessible?”

As modern travellers reject mass-market tourism in favour of authentic experiences, Onus said the city had an opportunity to double down on its reputation as a cultural capital by embracing and investing in the stories and traditions that had shaped it.

While interest in Indigenous tourism experiences is booming globally, the Yorta Yorta and Dja Dja Wurrung academic and artist said Melbourne was failing to capitalise on its own rich First Nations history.

He said many locals, let alone visitors, remained unaware of the history behind some of the city’s most iconic places and festivals – such as Moomba Festival’s origins in an Indigenous protest performance, or the MCG, once a corroboree ground, “turned into a cricket ground because it was a huge, flat expanse that had been beaten flat by the dancing of literally millions of feet over thousands of generations”.

Onus said the stories of diaspora communities who had fundamentally shaped the face of the city were also often lost, and that the recent Indian Film Festival was a perfect example of the kind of event the government should be investing more in. By leaning deeper into the rich history of the city and its diverse cultures, he said the city’s international appeal would only grow.

“[In the past] you travelled overseas, you’d come back with a suitcase full of gifts for everyone because of all of this strange stuff that you couldn’t buy elsewhere. You go to another country now, and it’s the same shops, it’s the same spaces, everything is the same,” Onus said.

“Now people are coming here [because they] want an experience … They want to learn something about a place … So we need to help those stories get told. And perhaps if we listen to them a bit more ourselves … we’d feel a little less threatened by one another, and we’d all be a little bit more excited about who we might be together.”

Melbourne Assembly will be held from October 19 to October 21. More information is available on the Melbourne Assembly website.

Continue this series

Melbourne’s cultural scene is thriving. That doesn’t mean artists don’t face challenges – even when they’re homegrown superstars.

A fan-friendly revamp of the MCG and better links to Melbourne Park would turn sporting events into festivals and cement Melbourne’s sports capital status.

Harry Kane doubles up on landmark night as England cruise past Czechia

The Guardian Tue, 06 Oct 2026 20:50:39 GMT

It was a night that belonged to Harry Kane. Yet another one. It began with him being shown a replay of his first England goal during a pre-match interview with ITV – the header against Lithuania in 2015, just 79 seconds after he came on as a substitute for his debut. It ended with him reflecting on two more in what was a supremely comfortable Nations League victory over Czechia. Some things never change.

It remains a numbers game for Kane. They are getting bigger and ever more impressive. On the ­occasion of his 125th cap, the one that took him level with Peter Shilton at the top of the all-time England list, he moved to an astonishing 91 goals. Nobody will be surprised if he reaches the century. The only question appears to be when.

England know how to beat the game’s smaller fry. Under Thomas Tuchel, they have played 16 matches against teams ranked outside the world’s top 20. They have won 15 and drawn one – against Ghana at the World Cup. They have conceded only once – against the Democratic Republic of the Congo, also at the World Cup. Czechia, who are ranked No 50, were never in the contest.

Kane is similarly inevitable. The captain even claimed the assist for the breakthrough goal with a cross into the corridor of uncertainty that spooked Vladimir Coufal so severely he shot into his own net. Kane’s passing was very good. When he was withdrawn in the 82nd minute, he left to a great ovation.

The victory meant that England virtually guaranteed their progress into the Nations League quarter-finals and, perhaps more importantly, saw them close out this elongated window with plenty of optimism. One of the main goals was to put as much distance as possible between themselves and the World Cup semi-final defeat against Argentina. It was mission accomplished.

Kane will break the caps record when England host Croatia in November and that will be the night when he is truly feted. As an aside, he would want to do it at Wembley rather than in Madrid against Spain where England’s next-but-one game will be staged. Was that why he was so keen to play in all four of the matches during this window? It might have been a part of it.

Then again, Kane always wants to play. He was one of only three England players to start each of the matches in this series. The others were Manchester City’s Marc Guéhi and Elliot Anderson. Was the City manager, Enzo Maresca, happy about that? Probably not. Does he have bigger problems at the moment? Yes.

Kane’s act of drawing level with Shilton was the box-office detail. His name was on everybody’s lips; his face on the big screen before kick-off. He was pictured alongside Shilton when his name was read out with the teams. The Wembley crowd roared.

Kane was at the heart of the opening goal, providing the teasing cross from the right and it was some finish from the player just inside the six-yard box. One that Kane would have been happy to call his own. The problem from a Czechia point of view was that it came from their right-back. Coufal could feel Eberechi Eze at his back as he faced towards his own goal, albeit the England winger was not that close. Coufal stretched and everybody had the time to have the same thought: you do not have to do this. Coufal did it. He could not check his momentum and steered firmly past his goalkeeper.

Trent Alexander-Arnold, who Tuchel recalled at right-back, was involved in the buildup and he caught the eye, especially when surging up and inside. He repeatedly got into advanced areas and there was one moment in the first half when he stormed into the No 9 position on to an Anderson pass. He just could not bring it under his spell. Alexander-Arnold had extended Lukas Hornicek with a whipped free-kick at the outset.

Jude Bellingham was excellent. Of course he was. There were fizzed passes from him that took the breath, getting England into dangerous positions, including one for Morgan Rogers in the 25th minute that the Chelsea attacker wasted. There were those strutting runs and it was Bellingham, as much as anybody, who advertised the fact that England were going to break through.

This now constitutes a rocky start for Sébastien Pocognoli as Scotland’s manager.

The claiming of four points from three Nations League games was adequate until Slovenia inflicted this defeat. It was the abject nature of Scotland’s display this time that was so stark. Pocognoli’s team were comprehensively outplayed by a side who themselves are no better than functional.

November feels significant for Pocognoli. Put simply, Slovenia met a Scotland who were far, far too easy to play against. Pocognoli has to prove this is the dawn of a new era as opposed to the beginning of an error. This is no patient football domain.

A pre-match presentation to Andy Robertson, who reached the 100-cap mark during Scotland’s win in North Macedonia on Saturday, carried wider meaning. Gordon Strachan and Alex McLeish, Robertson’s first two Scotland managers, were joined on the Hampden pitch by Steve Clarke. This marked a swift and welcome return to the national stadium for Clarke, who departed the Scotland job in unsatisfactory circumstances following failings at the World Cup. Clarke, bashful by nature, took as significant a bow as he was ever likely before supporters but Robertson’s warmth towards the Ayrshireman was clear.

Scotland find themselves in a post-Clarke state of flux. He was the manager who made this nation relevant on the wider stage once again. There was, however, a widespread criticism that Clarke’s team lacked ambition. Pocognoli has been charged not only with maintaining at least decent results while delivering an alternative brand of football. It remains to be seen whether the dual quest is fanciful or not.

The first quarter of the game mirrored the opening half when these teams met in Ljubljana. Scotland looked uncertain and ragged. This venue, which should be an asset to Scotland, was eerily quiet.

A short free-kick was played wide to Ben Gannon-Doak, whose deflected cross was headed on to a post by Hendry. Modern football’s madness means Oli McBurnie will be credited with an assist for the header he was undoubtedly trying to score with. Here, the Bournemouth player supplied breathing space.

Robertson demonstrated his ongoing value before the break. Zan Vipotnik seemed certain to equalise before the Tottenham left-back’s rescue act, courtesy of a sliding block. Ominously for Scotland, Danijel Sturm had totally bamboozled their three-man defence when supplying Vipotnik.

It was impossible to argue Slovenia were not worthy of their equaliser, which landed 11 minutes after half-time. It came from a Scotland throw-in, where possession was cheaply conceded. Sturm played through the centre and towards Aljosa Matko, who brushed Luis Binks aside as if the Brøndby defender was not even there. The Scotland goalkeeper, Angus Gunn, as is something of a theme, was weak in trying to deal with Matko’s shot. Sturm should have sent Slovenia in front two minutes later but saved the blushes of a hilariously open Scotland defence by shooting over. This had to be alarming for Pocognoli.

‘All I want to do is cry’: trauma of 7 October survivors three years after the attacks

The Guardian Tue, 06 Oct 2026 20:00:23 GMT

Israeli communities shattered by Hamas masacres are torn between rebuilding their lives and remembering lost friends and relatives

Keith Siegel spent many of his long hours in Hamas captivity in Gaza etching everything that happened after 7 October 2023 into his memory. For 484 days, he recited to himself every place he was held, the dates he was moved and every attack or humiliation he endured or witnessed.

He aimed to store intelligence that could help Israeli forces free other hostages if he was released, to keep track of time as the days slid by and be able to tell his family what happened to him. Now his body is free, but he cannot loosen those memories.

“I’m living a kind of dual life,” he said in an interview in Tel Aviv. “I’m here for some of the time, and I’m in Gaza some of time. It’s very challenging to convey in words what it was like.”

Siegel and his wife, Aviva, were among 251 people taken captive to Gaza on the deadliest day in Israel’s history, when Hamas militants broke across the border to launch a wave of attacks on kibbutzim, border towns, military bases and music festivals.

Israel’s security forces were caught by surprise, and by the time they regained control of the area, 1,209 people had been killed, the majority of them civilians, including 36 children, according to records kept by the Israeli newspaper Haaretz.

The cemetery at Nir Oz contains two lines of fresh headstones, marking lives that all ended on that same date. A shared plot for a family of five – a mother, father and their three young children – has been made into a garden with space left for their still-living grandparents.

Caretaker Shlomo Margalit, who will soon turn 89, points to the graves of three of his oldest friends, founding members of the kibbutz who came to Nir Oz from Haifa with him in the 1950s.

“This is my life project, as well as my home,” Margalit said, explaining why he has come back to a place of such loss. He is waiting for a new house but, for now, staying in the former home of Gadi Moses, 82, who survived 482 days as a hostage.

The graves he tends are a silent testament to the brutality of the attacks and the scale of the state’s failure, which in Nir Oz was staggering, even on a day of terrible failures.

A five-person volunteer defence force held Hamas at bay for at least two hours, Margalit said. When they had all been shot, the kibbutz was taken over and sacked, homes burned, families slaughtered and kidnapped.

Then, before the first Israeli soldier arrived, the Hamas forces, other Palestinian gunmen and civilian looters all left. Nir Oz had been forgotten by the army and ripped apart without the military firing a single shot to defend it.

In total, 47 people were killed and 76 taken to Gaza, including Shiri Bibas, her 10-month-old baby Kfir and four-year-old Ariel, who were killed in Gaza. The dead and hostages represented more than a quarter of the small community.

Revisiting that terrible day, and the trauma that followed, is painful and exhausting for Margalit, but he still accepts interviews for a simple reason. “I want people to know what really happened here,” the 89-year-old said.

The third anniversary of the 7 October attacks falls a few weeks before national elections, and much of the country is caught up in a furious debate about responsibility for the deadliest day in Israel’s history and the conduct of the war that followed.

Survivors and bereaved relatives are avoiding the political fray, still grappling with the trauma and the struggle to rebuild something like normality.

In Nir Oz, there is a terrible, almost irreconcilable struggle between re-establishing the kibbutz as a living community, and preserving physical testimony of the attack.

The cemetery echoes with the sound of construction and families have already moved into several rows of new houses near the kibbutz entrance.

But on the other side of the compound, paths still lead between blackened ruins and memorials to the dead. Some bereaved survivors want the homes of loved ones preserved this way as permanent monuments to mark their loss.

“There are families that can’t [bear to] live here, but want a memorial place to come to visit,” Margalit said. “On the other hand, can you build a new kibbutz where children grow up running around between burnt houses?”

He is on the remembrance committee and, two years on, they are struggling to reach a decision on this impossible choice. “Is there right or wrong here? No,” he said. “We are dealing with that, trying to find an answer.”

One compromise might be a memorial garden on the border of the kibbutz. For now, there are plaques with the stories of families attacked on that day and a memorial house to remember the dead and kidnapped.

When the kibbutz took a collective decision to return and rebuild, Margalit and his wife, Hanna, knew they wanted to join. His only concession to the trauma was asking for a new home that did not face Gaza.

“I’ve found myself building this place for the second time,” he said. “I know when I’m gone, I will have done something with my life. I took part in putting this spot on the map.”

The Siegels, who lived in the nearby kibbutz of Kfar Aza, also among the worst hit, have decided not to return as they focus on mental and physical recovery. Aviva was 62 when she was kidnapped. Keith was 64.

“What happened to me in Gaza, what happened with Keith in Gaza, it’s there all the time,” said Aviva.

“I understand that it’s going to be a process of healing. There’s always things that remind me, and if I don’t remember, then he reminds me. If I’m cooking lunch or making a cup of tea and I turn around and see Keith with tears in his eyes, because he just read something or let himself feel.”

The days approaching the anniversary have been particularly difficult, she said. Last year, at this time, she was still campaigning for the release of other hostages, her own emotions held at bay by the urgency of that campaign.

For a time, she tried to deal with the trauma by telling herself, over and over again “I must feel lucky,” simply because she had made it back alive.

Now she has allowed herself to feel again, and as 7 October approached, she has realised how raw the wounds still are. “Getting ready [for the anniversary] has been very very painful,” she said. “The last couple of weeks all I want to do is cry. Now I’m feeling things I didn’t feel before.”

“When I hear my grandson say he is afraid of being kidnapped in the middle of the night, it breaks my heart.”

She has written a book, Survived to Tell, about the ordeal, which she describes as therapy and an act of celebration. She wrote so her grandchildren could read about what she and Keith endured, for other hostages who couldn’t tell their own stories and to inspire a broader audience in Israel and beyond.

After the exhausting campaign to get Keith and other hostages home, she said she had struggled to concentrate on the election. Keith’s political focus is an independent inquiry into 7 October to prevent other families suffering as his has.

He said: “There needs to be an investigation to understand how this happened, in order to do everything possible that it won’t happen again. So many people were killed, injured, traumatised.”

Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister, has fiercely opposed an independent state commission of inquiry. Critics say he is afraid it would expose his own failings.

In the immediate aftermath of the attacks, few people inside or outside Israel expected him to stay in power long, particularly as the country’s coalition governments have rarely served out their full terms.

Netanyahu had for years championed a foreign and security policy based on the premise that Hamas was “contained” in Gaza, behind unbreachable layers of fortifications.

The security officials who were in command that day have all stepped down yet, three years on, Netanyahu is still in power, having deflected all demands for his resignation.

Yaakov Godo, a bereaved father, interrupted Netanyahu’s speech at the official commemoration event this year to accuse him of negligence.

“You did not protect my son on 7 October, you did not protect 1,200 people murdered in one day. Shame!” he shouted, before being ushered away.

Both US and Israeli officials have said Netanyahu rejected ceasefire deals that could have halted the war in Gaza and brought many Israeli hostages home sooner. But criticising the prime minister means venturing into a vicious political debate where age and loss offer little protection.

Yocheved Lifshitz, 88, was taken hostage from Nir Oz with her husband Oded, whose magnificent cactus garden blooms at the heart of the kibbutz. He died in Gaza, she survived and since her return she has been a vocal critic of Netanyahu.

A candidate for Netanyahu’s Likud party, Itzik Bonzel, said last month that he wished he could turn back the clock and return her to Hamas captivity. He later apologised, blaming grief for his son who died fighting in Gaza, but Lifshitz denounced it as a proxy attack driven by the prime minister.

Netanyahu, who is battling a corruption trial and could be more vulnerable legally if he loses power, is pushing to intensify Israeli attacks on Gaza and his coalition partners are calling for ethnic cleansing and annexation of Palestine.

The war Israel launched in response to 7 October has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, the majority of them civilians, including about 20,000 children.

Netanyahu has also waged a years-long campaign to dismantle institutions protecting democracy inside Israel’s 1967 borders. Palestinians under Israeli military rule in the occupied West Bank do not have the rights of Israeli citizens.

Many Israelis opposed to this rightwing vision of perpetual war in a state with diminished institutions consider this election the most critical since Israel was founded in 1948, among them Margalit.

Nir Oz, like many communities targeted by Hamas, had its roots in the leftwing Zionist movement, and although the brutality of 7 October pushed some to the right, others saw their pain as bitter proof that war alone cannot offer long-term security.

“I don’t believe we can ignore the fact that Palestinians live here,” Margalit said. “We have to find a way we can live here with them and be secure. I don’t have an answer, I just know we are here to stay and they are here to stay. Maybe we need someone from the outside.”

Chancellor plans major intervention to help poorer UK households with rising energy bills

The Guardian Tue, 06 Oct 2026 19:27:59 GMT

Exclusive: Officials working on further radical changes that would change how much energy companies could charge customers

John Healey is planning a major intervention to cut energy bills for poorer households in this month’s budget, after ministers became alarmed at forecasts that show bills rising by hundreds of pounds in January.

The chancellor is working on plans to spend more than £1bn to help energy consumers, the bulk of which is likely to go towards increasing the discount given to households on certain benefits.

Sources say final decisions have not been made, but Healey is set to rebuff a call from the energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh to spend billions more on removing levies from bills altogether.

Energy officials are working up more radical changes to bills, however, which could be implemented after the budget and would change how much companies could charge customers, rather than subsidising their bills.

If approved, the energy discount will form a major plank of the budget, which government sources say will be low-key but focused on reducing voters’ cost of living.

The chancellor is facing a cash crunch as he looks for money to fund an additional £4.7bn in defence spending and rebuild his fiscal buffer, which has been eroded by higher borrowing costs.

He is likely to raise taxes to pay for the additional spending, and is rumoured to be looking at higher bank taxes in particular.

Government sources had previously insisted the VAT cut to electricity bills which Andy Burnham announced soon after becoming prime minister would be the last support to be offered this year.

But they have become increasingly concerned by forecasts showing that the Iran war will push the energy price cap up by as much as £442 in January – entirely eroding the impact of the VAT cut.

As a result Healey has been considering submissions from the energy department on how to ease the pressures on households in the coming months.

The most likely solution is understood to be increasing the warm homes discount – a £150 discount to energy bills offered to households on certain benefits.

Healey is understood to be considering increasing this by a further £100, which would be funded by taxpayers, rather than bill-payers as the existing discount is.

Fahnbulleh, meanwhile, has been pushing for more sweeping action to reduce bills for all consumers by as much as £120 by removing all levies.

Under the energy secretary’s proposals, the levies, which fund renewable energy and efficiency schemes, would be paid for through taxation instead.

She told the Guardian last week: “If we want a system that is resilient, if we want a system that can cope, if we want a system that ultimately can deliver the diversity of energy that we want, what is the fairest way in which we pay for it?

“That is both across the exchequer versus our bill-payers, and then within our bill-payers. So we have to ask that question. Every other country is asking that question, and ultimately we’ve got to come to a fair deal.”

Removing levies from bills would reduce inflation, but would cost as much as £3.2bn and would be difficult for the government to unwind should energy costs come down in the future.

Officials in the energy department are working on more radical proposals for after the budget, meanwhile, including proposals to reduce tariffs for poorer households or those that use less energy.

Burnham told the Labour conference last week: “British businesses and bill-payers pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe. Within 10 years, I want those costs to be in line with our neighbours.

“This means reforming a broken energy market so it better serves the public interest.”

A so-called “social tariff” would force energy companies to charge poorer households less for each unit of electricity they consume than richer ones.

Creating such a scheme, however, would involve a large amount of data collection from tax authorities, the Treasury and energy companies – an exercise likely to take far longer than the next few weeks.

An alternative plan, known as a “rising block tariff”, would also vary the tariffs that energy companies can charge, but by consumption levels rather than income.

The idea, which was proposed by the New Economics Foundation (NEF) thinktank when Fahnbulleh ran it, would charge consumers less for a set amount of “essential” use and more once their consumption crossed that level.

Alex Chapman, head of economic and environmental policy at NEF, said: “A serious price spike is coming, and without action, bills will exceed the peak of the last crisis. The government must use the budget to put in place both targeted support for the most vulnerable and, critically, a safety net for all.”

He added: “Repeated crises have exposed the flaws in our privatised energy system – these can only be fixed by fundamental reform. This means capturing the benefits of cheap renewables and offering every household a ‘block’ of essential energy at a truly protected and affordable price.”

Alfie Stirling, economist and director of policy at the Joseph Rowntree Foundation, said: “Energy support for this winter needs to tick three boxes. It needs to support the majority of households; within this, it needs to target the most support towards those in greatest need; and – as far as possible – it needs to actually lower the price, thereby bringing down inflation.

“The UK does not yet have the right toolkit to respond effectively to energy price shocks – building better tools is now a critical priority for our future security and living standards.”

A spokesperson for the Treasury said: “As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”

A former high-ranking Department of Justice official will look at how Cornell handles sexual misconduct complaints, university trustees announced on Tuesday as they tried to address an outpouring of anger over allegations of a 2024 gang rape at a fraternity house.

Sally Yates, who was a deputy attorney general in the Obama administration, will spearhead the review, the trustees said. The assessment is to include how the Ivy League university investigates reports of sexual assault and sexual harassment, how the disciplinary process works, the adequacy of campus police responses, and more.

“It is imperative that Cornell be willing to examine itself with the same rigor we expect of others,” the trustee chair, Anne Meinig Smalling, said in a statement.

The announcement comes after days of outrage and a large demonstration over Cornell’s response to a complaint from a woman known publicly only as Jane Doe. She told campus police in November 2024 that she had been sexually assaulted by multiple Chi Phi fraternity brothers the month before after being pressured into drinking and taking drugs.

No criminal charges have been filed. The Chi Phi chapter at Cornell was shut down, and the Ivy League university has said it expelled some students and suspended others.

Yates will look at how the woman’s complaint was handled and at the oversight of fraternities, sororities and other campus groups, Cornell said.

The woman sued the university, seven former students, the fraternity and others last month.

Lawyers for two of the former students denied they participated in a sexual assault. Attempts by the Associated Press to reach the other men or their representatives have been unsuccessful. Court records show that during an investigation that Cornell conducted under the federal Title IX law, some of the accused students contended that the sexual activity was consensual.

The lawsuit put a new, nationwide spotlight on the allegations and how the campus police, university and local prosecutor had reacted.

New York’s attorney general is now conducting a criminal investigation, and the state’s governor called for an independent review of Cornell’s handling of the matter – the review that Yates now will lead.

Cornell students, professors and others thronged a campus plaza on Monday to protest the university’s response to the matter and demand more accountability, greater transparency, an overhaul of the disciplinary process and other changes.

Yates had a decades-long career at the justice department, serving for years as the top federal prosecutor in Atlanta and later as a deputy attorney general.

She achieved particular prominence in January 2017, when, as acting attorney general in the early days of the Trump administration, she directed justice department attorneys not to defend the constitutionality of Donald Trump’s refugee and immigration ban. She was swiftly fired, with Trump accusing her of betrayal and insubordination.

Yates also generated headlines when it emerged that, in a conversation days before her departure, she had expressed alarm to the Trump White House about contacts that Trump’s new national security adviser, Michael Flynn, had had with the Russian ambassador during the presidential transition period. Flynn later was fired.

Yates has been in private practice since her departure from the justice department. Her practice at the King & Spalding law firm includes conducting independent investigations for outside organizations and companies.

She led a high-profile inquiry into alleged abuse and misconduct, including claims of harassment and coercion, at the National Women’s Soccer League. The investigation concluded in 2022 with a finding of systemic abuse.

Senior academics set out key questions Cambridge must answer over Jason Arday’s death

The Guardian Tue, 06 Oct 2026 18:44:25 GMT

Letter from more than 40 signatories says university has backed away from promised thorough review of events before death

Senior Cambridge academics have criticised the university’s plans to investigate Prof Jason Arday’s death as inadequate, and said those responsible for “serious failures of leadership” should face consequences.

In a letter to Chris Smith, Cambridge’s chancellor, the academics said “it is not yet clear” how the proposed review will answer difficult questions about the university’s involvement in the events leading up to Arday’s death, including its handling of the criticism Arday suffered after his appointment as professor of sociology of education in 2023.

Arday died at his home in London on 14 August, nine days after he resigned amid allegations of plagiarism and inconsistencies in statements about his career.

An inquest will be held to determine the cause of death.

Arday’s family said he was subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse for more than three years.

Now, a letter signed by more than 40 professors, associate professors and fellows raises concern that Cambridge has backed away from initial promises by Deborah Prentice, the university’s vice-chancellor, to carry out a “thorough and transparent” examination of the circumstances that led to Arday’s appointment and treatment.

Rather than reviewing the “lessons learned”, the group wants the investigation to pinpoint the crucial advice given and decisions made during Arday’s hiring and subsequent career.

“The investigation must establish who authorised and directed the university’s public promotion of Professor Arday; what assessment was made of the risks that accompanied it; who authorised any legal or other communications with journalists investigating the story; what the university knew as racist and ableist abuse and media hounding escalated; and how responsibility for Professor Arday’s protection was allocated and exercised across the university,” the letter says.

The signatories included Cahir O’Kane, a professor of genetics; Caroline Bassett, a professor of digital humanities; Clair Wills, the King Edward VII professor of English literature; and Clément Mouhot, a professor of mathematical sciences.

Cambridge last month announced a two-part review, with part one to be led by Nazir Afzal, a former chief crown prosecutor for north-west England, focusing on the support given to Arday immediately before his death.

The university has not yet named a chair for part two of the review, which it said would be “a broader review of institutional processes and practice” and only consider “the wider context” of Arday’s period at Cambridge, including general appraisals of recruitment and support available to academics facing media scrutiny.

The group behind the letter, which was also sent to Cambridge’s governing council, said the “scope and investigative character” of the second part of the review would be crucial in settling the decisions, structures and processes involved.

They wrote: “To this end, it is vital that the university establishes a clear chain of responsibility for the institutional decisions made in the period following Professor Arday’s appointment, through the events leading to his death and the university’s subsequent responses.

“The university should state clearly how responsibility will be acted upon if the review establishes serious failures of leadership or responsibility … Serious findings must have consequences for the individuals and offices responsible.

“At the same time, individual accountability cannot substitute for the institutional changes required where failures arose from structures of decision-making, scrutiny or governance.”

Saudi Arabia’s then crown prince said peace required “two equal parties” and could not survive “oppression and humiliation”. His words remain as relevant now as then.

The Green party has now rejected that two-state framework in favour of a one-state solution. The Guardian strongly disagrees with this move. Peace needs to acknowledge reality: the latest polls in Gaza and the West Bank suggest that a majority support a two-state formula based on the 1967 borders compared with just 10% who back a single democratic state with equal rights. The European Greens also disagree with the new direction of their English and Welsh sister party. The EU-wide representatives argue that the policy is incompatible with previously agreed positions. The international consensus has plainly failed to deliver Palestinian statehood, or indeed prevent the near-total destruction of Gaza by Israel. But a “single democratic” entity in Palestine seems even more remote. There may need to be fresh future thinking about peace, including confederation models being considered as the crisis deepens in the occupied Palestinian territories. The ultimate test of any solution to the Israel-Palestine conflict is whether it ends domination by any one group and provides equal rights so both peoples have a secure political future.

The vote at the Green party conference to adopt a controversial set of policies was decided by about 200 votes – less than one-thousandth of the membership. The Greens’ leader, Zack Polanski, who is himself Jewish, has become embroiled in a row over antisemitism around the third anniversary of the 7 October attacks, at a time when he is fighting a parliamentary byelection in London. The motion defines Zionism as being “to the exclusion and/or domination of the non-Jewish population” in historic Palestine. Whatever the motion’s eventual impact, it is clear that Green party structures urgently need to be reformed for a mass membership base. The Guardian view on the French school protests: the political class needs to heed the voice of students

The Guardian Tue, 06 Oct 2026 18:31:54 GMT

A generation facing unprecedented challenges deserves better than an underfunded education system

One of the most famous slogans in France’s May 1968 student protests declared “L’imagination au pouvoir” (Power to the imagination). In a postwar context of steady growth, the ’68ers dreamed of shaping an egalitarian society, freed from the social constraints of their parents’ generation. Nearly five decades on, in a very different economic climate, the goal for most of the tens of thousands of pupils disrupting schools across the country is more modest. As one placard on display had it: “I’d like to be worrying about my maths exam, not my future”.

A huge turnout of hundreds of thousands of protesters on Tuesday – a number that included many parents and teachers – confirmed the depth of resentment at years of budget cuts leading to crumbling school buildings, overcrowded classes and chronic staff shortages. Other complaints point to a lack of resources to deal with the now frequent heatwaves that make classrooms intolerable in May and June, and the unfairness of an opaque, algorithmically driven selection process for universities.

Confronted by the anxieties of a generation facing challenges ranging from the climate emergency to the impact of AI on future job opportunities, the response of Emmanuel Macron’s government has been disastrously heavy-handed. Instead of being instructed to show maximum restraint, given the age of most of those involved, security forces were urged to intervene to break up the school “blockades”. The result has been heightened confrontation and unacceptable violence on both sides. More than 200 students have been injured, as well as over 700 police officers and a number of teachers. One 15-year-old boy had his hand blown off during a protest in Lens, another lost an eye, and more than 4,000 minors were taken into custody, with nearly 1,500 facing prosecution.

At a political level, the eruption of anger over the underfunding of education has underlined the folly of Mr Macron’s ongoing attempt to balance France’s books by taking an axe to social spending. During his chaotic second term as president, five prime ministers have attempted to force through austerity budgets in order to cut the deficit and satisfy increasingly restive bond markets. The latest, Sébastien Lecornu, has belatedly said that the students’ core demands should be addressed. But last month he proposed cuts worth €54bn, including a real-terms reduction in schools funding. A credible approach would require more resources, not less.

Six months out from a presidential election in which Marine Le Pen is the frontrunner, the spectacle of burned-out schools, baton rounds and teargassed protesters feels ominous. As French politics polarises amid a crisis of faith in mainstream leaders, Ms Le Pen has accused the hard left of fomenting the school protests and called for a toughening up of “anti-riot” legislation. Public sector workers were on the streets on Tuesday, demonstrating against wage freezes. The major unions are jointly planning further demonstrations for November. An autumn of discontent now seems possible, as a lame-duck government enters its final months.

Mass protest in the streets is hardly an unknown phenomenon in France. But as calls mount for government spending to be further cut to appease market sentiment, the scale and intensity of the school protests should be heeded by the political class. As the social contract in France comes under increasing strain, the voice of its protesting students needs to be heard.
