A seventh man has been arrested in London on suspicion of terrorism offences as part of the investigation related to threats to RAF Fairford, police have said.

The 22-year-old British national was arrested in Westminster, central London, on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts under section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006, counter-terrorism police said.

Police are continuing to investigate a so far unexplained incident on 27 September, when five men from London driving three white vans were arrested in the small hours in a village outside the Gloucestershire airbase used by bombers from the US air force.

A week later, on Sunday, the US decided to hastily withdraw all 12 of the B-1 Lancer bombers that had been based at Fairford back to the US. Some had only arrived at the base a week earlier, and refuelling aircraft had to be scrambled in order to complete the evacuation.

There remains speculation that Iran wants to target the base, which was used for US bombing runs on the country earlier this year, but the US and UK appear to have divergent views about the security situation and level of threat.

UK sources question whether Iran would have the capability to launch a Ukraine-style drone attack on military aircraft at the base, given the complexity of such an operation. On Monday, Downing Street said the base was safe.

But some reports suggested the US feared a drone strike along the lines of Ukraine’s Operation Spiderweb attack on Russian airbases last year, and so did not want to leave its bombers stationed at Fairford.

On Monday night Donald Trump, the US president, said the aircraft had been moved because “there were some threats, and rather than tempting the enemy – we’ll capture the enemy and beat the enemy, but why should we leave them there?”

So far there has been no breakthrough in the investigation by counter-terror police. The five men detained in Whelford on 27 September were released on police bail a day later, without charge.

No explosive devices were found in their vans, though a barrel of petrol was recovered. One of the five had also called 999, and their intentions remain publicly unexplained.

On Thursday, a 25-year-old dual UK-Iranian national was arrested in Westminster on suspicion of terrorism offences. He was also released on bail on Saturday.

Speaking on Tuesday, the senior national coordinator for counter-terrorism policing, Vicki Evans, said: “This remains a live investigation and our specialist teams continue to pursue multiple lines of inquiry into the circumstances surrounding events near RAF Fairford.

“Once again, I’d like to thank the public for their continued support and patience whilst we work through this highly complex investigation.

“We’re acutely aware of the public interest in this investigation, and we are working around the clock, and at pace, to identify the motivation behind events in Gloucestershire. We remain committed to investigating all possible angles.”

The 22-year-old is being held under rules that allow detectives to bail him, just like the other six men who have been arrested on a terrorism charge.

People arrested for terrorism offences can be held under two legal schedules which dictate how long they can be detained without charge. Under the terrorism schedule a suspect can be held for up to 14 days, but cannot be bailed, meaning police have a fortnight to charge or release them.

The 22-year-old arrested for alleged preparatory acts is being held under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act, a spokesperson for counter-terrorism police said on Tuesday. That means he could be released under investigation on bail, but detectives have much less time to hold him.

The five men arrested close to RAF Fairford were held under the same act before being bailed the next day, to the surprise of some.

Tensions have been high at RAF Fairford since Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said in July that the base was a legitimate target. Iran’s embassy in London has denied any involvement in the events of the past few days.

Ministers have been briefed that Iran has various reasons for hiring proxies, who sometimes are unwitting, to carry out acts that aim to eat up resources and create chaos.

The Iranian embassy in London has said it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations” of Iranian involvement.

Senior US politicians, including the president, Donald Trump, have expressed surprise that the suspects were released on bail.

Counter-terrorism police last week defended the move. “I understand why this development will have come as a surprise to many, but I’d like to reiterate that it was an investigative decision, and one which is grounded in experience and careful consideration of policing powers,” Britain’s head of counter-terrorism police said.

Morrisons is not a must-do deal for Sainsbury’s

The Guardian Tue, 06 Oct 2026 18:10:08 GMT

Odds are good the CMA would approve of a supermarket merger. But does Sainsbury’s need Morrisons?

Would competition regulators really smile upon a combination of Sainsbury’s and Morrisons? One must assume the two companies believed the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) would give a thumbs up if asked, otherwise they would not have initiated their now-aborted merger talks.

It’s easy to list the arguments the duo could make. First, the combined market share of Sainsbury’s (15.2%, on the latest numbers from Worldpanel analysts) and Morrisons (8.4%) would still be less than that of mighty Tesco (27.8%). It would not be a case of leap-frogging the market leader, which was Sainsbury’s big idea back in 2018 when Asda was in its sights.

Second, Aldi and Lidl are a stronger force in the land. Together, the German discounters represent almost a fifth of the UK market and, since they’re backed by serious international buying muscle, their role as the country’s grocery price police might not be affected one jot.

Third, since Morrisons has already sold its petrol stations, the CMA needn’t worry about the touchy issue of fuel. Fourth, at a push, Sainsbury’s and Morrisons could argue that the UK’s food security (a growing political worry) would improve if the latter’s 18 food-processing factories were housed within a stronger company that could boost local production.

So, yes, one would probably bet that the CMA would ultimately approve some version of a deal. But what version? How many store disposals would be demanded?

The CMA, as in 2018, would presumably conduct a site-by-site analysis of drive-times to judge local competition. The regulatory instinct, one suspects, would be to err on the side of intervention in light of the overall national picture. Never mind Tesco’s size, it would still not be a simple decision for a competition regulator to sanction a supermarket setup in which half the trade, or thereabouts, would be in the hands of just two companies.

Would a deal still make sense after the CMA’s remedies? It’s impossible for Sainsbury’s and Morrisons to know until they go through the process. That’s the distraction factor for Sainsbury’s. Does its chief executive, Simon Roberts, really want to spend a year bogged down in regulatory back-and-forth? In the Asda episode, the effort sucked the life out of his predecessor’s reign.

It’s not as if Sainsbury’s is struggling today. The group is winning market share, profit margins are stable, there’s enough spare cash for share buy-backs and the strategic headaches of its bank and Argos have been solved by selling both. While it would be preferable to square up to Tesco’s buyers on more equal terms, life ain’t bad.

Five years after buying the chain for £7bn, owners Clayton, Dubilier & Rice’s thoughts will be turning to how to exit a tricky investment. Kemi Badenoch is the most rightwing leader in Tory history. Isn’t it time she got some actual scrutiny?

The Guardian Tue, 06 Oct 2026 18:04:53 GMT

Farage’s scandals have allowed Badenoch to get her party back in the race. But her programme would be no less ruinous for our country

The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, will march on to the conference stage in Birmingham feeling buoyed. “Kemi’s soaring,” coos the Sun, and that sums up the prevailing wisdom. More than four in 10 Britons think she is doing well as Tory leader, compared with a third who think otherwise. As Nigel Farage’s stock has plummeted thanks to scandals over a £5m personal gift and donations from crypto billionaires, the polling suggests that the Conservatives could regain the mantle of Britain’s main rightwing force.

Yet Badenoch has been the beneficiary of circumstance. Her tenure as opposition leader has been defined by Keir Starmer’s project imploding almost as soon as it gained power. When Reform UK enjoyed its seismic polling lead, the Tory plight was double-edged: they were starved of attention, but that inevitably resulted in a lack of scrutiny, too. It has been easy for Badenoch to appear formidable while her opponents have disintegrated.

With the Conservatives now back in the race, the spotlight falls on Badenoch. Let us consider the absurdity of her proposed air defence system. Our would-be prime minister denied comparing it to Israel’s Iron Dome, despite the term appearing in both a press release and a newspaper article under her own name. This amateurishness is one thing, but even on its own terms, her proposal is a mess. It will “protect the whole United Kingdom, our sovereign territories and British bases overseas”, she claims, which would be impossible for the £10bn over 10 years she is proposing to spend on it. The former British general Richard Barrons suggests such a system would cost more than £100bn.

What does this say about Badenoch’s sense of priorities? The actual urgent national security threat Britain faces is not volleys of missile attacks, but the climate emergency. There were estimated to be thousands of excess deaths from heatwaves this summer, while our intelligence services warn of serious disruption to our food supply from 2030. Yet Badenoch has committed to repealing the Climate Change Act and claimed that net zero by 2050 is “impossible” without bankrupting Britain. This not only contradicts the conclusion of the government’s statutory climate scientific advisers, but Badenoch herself. As a Treasury minister in 2021, she told parliament that it would cost less than 2% of GDP, largely from “increased investment in growth markets of the future”. Even three former Tory prime ministers have criticised Badenoch’s shift against net zero – including the former rightwing pin-up Boris Johnson.

Then there’s her economic agenda. A year ago, Badenoch declared that she sought to become Britain’s version of Argentina’s far-right president, Javier Milei. His government has imposed devastating cuts to pensions, universities and public healthcare, while poverty is once more surging. Badenoch proposes welfare cuts worth £23bn, and misleads the public as she does so. In May, she declared: “For the first time ever, the total welfare bill is now higher than total receipts from income tax.” This has been the case since 2011, and as the UK Statistics Authority noted in a letter rebuking her, this was misleading for other reasons: the gap had actually narrowed in recent years, and most of the welfare bill goes to pensioner benefits, including the state pension.

What would £23bn in cuts mean? They would include stripping workers with indefinite leave to remain of social security – people who have lived here for years, worked and paid taxes. That would not only be an injustice to them – consider that there is already a staffing crisis in sectors such as social care that immigration restrictions are worsening. She would reinstate a two-child benefit cap that would drive hundreds of thousands of children into poverty. Most of the rest would fall on the shoulders of sick and disabled people, including those receiving support while they work.

Consider this too: while we still live with the consequences of the 2008 financial crash, Badenoch proposes ending the ringfence for big banks separating retail and investment activities, and reducing their capital requirements.

What of her authoritarianism? Badenoch has declared free speech to be “the birthright of every citizen”, yet has advocated a blanket ban on pro-Palestinian protests. The justification is conflating opposition to genocide with threats to Jewish people, but this is a Tory leader who, when asked about Gaza, said that “Israel is fighting a proxy war on behalf of the UK”. Withdrawal from the European convention on human rights and repealing the Human Rights Act would strip citizens of crucial protections against an overbearing executive and abuses of state power. Badenoch advocates an ICE-style mass deportation apparatus with sweeping powers of surveillance – directly mimicking an institution across the Atlantic that snatches people from the street and kills migrants and US citizens alike.

Her attitude to the rights of minorities, meanwhile, is underlined by her commitment to scrap the public sector equality duty in its entirety. As a minister in 2021, she backed it, saying it helped ensure “that fairness is at the heart of everything we do”.

Yet the average punter knows little about Badenoch. The increasing extremism and scandals of Farageism have allowed her to appear somehow more reasonable and stable in comparison. But Badenoch is easily the most rightwing Tory leader in the party’s history. Her programme is a wishlist of rightwing zealots – one which would be ruinous to our social fabric. Yet few have bothered to look under the bonnet. The danger is that Britain discovers what Badenoch really stands for only when she is close enough to power to put it into practice.

Tuesday’s marches came after two weeks of protests that ⁠began in the northern suburbs of Paris and have snowballed nationwide. Besides the injuries to protesters and staff, 715 police officers have been wounded in the clashes, Lecornu’s office said.

Demonstrators have set dustbins on fire outside their schools, destroyed bus shelters and hurled projectiles at riot police, who have responded with batons, teargas and riot-control rounds.

Twenty-four schools have been burned or ransacked since mid-September, while more than 6,100 people have ​been arrested, almost all of them minors. More than 1,800 are being prosecuted, nearly 1,500 of them under 18, the justice ministry said.

The education ministry said more than 900 of the country’s 3,700 high schools were blockaded or had been closed for the day on Tuesday, although student groups put the number at 1,800. Some local education authorities moved classes ‌online.

Océanne, 18, was among the marchers in Marseille. “We just want to save our education and be educated,” she said, adding that she had suffered from absent teachers who were replaced either by “pointless substitutes” or not at all.

Many teachers were also demonstrating. In the western city of Rennes, Romain Dubourg said he and “about 30 colleagues” had “talked about the police brutality that we’ve witnessed, and decided to be there for our students if they need us”.

Trade unionists were also on the marches, with the head of the CGT union, Sophie Binet, urging members to “protect high school students”. The Green party leader, Marine Tondelier, urged local officials and parents to wear white and “go and protect our children during demonstrations”.

Anne Savinel-Barras, the president of Amnesty France, said: “The images and testimonies widely circulated over the past week raise alarming concerns about the dangerous use of teargas, batons and policing techniques by the police.” The interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said police had launched 10 internal investigations into allegations of brutality since the protests started.

On Monday, a 15-year-old’s hand was blown off as protesters battled riot police in northern France.

A 16-year-old lost the use of his right eye after he was seriously injured in the head on Wednesday during the blockade of a high school in Tours. The local prosecutor, Catherine Sorita-Minard, said the wounds were “compatible with the impact of a defensive bullet of the blast ball type”.

In another incident, a 14-year-old lost most of his teeth on Monday when a police officer appeared to fire a grenade at him at close range during a protest north-west of Paris. “His jaw is sealed shut, he can no longer speak and he eats through a straw,” his mother told reporters.

Lecornu has ordered his ministers to tackle the students’ core demands, which include ensuring absent teachers are replaced, reviewing the length of the 8am to 6pm school day and repairing ‌ageing buildings.

He denied accusations of routine excess force by police, saying officers had mostly acted proportionately. He told MPs on Tuesday that “extreme violence” had come “knocking on high-school doors, and must be condemned”.

“Setting fire to a school will not help repair it. Attacking a teacher will not help replace missing staff,” he said.

The protests, seven months before crucial presidential elections to choose a successor to Macron, have piled pressure on a government trying to reduce a ballooning budget deficit amid mounting investor concern over France’s ​mountainous debt and weak economic growth.

The government has accused the radical-left La France Insoumise party of encouraging and even orchestrating the movement after numerous LFI MPs attended school blockades. The party’s veteran leader and presidential candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, has strongly supported the protests, while urging non-violence.

Alleged Iranian spies planned ‘serious violence’ against UK journalists, court hears

The Guardian Tue, 06 Oct 2026 17:34:43 GMT

Mostafa Sepahvand, Farhad Javadi Manesh and Shapoor Qalehali Khani Noori did not dispute they surveilled targets

Three alleged Iranian spies carried out surveillance and reconnaissance to target journalists in the UK as part of a plan to commit “serious violence”, a court heard on Tuesday.

Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, and Shapoor Qalehali Khani Noori, 57, are charged with offences under the National Security Act.

Their “subjects” included Mojtaba Pourmohsen and Kambiz Hosseini, journalists for London-based Persian broadcaster Iran International, as well as a founder member of UK Lawyers for Israel, Jonathan Turner, the court was told.

The prosecution alleges Sepahvand intended to physically carry out a “violent attack” against at least one of the targets, while Manesh and Noori assisted in planning.

Sepahvand claims he was threatened into conducting surveillance against his will, but the prosecution described this as an “entirely bogus claim”, telling jurors he did it to get paid and have his theft conviction in Iran “fixed”.

In a voice note read out to Woolwich crown court in London, Sepahvand told an associate he would “finish off” a target if he was paid £150,000.

“They made me a promise and said: ‘We’ll sort out your matter/court case, and we’ll give you £150,000 as well. Finish the job. We’ll show you him/her (the target),’” he said.

“This is an illegal job. It’s something that constitutes a criminal offence, and it carries a heavy prison sentence. At the absolute minimum, they should transfer £10,000 for now.

“Wherever they tell me, I’ll go there and stand there. If the person (the target) is inside, they pay the £150,000, and I’ll finish him/her off.”

The defendants were said to have visited addresses linked to their targets, taken photos and videos and used platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online between August 2024 and March last year.

There was no dispute that the three defendants conducted the surveillance and reconnaissance, the jury was told.

Sepahvand accepts he was doing so for the benefit of the Iranian regime but claims he was threatened or bullied into doing it, and that he “deliberately did a bad job of it”, the prosecution said.

The crown added that Manesh and Noori claimed they did not know they were carrying out the surveillance to assist the Iranian intelligence service.

The defendants are charged with engaging in conduct likely to assist a foreign intelligence service.

Sepahvand, of St John’s Wood, north London, is also charged with engaging in surveillance, reconnaissance and open-source research with the intention to commit serious violence against a person in the UK.

Manesh, of Brent, and Noori, of Ealing, are also charged with engaging in surveillance and reconnaissance, with the intention that serious violence against a person in the UK would be committed by others.

The three men, who deny all the charges, were assisted by interpreters in the dock. The trial continues.

Three men jailed for raping teenage girl before fleeing UK in back of lorry

The Guardian Tue, 06 Oct 2026 17:23:48 GMT

Trio and 17-year-old boy convicted of rape after they persuaded girl to travel into Bristol alone and got her drunk

Three men who raped a 17-year-old girl before escaping from the UK to France in the back of a lorry have been sentenced to a total of 33 years in detention.

Mehrab Safi, 21, Salman Habibkheil and Awal Ahmadzai, both 19, and a 17-year-old boy plied the girl with alcohol after she had been persuaded to travel into Bristol alone, and all four raped her at a house in the city.

Safi was found guilty of two counts of rape, and Habibkheil of one. Both were convicted of arranging or facilitating the travel of a female with a view to exploitation. Ahmadzai was found guilty of one count of rape and one of sexual assault. The 17-year-old was convicted of one count of rape.

Safi was jailed for 15 years while Habibkheil and Ahmadzai were each sentenced to nine years in a youth detention centre. The 17-year-old was sentenced to two years and seven months in youth detention.

The victim had met Safi in Bristol during a trip she made in November 2025 to do some Christmas shopping with a friend – her first trip to the city from her home in Somerset, Bristol crown court heard.

Immediately after they left, Safi began messaging the girl. He told her he loved her and asked her to send indecent images.

Four days later, Safi, in collaboration with Habibkheil, arranged for her to be collected by a taxi and brought into Bristol. She was taken to his house where she was raped over several hours.

The victim’s mother reported her missing and police found her and the 17-year-old boy at Safi’s house.

As officers arrived, the three men fled, eventually managing to make their way across the Channel in the back of lorry carrying frozen goods.

Footage from Safi’s mobile phone showed the men laughing and gesticulating in the back of the lorry, which the prosecution suggested showed they thought they had escaped. But they were swiftly arrested in France and returned to the UK.

The girl had been raped five times by the four offenders. In a victim personal statement, the girl said she felt like a different person now and could not leave her home alone. She had put on hold her dreams of going to college and working with children.

Bristol crown court was told the four were born in Afghanistan and displaced as young people by the “brutality” of the Taliban regime.

Habibkheil had lost his father to the Taliban and was instructed by relatives to travel to England. Ahmadzai had ambitions of being a mechanic when he arrived in the UK but was unable to as an asylum seeker. He is believed to have post-traumatic stress disorder and was terrified of being deported to Afghanistan.

The 17-year-old offender lost his parents in Afghanistan and fled to the UK aged 11. The court heard he suffered “horrendous abuse” en route to England, arriving aged 12. He had flashbacks and nightmares.

But Judge Cullum said their experiences did not excuse the serious psychological harm they had caused to a “vulnerable” girl who had been “groomed and trapped”.

DS Jo Babbage, of Avon and Somerset police, praised the girl’s bravery in telling police her story and being questioned in court. “It’s impossible to overstate the courage she has shown,” she said.

Babbage said: “We do understand there is going to be anxiety in communities, but we need to be clear that this is not about a culture, a community, any religious belief. This is about deep-rooted misogyny and criminal behaviour in individuals.”

Lord Archer of Weston-super-Mare obituary

The Guardian Tue, 06 Oct 2026 17:05:18 GMT

Bestselling author and Conservative politician whose scandal-ridden career ended with a prison sentence

Jeffrey Archer, who has died aged 86, was irrepressible, though not necessarily in a good way. Ordinary humans would be sunk by the allegations of lies, thefts, frauds, gussied-up CVs, expenses fiddles, charity swindles, plagiarisms, insider trading deals, funding illicit coups and – perhaps most unforgivable of all – unpleasantness to underlings that dogged Archer’s life. But Lord Archer of Weston-super-Mare – bestselling novelist, disgraced politician, one-time athlete and convicted liar – was not ordinary: he was what the Titanic was designed to be, unsinkable.

One morning in September 2000, for instance, Archer emerged from Wimbledon police station. He had just been charged with perjury for persuading a friend to lie for him during his 1987 libel action against the Daily Star newspaper, which had claimed he had paid a sex worker to buy her silence.

That morning, Archer’s life had started to unravel: the following July he would be jailed at the Old Bailey for this crime. But instead of returning to his sumptuous Thameside apartment overlooking parliament to consult with lawyers or have a good cry, he smiled for the media, climbed into a chauffeur-driven BMW and went on to his next appointment. The Archer show had to go on. That evening he made his senior stage debut in a production of his own play at the Theatre Royal, Windsor.

The Accused was, if nothing else, strikingly topical. In it, Archer played Patrick Sherwood, a GP accused of poisoning his wife. Posters for the play read: “See You in Court”.

The stage was a simulacrum of the Old Bailey courtroom where he would later stand in the dock. Critics noted that it was a good job Agatha Christie was no longer alive to add the charge of plagiarism to the list he was soon to face. The Accused, they pointed out, bore a striking resemblance to her play Witness for the Prosecution. This was not the first time he faced allegations of plagiarism: Archer once judged a short story competition and duplicated many of the features of the winning entry in one of his own.

The theatre audience was the jury, giving their verdict on keypad. Most nights, Archer got off. In the real world, he was not so fortunate. But Archer’s comeuppance was not fatal. In jail, he wrote the three-volume memoir A Prison Diary and was regularly visited there by literary editors, eager to work up the raw copy of Britain’s most bankable novelist into publishable form in time to capitalise on the Christmas market.

Born in London, two weeks later Jeffrey moved with his family to Weston-super-Mare, in Somerset. He was the third child of Lola (nee Cook) and William Archer. The first two of Lola’s children, including another Jeffrey, were born outside marriage and given up for adoption. His father, a convicted fraudster and bigamist who was 64 when Archer was born, left the family home not long after and died in 1956, when his son was 15.

His doting mother spoiled him in compensation for that loss. She wrote a column for the local paper called Over the Teacups, about her scamp of a son who featured as “Tuppence”. He attended Wellington school, in Somerset – though he later implied he had attended the grander Wellington college, in Berkshire – where weedy Jeffrey was nicknamed The Pune, for his puny skin-and-bones physique, and bullied. He took up bodybuilding and athletics in response and was so successful at the latter that he became a blue at Oxford and later ran for Britain.

He left school with three O-levels (English literature, art and history), trained for the army and the police, and then found a niche at private schools as that rare thing, a popular PE teacher.

Then he went to Oxford, where he studied for three years at Brasenose College, though he was never registered there as an undergraduate. Rather, he studied for a teaching qualification on a course based at the college.

At Oxford, Archer also raised money for Oxfam, and succeeded in inviting the Beatles to visit Brasenose to sign a cheque and mingle with the dons in the senior common room. During that February 1963 soiree, undergraduate Sheridan Morley and Beatles drummer Ringo Starr found themselves at adjacent urinals. “[Ringo] asked if I knew this Jeffrey Archer bloke,” theatre critic Morley later told the Guardian. “I said everyone in Oxford was trying to work out who he was. Ringo said: ‘He strikes me as a nice enough fella, but he’s the kind of bloke who would bottle your piss and sell it.’”

While at Oxford, Archer wooed the student Mary Weeden, who in 1966 became his wife and later a chemistry lecturer at Cambridge University. Despite her husband’s shaming bankruptcies and his reported infidelities, Mary Archer justified standing by her man with more imaginative verve than, say, Tammy Wynette. She said much later: “I think I would find it a little monochrome, a little grey, to have a sort of a more conventional life with a more conventional husband.”

After leaving Oxford, he continued as a charity fundraiser, working for a medical charity and for the United Nations Association, whose chairman, the former Conservative MP Humphry Berkeley, alleged that Archer fiddled his expenses. He also served as a Conservative councillor on the Greater London council from 1967 to 1970, during which time he was accused of fiddling other councillors’ expenses. Despite these allegations, and despite Berkeley striving to convince Conservative central office that Archer was an unsuitable parliamentary candidate, he beat the future Tory minister Ian Gow to become Conservative candidate for Louth in Lincolnshire. He took the seat in a byelection on 4 December 1969, becoming – or so his book blurbs repeatedly claimed – the youngest MP in the House of Commons, aged 29. In fact, as Michael Crick points out in his biography, there were four younger MPs already in the Commons.

In 1974, he became one of the youngest MPs to relinquish his seat. That year, as a result of a complicated speculation he was involved in, Archer lost £500,000 in a fraudulent Canadian company called Aquablast. At the edge of bankruptcy, he resigned from parliament. In terms of fulfilling his ambitions, he may have been prudent: “I realised there would never be a career for me there,” he said of the Commons later.

Facing bankruptcy, he told his wife, then pregnant with their second child: “The only way I can get out of this is to write my way out of it.” Friends were sceptical that Archer could make capital from novel writing, having failed to do so from property deals. “Jeffrey, you can barely spell,” his friend Adrian Metcalfe told him, “let alone write.” “No, but I can tell stories,” Archer is said to have replied.

He was right. His first novel, Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less, published in 1976, became a bestseller, as did many of the more than 50 novels, prison journals, children’s books and short story collections that followed.

That fictional debut was something of a roman a clef, since it told the story of four men swindled out of $1m – roughly what Archer lost in business deals. The novel’s denouement though, in which the men revenge themselves on their swindlers, was part wish fulfilment and partly cribbed from the then popular movie, The Sting. His wife reportedly helped him edit it, correcting his spelling and grammar.

Later, teams of editors worked on making his novels publishable. They were impressed by his capacity for work: he would address the task in blocks of two hours at a time, then wrote as many as 17 further drafts at their behest.

Jonathan Coleman, one of four editors who worked on Archer’s international bestseller Kane and Abel (1979), said that, though the book was heavily edited, “he did the rewriting ... I mean, he wasn’t trying to write a literary masterpiece.”

He was, rather, trying to make money – and he did. Much came from TV adaptations, but he was a publishing phenomenon whose books were bought at the rate of 25,000 a month at the peak of his literary bankability, resulting in overall sales of around 300m copies.

By the mid-70s, then, the disgraced ex-MP was back. Yes, there was a report that he had stolen some suits from a Toronto store when he was giving evidence at the Aquablast trial in Canada in 1977, but that was never proved. And yes, some did complain that he trod on the little people as he rose again (“The sales people at HarperCollins loathed him – absolutely loathed him – because he was so awful to booksellers,” one company manager told Crick, referring to the sales rep as a “waste of space, being very abusive and unpleasant”), but none of this would stop him becoming rich and famous.

In 1979, Archer bought the Old Vicarage, Grantchester, a house associated with the poet Rupert Brooke. He also began to hold shepherd’s pie and Krug parties for politicians, business people and even journalists at his Thames-side apartment. He loved to give directions to the toilet: “Past the Picasso and left at the Matisse.”

He even returned to politics. Margaret Thatcher made him Conservative deputy chairman in 1985 – despite the misgivings of the senior Tories Norman Tebbit, Edward Heath and Willie Whitelaw – partly in gratitude for the sums he had funnelled into Tory party coffers.

The political return was shortlived. The following year he resigned because of newspaper allegations that he had paid Monica Coghlan, a sex worker, £2,000 through an intermediary at Victoria station to go abroad. In 1987, he sued the Daily Star for claiming he had slept with her.

In one of the case’s more memorable moments, Mr Justice Caulfield spoke to the jury: “Remember Mary Archer in the witness box. Your vision of her probably will never disappear. Has she elegance? Has she fragrance? Would she have, without the strain of this trial, radiance? How would she appeal? Has she had a happy married life? Has she been able to enjoy, rather than endure, her husband Jeffrey?” He said of Jeffrey Archer, “Is he in need of cold, unloving, rubber-insulated sex in a seedy hotel round about quarter to one on a Tuesday morning after an evening at the Caprice?” The judge’s questions, counterintuitively, were rhetorical. Archer won and was awarded £500,000 damages.

In 1992, thanks to the prime minister, John Major, Archer was politically rehabilitated again. Major made him a life peer, Lord Archer of Weston-super-Mare, chiefly because of his role in the previous year’s fundraising concert for Kurds. Archer, with the Red Cross, set up the charity Simple Truth.

But once more his philanthropy was questioned. Archer had claimed to have raised more than £57m for Kurdish refugees. Kurdish disaster relief groups claimed only £250,000 had been received by groups in Iraq. Years later, Scotland Yard investigated these discrepancies, but Archer was never prosecuted.

In 1994, Archer was back in trouble over alleged insider dealing involving shares in Anglian Television, of which his wife was a director. An inquiry by the Department of Trade and Industry concluded that Archer would not be prosecuted.

In 1999, aged 59, Archer was poised to fulfil one of his ambitions – to hold high political office – when he was selected as Conservative candidate for the London mayoral election of 2000. But that ambition was thwarted when the News of the World reported that he had perjured himself in the 1987 libel case.

His former friend, the TV producer Ted Francis, and his former personal assistant, Angela Peppiatt, decided to reveal that he fabricated an alibi at the trial because they thought he was an unsuitable mayoral candidate. He withdrew his candidacy the next day and was, in February 2000, expelled from the Conservative party for five years. The then party leader William Hague, who had hailed Archer’s “probity and integrity”, said: “This is the end of politics for Jeffrey Archer. I will not tolerate such behaviour in my party.”

Archer’s trial for perjury began in May 2001. Once more, his wife Mary gave evidence. Archer did not, though he had to hear his former secretary, Peppiatt, detail alleged marital infidelities with a former employee. During the judge’s summing up, his mother died. As a result, she missed seeing her son sentenced to four years’ imprisonment by Mr Justice Potts. He served only two years in jail and retained his life peerage.

Archer’s scandals were not over yet. A year after his release, he was accused by Equatorial Guinea’s government of co-financing the failed 2004 coup d’etat attempt.

He continued writing after his release. In 2007, he collaborated with the Catholic scholar Francis J Moloney in a book entitled The Gospel According to Judas. In this version of the story, Judas did not betray Jesus. The treatment of the story must have appealed to the disgraced peer, since in it he rehabilitated Judas. Perhaps in his mind, Archer – similarly maligned though more fairly – hoped for a similar rehabiliation.

Archer’s life was lived, if not told, in heroic denial of what he was. “He will dive over a cliff and then be amazed that he’s falling,” said his college friend Morley who, like many politicians in the party that Archer disgraced, remained supportive. “He thinks he’s Peter Pan, that he’ll never die. Everything he does he thinks is going to be all right in the end.”

In fiction, if not reality, Archer was rehabilitated. The maligned Judas became a national hero when in 2002 the writer Guy Jenkin wrote a TV comedy called Jeffrey Archer: The Truth. It told the version of the Archer story that never gets told (least of all in the newspapers) – about a misunderstood man who took the blame selflessly, suffered abuse, disgrace and imprisonment for the nation’s good.

“My Jeffrey Archer is the man who has frequently saved Britain over the last 30 years,” said Jenkin. “He’s beloved of all women he comes across, all men, all dogs – he’s a superhero.” If only the real Jeffrey Archer had been like that. But his life did not imitate art because it could not: it was rather, in the title of Crick’s biography, Stranger Than Fiction.

Archer retired from the Lords in 2024, and said that his final novel would be Adam and Eve. His death came unexpectedly, on the day before its publication.

He is survived by Mary, and his sons, William and James.

Jeffrey Howard Archer, Lord Archer of Weston-super-Mare, author and politician, born 15 April 1940; died 5 October 2026

Artificial review – Luca Guadagnino takes on OpenAI in muddled tech satire

The Guardian Tue, 06 Oct 2026 16:58:15 GMT

New York film festival: The origin story of Sam Altman’s company is reimagined as a campy comedy starring Andrew Garfield

On the day that Luca Guadagnino’s film about Sam Altman and OpenAI premiered, Vanity Fair released a cover story on Altman. Alongside glossy portraits from Annie Leibovitz, the world’s pre-eminent portrait photographer, the story describes him as the Oppenheimer of his day, evoking the image of a man leading humanity towards its own inevitable demise at the hands of sentient robots. Altman doesn’t seem to be grappling with much existential angst about the whole thing though: in an interview also released this week, he said that we should be prepared to accept “bad things” in return for the benefits of AI.

How much worse can things get? AI agents have already gone rogue, hacking into government systems and “bruteforcing” UN databases. Last year, a young woman used ChatGPT as a therapist before she killed herself (the software helped her write her suicide note). Studies show that using AI is probably leading us all towards something called cognitive surrender, which does not seem like the best use of your one wild and precious life.

Artificial is a stylish and blunt satire that is unambiguous in its perspective: that Sam Altman is an amoral manipulator who might be dead inside. That goes some way towards explaining why Amazon MGM Studios pulled out of distributing the film in June (Jeff Bezos’s company has a $50bn investment in OpenAI). I found it to be more of an op-ed than a movie, with little insight into what makes Altman and the tech elite tick. Neither does it have much to say about the world – glossy magazines included – that has welcomed them with open arms.

In 2003, a young math prodigy named Ilya Sutskever (Yura Borisov, the heartbeat of the film) visits Prof Geoff Hinton (Mark Rylance) in his office hoping for a job with the man known as the godfather of AI. “Have you ever considered the link between knowledge and patience?” Hinton serenely asks his young charge. You can almost feel Guadagnino is turning to the audience and giving us a big stage wink.

Nine years later, Sutskever and Hinton’s technology is starting to work “much the way your mind does”, with an ability to differentiate between cats and dogs, but Sutskever is growing increasingly impatient with what he sees as Hinton’s conservative ambitions for the technology. It’s at this point that Elon Musk (Ike Barinholtz) introduces Sutskever to Sam Altman (Andrew Garfield), who is fresh from selling his Loopt app, a kind of proto-Find My Friends, for $40m.

These guys are total dweebs, peppering each other with puerile jokes while doing shots in upscale restaurants as servers grimace and pray for a tip. Everyone is starting to want what these guys are selling, and one prospective investor speculates that AI will soon be able to reverse climate change and cure cancer. When talking about the technology, Sutskever’s eyes light up. “All pain, all loneliness will cease,” he says, as knowingly over-the-top haunted house music plays. “We will be free.”

The film’s dramatic tension rests in the opposing poles of thought represented by Sutskever, a delusional optimist, and the self-motivated hubris of Altman. As we move into the recent past, cracks and fissures appear in their partnership as OpenAI’s self-learning technology begins to first outsmart humans at video games, and then becomes a different beast entirely. Garfield is brilliantly slimy, nailing Altman’s evolution from demon twink to a narcissistic grifter with a victim complex that climaxes with him being fired as the CEO of OpenAI and then rehired five days later. “They’re being very mean to me,” he pouts in one scene after his board airs one of its many legitimate concerns over the ethics of his product.

Artificial is the most outwardly comedic Guadagnino film to date, with a script by the New Yorker essayist Simon Rich. The humor can be frustratingly broad, and it often feels like Barinholtz is impersonating Mike Myers doing Musk on Saturday Night Live than the Tesla founder himself (Rich is a former writer on SNL). Garfield seems to be playing Altman, who is an out gay man, as more effete than he actually is, which is strange as there are plenty of reasons to laugh at the tech oligarch that don’t involve him being light in his loafers. At other times, the script is satisfyingly savage. After being questioned over safety concerns by his associate Mira Murati (Monica Barbaro), Altman snaps, “I didn’t invent teen suicide, Mira.”

I could have done without some Artificial’s clangingly obvious visual metaphors, such as a random shot of a unhoused person wearing VR goggles, or the sudden plunge into a simulator-like sequence of a car accelerating over a foggy Golden Gate Bridge (we get it, we’re taking a reckless leap into the unknown). The film comes with a score by Damon Albarn, and the Blur frontman contributes one original composition that an ASPCA advert would reject for being too on-the-nose with lyrics like, “In a corrupt world, we’ll sing the saddest song.”

It’s tech oligarch season at the movies, with films about Elon Musk, Elizabeth Holmes and Mark Zuckerberg also due for release over the next few months as film-makers try to respond to the zeitgeist in real time. “We opened Pandora’s box,” Altman says in a standout monologue towards the end of the film. “Countries will fall, industries will collapse, and we get to be the ones to usher people into this new world.”

It’s a grim prophecy that gets lost in Guadanigno’s tonal jumble of a film, which has a certain self-satisfaction in telling us that dystopia is upon us. I couldn’t help but crave a leaner, meaner version of this movie. Despite some genuinely chilling moments, Artificial shows the limits of holding up a mirror to the world.

Artificial is screening at the New York film festival and wil be released in the US on 25 December, in Australia on 21 January and in the UK on 27 January

Why a PR voting system is the best bet for Britain

The Guardian Tue, 06 Oct 2026 16:56:09 GMT

Tom Walker responds to a letter that said first past the post is the lesser of two evils for voters. Plus letters from Susanna Dammann and Steve Smart

It is common in the argument against proportional representation (PR) to reach for Italy as a cautionary tale, as Gian Lorenzo Spisso does in his letter (A proportional representation voting system could spell disaster for Labour, 30 September). The irony is that Italy does not actually have a proportional system: it has a mixed system. If we want to assess PR, we should look at countries that actually use it – Germany, Sweden, the Netherlands, Denmark – hardly synonymous with political instability.

Also, small parties or weak local representation are not unique to PR. The tiny Democratic Unionist party held the balance of power at Westminster less than a decade ago under first past the post (FPTP), while the Scottish National party and Plaid Cymru wield influence disproportionate to their UK-wide vote because their support is geographically concentrated.

Germany limits fragmentation with a minimum electoral threshold. And systems such as Germany’s combine PR with constituency MPs, while Ireland’s single transferable vote system retains a strong geographical link between voters and representatives.

Gian’s letter does raise a more interesting point: FPTP encourages major parties to contain competing tendencies within broad internal coalitions rather than allowing them to form separate parties. But is it preferable for those coalitions to be internal and opaque, forcing voters into tactical choices, rather than external and explicit, requiring parties to negotiate and find common ground?

The fundamental problem with FPTP is that millions of votes have little bearing on parliament. If your preferred candidate has no realistic chance of winning, voting for them does not translate into representation. In 2024, Labour won 33.7% of votes cast but 63.2% of the seats. That distortion is not a minor technical flaw. Who wields power depends heavily on where votes are cast rather than who people vote for. This disconnect is precisely why Britain needs electoral reform.

The question isn’t whether PR is perfect, but whether we can design a system in which parliament reflects the votes people actually cast. Other stable democracies do so. Britain can too. Tom WalkerLondon

Re Gian Lorenzo Spisso’s letter and Zoe Williams’ article (Electoral reform could be a gamble too far for Burnham, 30 September), there are several reasons for the UK to adopt a more proportional voting system of which the most important is the moral one: it’s fairer.

In the last general election, the current system gave us a government that only about 20% of the electorate had voted for. No wonder the public has been hostile since the start of this administration: almost 80% of us didn’t vote for it.

There are other, more pragmatic reasons, particularly for those of us on the centre/soft left: if we are anxious to avoid having an extreme party in power, we need to ditch first past the post – and fast. Reform UK may be lagging a little in the polls at the moment, but with £76m behind them, they may be able to mount a campaign of mis- and disinformation that could persuade 30% of the electorate to vote for them – and they might win. If we don’t want an extreme right (or left) party in power, we need a way to elect MPs that reflects that view. We need proportional representation.

Of course, not all PR systems are the same. Italy uses a mixed system similar to the one used in Scotland for elections to Holyrood. However, as a report published by Make Votes Matter on possible future electoral systems points out, the Italian system “tilts the playing field rather than levelling it”. Its results do not reflect the views of the Italian population accurately.

The crucial effect of any proportional system that meets the criteria of the “good systems agreement” (which sets out the standards that a system should meet to be considered by the proposed national commission) is to encourage cross-party collaboration and cooperation. It undermines the tit-for-tat squabbling so typical of our House of Commons and reduces the policy flip-flop of right-left-right administrations that makes it so hard for businesses, and individuals, to plan long term. It is precisely that collaborative, creative approach to policy that would encourage the stability and prosperity our people are longing for. Susanna Dammann London

Gian Lorenzo Spisso’s letter arguing against proportional representation voting in the UK is superficial and wrong-headed. Up and down the country there are huge numbers of voters like me whose entire lifetime has been spent thoroughly fed up with our unfair system. I am 79 now, and my vote has never elected an MP since I lived in an urban area private rental in my early 20s.

As a middle-class, left-leaning voter living in mainly middle-class towns and suburbs, my vote has been wasted in a succession of places. Of course PR could elect a rightwing government; it could also lock the right wing out of power for a long time, and as a democratic socialist I would be happy to live with the prospect of a long-term progressive coalition. PR would also give the Greens the scale of representation in parliament that their increasing national support deserves. Steve SmartMalvern, Worcestershire

Is regulation enough to stop AI systems killing us all?

The Guardian Tue, 06 Oct 2026 16:56:04 GMT

Martyn Thomas wonders how any rational person can argue that independent oversight and regulation will be sufficient

Once again a frontier AI model has been withdrawn because it fails safety tests (OpenAI scraps release of new model over safety concerns in internal testing, 28 September). There is the usual call for “independent oversight and regulation”, though never any explanation of how this would work or, most importantly, what evidence should persuade a regulator that an AI system is adequately safe.

There is a long engineering tradition of regulating safety-critical software systems, such as those controlling aircraft or nuclear power stations; international standards require “safety cases” – rigorous analyses that show that the possible hazards have been identified and controlled and that the probability of an accident is extremely low.

Typically, the safety case should show, with a probability of at least 99%, that an accident that could cause multiple fatalities will not occur more often than once in 1,000 years. It is extremely hard to provide evidence for such low probabilities, even for aircraft that at worst might kill 1,000 people in a single accident. The developers of frontier AI systems tell us that their systems might kill the whole of humanity, yet they have provided no detailed risk analyses, no safety cases that could be independently assessed, and no evidence that such safety cases could ever be produced for frontier AI systems.

How, then, can any rational person argue that independent oversight and regulation will be sufficient? Policy must be based on rigorous analysis of the facts, not on fantasy. Martyn ThomasFellow and emeritus professor of IT, Gresham College

Too nice: do Arsenal lack the grit and tenacity to end WSL title drought?

The Guardian Tue, 06 Oct 2026 16:55:59 GMT

Renée Slegers’ team have the technical ability, but doubts remain over the nastiness needed to rival Manchester City and Chelsea

Arsenal, 10 points adrift of the Women’s Super League leaders, are poised to undertake a “big review” of their season during this international break to try to determine where things have gone so horribly wrong – again – in the early stages. After their 4-2 loss at Manchester City on Sunday, it felt as if the agenda needs to include an unusual but potentially critical question: is this team nasty enough to win a WSL title?

The technical ability throughout the world-class squad Arsenal have assembled could hardly be higher but the levels of grit, resilience and tenacity need examining in a group that appears unable to match Chelsea and Manchester City when it comes to the mental aspects of a title race. Arsenal last won the WSL in 2019.

When speaking to sources close to the Arsenal players, it is common to hear of the squad being like a “family”, very supportive of each other and full of “great people”. Those admirable traits, and a general sense the club is full of nice characters, often come across when watching games or during player interviews. Arsenal have built a team of good eggs; polite, courteous and professional individuals who people would be glad to call friends. In the vast majority of scenarios in life this is, quite obviously, a good thing. But are they too nice to beat City?

It is quite hard to imagine many of the Arsenal squad raising their voices in anger. It is equally hard to recall the last time anybody at the club engaged in so-called “housery”; perhaps not since Katie McCabe’s hair pull against Chelsea in last season’s Champions League quarter-final. The irony is that McCabe is one of the senior, influential players who left this summer – in her case to join Chelsea – and McCabe, regardless of what fans might think of her, is someone Arsenal could rely on to roll up her sleeves and get stuck in, to raise her game in a hostile atmosphere and be combative.

Last term, no Arsenal players – not even McCabe – registered in Stats Perform’s list of the top 20 WSL players for percentage of duels won. Only one Arsenal player has been shown a red card in a WSL game since 2021-22. Admirable discipline, yes, but are they lacking that fire in the belly?

This season, the team appear to be without a dogged, refuse-to-lose type of character in the mould of Lucy Bronze, whose never-say-die attitude has frequently come to England’s aid in crucial moments at major tournaments; or the gritty battling spirit of Erin Cuthbert, who has helped Chelsea lift seven league titles; or – to take an Arsenal example – a leader such as Gabriel Magalhães, a rock for others to lean on during tough games.

It is possible to be successful without a Roy Keane in your squad and Arsenal do have Leah Williamson, who has led England to two European titles, so it would be wrong to imply there is no leadership in this group. Leaders can step up in different ways but recently Renée Slegers, when praising her senior players’ reactions to their disappointing draw in Paris, mentioned there had been “lots of hugs” and praised how supportive everybody had been for each other. That sounds like the sort of unified workplace culture millions would envy, but to win titles sometimes you need to fall out, yell, be angry and demand higher standards.

On Friday I asked Slegers whether Arsenal had enough of a nasty edge to win the league, and she replied defiantly: “I think so, and nastiness or that grittiness, that can express itself in different ways, and I think we have certain ways in which we express that and [in] which we can do that. But of course, with our performances where we haven’t been at our best, you maybe don’t see those moments as much which we can bring, but we’re convinced that we can bring that to games as well, in our way, the Arsenal way, because it’s definitely there.”

That was not evident on Sunday in the little – but important – moments, such as shortly after Arsenal had twice taken a lead they would surrender. City seemed unfazed and carried the resolve of a team who had no doubt they would win.

Part of the way that belief has been instilled into the defending champions was evidenced in a clip, released by Sky Sports, of Andrée Jeglertz’s pre-match team talk, which he concluded with the words: “The most important thing: we are Manchester City, we are playing at home and we are winning this game.” The matter-of-fact, defiant instruction was not easy to imagine hearing in this Arsenal dressing room with any real conviction right now, not from the players and not from Slegers, who has many excellent qualities as coach, and is, by all accounts, an intelligent, detail-oriented coach of whom the players are very fond.

In decades to come, all the nice characteristics this Arsenal squad demonstrate will no doubt stand them in good stead in the real world, with their friendships, but the cliche “nice guys finish last” is starting to feel increasingly appropriate for this amiable side.

Unemployment and the rise of the Nazis

The Guardian Tue, 06 Oct 2026 16:55:55 GMT

John Plowright reflects on how unemployment was viewed by Germans and the fear the KPD sparked

Philipp Ruch believes that the impact of the 1929 Wall Street crash cannot explain the Nazi breakthrough at the 1930 Reichstag election, as the full effects of Black Thursday “didn’t fully arrive in Germany until July 1931” (‘Hitler was a lazy criminal who slept in until noon’: why most of what we think we know about the rise of the Nazis is wrong, 1 October). But unemployment more than doubled between 1928 and the 1930 election, and that fact alone might be thought sufficient to explain the change in Nazi fortunes. Not so, says Ruch, for “in regions where unemployment was high, the Nazi party performed relatively poorly. If anything, unemployment was a factor contributing to anti-fascist resilience.”

This, however, marks a failure to appreciate how rising unemployment was seen by most Germans at the time. Not only did they see it as signifying one aspect of the failure of the coalition parties in government to manage the economy competently, but they also rightly regarded it as fuelling the rise of the Communist party of Germany (KPD) – with it being the other great political beneficiary of the Wall Street crash along with the National Socialist German Workers’ party. As the KPD grew, so the Nazi party grew – as it was perceived as the only party with the resolve and the numbers (thanks to the brownshirts) to stop the communists seizing power on the streets.

The fact that the KPD proved a damp squib should not blind us to the fact that the party once inspired genuine, strong and very widespread fear. John PlowrightRepton, Derbyshire

Greek prime minister vows to ‘ramp up’ efforts to regain Parthenon marbles

The Guardian Tue, 06 Oct 2026 16:50:19 GMT

Kyriakos Mitsotakis says his UK counterpart, Andy Burnham, has been supportive of restitution efforts in the past

The Greek prime minister has vowed to “ramp up” his country’s claims to get back the Parthenon marbles from the British Museum, emphasising that his UK counterpart, Andy Burnham, was hugely supportive of restitution efforts before he moved into Downing Street.

Kyriakos Mitsotakis said he would raise the issue in the strongest of terms when he met Burnham, who was culture secretary in a previous Labour government.

“Unfortunately they have not progressed,” he told a conference in Athens when asked about talks with London over a muted “hybrid” deal to repatriate the fifth-century BC marbles in return for a treasure trove of other antiquities.

“We will very clearly ramp up the intensity of our claims, not just with the British Museum, but also with the British government. I would also like to remind the audience that the new prime minister of the UK, unequivocally, was supportive of the return of the Parthenon sculptures before he became prime minister.”

It was the first time Mitsotakis had conceded that negotiations with the British Museum, under the aegis of its chair, George Osborne, had failed to make headway.

Upping the ante, he suggested the fate of the artworks was also connected to Burnham’s stated desire for the UK to have closer ties with the EU. Sculpted to adorn a monumental frieze that embellished the Parthenon, the carvings have been split between Athens and London since their controversial removal at the behest of Lord Elgin, Britain’s ambassador to the Ottoman empire, more than 200 years ago.

“For those of us who were saddened to see the United Kingdom leave the European family, we took great interest in the comments made by the UK PM,” said the Greek leader, citing the possibility of “a stronger relationship between the UK and Europe”.

“The Parthenon sculptures will be part of this debate, this is not just an issue for Greece. It’s an issue for Europe.”

The combative remarks come amid thinly disguised disdain in Athens for Burnham’s seeming about-turn on the sculptures. In private, Greek officials have voiced dismay that within days of assuming office, he should so publicly reverse his position, stating in one of his first interviews that the dispute was “an issue for the British Museum” to resolve.

Long seen as an advocate of repatriation, Burnham’s support for the antiquities to be returned to Athens dates back 25 years with Greek officials seeing his elevation as the best hope yet of finally ending the row.

In 2023, as mayor of Greater Manchester, he appeared to go further than ever before, posting on social media: “Send them back, no strings. And let’s use culture to change how Britain is seen around the world.”

“His change in stance caused great disappointment,” said one well-placed Greek heritage expert who has legally advised successive governments on the issue. “There was more than an element of perfidious Albion about it.”

The British Museum has been home to about 160 metres of the frieze since 1816, when a bankrupt Elgin was forced to sell the marbles in what, even then, was viewed as a controversial acquisition by the British government.

Mitsotakis, whose centre-right administration has sought to refocus the campaign on the idea of reunifying the masterpieces within view of the Acropolis, said on Tuesday that changing attitudes in Britain could not be dismissed.

There was, he said, still room for a “win-win” solution with the imminent closure and renovation of the National Archaeological Museum in Athens allowing gems that had never been seen outside Greece to be sent to the UK in exchange for the sculptures.

“[The marbles] reunification in Athens would also set a precedent for a unique cultural partnership between Greece and the UK, and in particular between Greece and the British Museum,” he said. “I will certainly make the case very forcibly to the British PM when I meet him. I think the time has come. British public opinion supports reunification of the sculptures and I do believe that now is the time to push in this direction.”

Don’t mention the Iron Dome: comedy genius Kemi on warpath at Tory conference

The Guardian Tue, 06 Oct 2026 16:49:03 GMT

‘It’s a Britannia Shield’ announcement proves no one does farcical improv better than the Conservative leader

Just another day in Crapland. It’s amazing what you can get used to. You can’t say the Tories haven’t put a lot of thought into their party conference. It takes some programming skill to make every day even more dismal than the last. You come expecting very little and get even less.

Schopenhauer would be in dreamland. The very act of being has never felt so inconsequential. Yet there’s something very comforting about this. You leave the Birmingham theme park attraction feeling better about yourself than when you arrived. Who knew abject failure could be so much fun? You find yourself congratulating some members on being able to dress themselves. A curious hybrid of an endangered species and care in the community?

You might find yourself wondering if you are being gaslit. Small pockets of people roaming around aimlessly with a smile on their face, insisting that it is very heaven in this dawn to be alive and repeatedly crossing themselves before images of the beatific Kemi Badenoch. But then you realise that the people the Tories are really gaslighting are themselves. It’s almost painful to watch. Almost. But mostly it’s like a remake of The Truman Show. Everyone waking up each day and believing they are engaged in something meaningful. When the reality is nothing is happening. They are living in a Potemkin village. A series of distractions designed to look like a party conference.

The breakout star is, of course, Kemi. She is the Tories’ chosen one. KULT KEMI. The leader who has rescued them from one black hole and is plunging them straight back into another. I’ve come to realise I’ve got Kemi wrong. Sure, she’s short-tempered and can’t tolerate dissent. But she’s actually a supremely gifted entertainer. A comedy genius. A woman whose one-liners often get mistaken for serious comment. A female Jack Dee. She would be far more successful taking her show to the Edinburgh fringe than Birmingham.

Kemi’s act on the morning media round was one of her best yet. No one does improv better. Understandably, every interviewer wanted to ask her about the Tories’ overnight announcement of a £10bn Iron Dome to rival the Israelis’ that would protect the UK from any kind of drone or missile attack. Like, how did she imagine she was going to build the Iron Dome for about a tenth of the money that all the experts said it would cost? And wasn’t this just some bullshit nonsense designed to make the front pages of the Tory press that wouldn’t stand contact with reality?

“Stop calling it an Iron Dome,” Kemi dead-panned. She really is a comedy pro. Even at 8.10am she’s still in role. “It isn’t an Iron Dome. I’ve never called it an Iron Dome. It’s a Britannia Shield.” Genius. She couldn’t think for the life of her why everyone was calling it an Iron Dome. Mmm. It might have been something to do with the Tory press office releasing a statement calling it an Iron Dome? And the opinion piece in the Sun, written by Kemi herself, calling it an Iron Dome? There are clearly a lot of replicant Kemis rushing around pretending to be the real one.

OK, OK, we’ll call it a Britannia Shield, said the radio and TV presenters. Sometimes it’s easier to humour a guest. So when was it going to be operational, what would it look like and how much of the UK would it cover? Kemi laughed. She hadn’t a clue. She was just the one with the ideas. The details she left for others. But it definitely would be up and running before Penny Mordaunt returned to parliament to reprise her role in Sky’s The War Game. As for the shield itself, that would be a few Sopwith Camel biplanes and barrage balloons that could be diverted to Scotland at a fortnight’s notice if required.

Are you really just a one-woman band? Anna Foster asked on the Today programme. Your personal polls are higher than your party’s. A polite way of saying the Tories are tanking in third place. Not at all, Kemi ad-libbed. Even Jeffrey Archer would have struggled to lie quite so shamelessly. Everyone knows who my shadow cabinet is. Er. I’m not sure I could name them all. I’m not even sure the shadow cabinet could. Just an array of nodding dogs on a dashboard. But maybe we’ve underestimated the public. They do know exactly who the shadow cabinet is. And that’s why the Tories are still bottom-lining.

Back in the conference centre, those members who were still alive were struggling to find something to do. The morning’s entertainment was centred around the “Main Hall”, AKA the converted cupboard. For Laura Trott, the shadow education secretary, there were about 15 people in the room. The rest of the audience had disguised themselves as seats again. Still, not all bad news. Eight people were watching online. A figure that soon went down to one. For a while I wondered who this one poor sod was. Then I realised it was me.

Laura looked close to tears by the time the session was over. She was met beside the stage by someone who I hope was a therapist. Quite where everyone else had got to was a mystery. There was also no one to hear Rebecca Paul – me neither – talk about £50k handbags with a woman called Plum. Self-selecting, I guess. Maybe there’s a separate hall for those experiencing extreme catatonia.

By the afternoon we lucky few were stretched out into the much-reduced Symphony Hall to prepare for war with a Shahed drone hanging above our heads. First up was the shadow foreign secretary, Tom Tugendhat, a man who has sold his one-nation soul for a job in Kemi’s Kabinet. “I am coming back to serve,” SuperTug announced, matching the oratory skills of Andrew Griffith. He is a man who wakes up every day, and seems disappointed not to find himself at war. He rather died on his arse.

Then we got the special guest. The rightwing historian Niall Ferguson. A more swivel-eyed, deranged Dr Strangelove. He had come to tell everyone that he too fancied a war, even if you didn’t want one. “A world war is coming,” he said, trying not to show if he had become sexually aroused. “And there is nothing we can do about it.” All of which made the later speeches of Kemi-come-latelies Helen Whately and James Cartlidge somewhat redundant. There’s no need to starve benefits claimants or build an Iron Dome when the apocalypse is upon us.

Suddenly the Tory conference made sense. It wasn’t just a place where hope came to die. It was a place where we all came to die.

‘We live in grief-phobic societies’: experts on how to get more comfortable with death

The Guardian Tue, 06 Oct 2026 16:00:18 GMT

We are all going to die, and so is everyone we know. So how can you not be terrified?

For most people, death is not a standard conversation topic. Once, at lunch, a friend began talking about her mother’s death several years earlier. Her voice caught occasionally, but she spoke about it plainly – like a simple fact of life. As we talked, I noticed another friend was shifting uncomfortably in his seat; he didn’t say much.

Afterwards, I asked him what was wrong. “I really don’t like talking about death,” he said, his hands twitching anxiously. “I don’t even like thinking about it. It freaks me out.”

His discomfort struck me as silly – and also the most normal thing in the world. We are all going to die, and so is everyone we know. So why be terrified? And how can you not be terrified?

My friend is far from alone in his discomfort. “We live in grief-illiterate and grief-phobic societies,” says Dr Lucy Hone, a resilience and grief researcher and author of the book How Will I Get Ever Through This?: A Practical Guide to Navigating Life’s Toughest Times.

Hone began researching grief over a decade ago, after the sudden death of her daughter, Abi. On our video call, she wears one of Abi’s old hats, an orange and white beanie with polka dots and a big orange pouf on top. It’s ridiculous, Hone says, but it makes her laugh.

For someone who has experienced such intense loss and spends so much of her time talking to people about their grief, Hone is remarkably cheerful and bubbly. This is in part because of her work, she argues. Hone and several other experts I spoke with said that thinking and being around death was “life-affirming”.

Below, experts share why so many of us are so scared of death, and how we can learn to get a little more comfortable with it.

Death disrupts the usual orientation of our lives, argues Dr Todd May, instructor of philosophy at Warren Wilson College.

“People in the west and elsewhere are forward-looking,” May says. We do not just exist in the moment – we engage in projects and relationships that we see unfolding over time. “The thought of our lives ending violates this future orientation we all have,” he explains.

The typically western, individualistic approach to life affects how we feel about death, says Sister Chȃn Trì Nghiȇm, an Australian-born Zen Buddhist nun. In the Judeo-Christian tradition, “there is a strongly shared belief that God created individuals separate from each other … we have a certain lifespan, and we die at a certain time”. This view causes fear and anxiety, argues Trì Nghiȇm.

In the Buddhist tradition, beginnings and endings are far less defined. Take a question as simple as when you first began to exist: was it when you were born? The nine months you were in your mother’s belly? When you were just a precursor cell within your unborn mother? “In Buddhism, we have always existed and there was no time when we didn’t exist,” says Trì Nghiȇm. Seen through this lens, death is less of an ending and more of a continuation.

The idea of finitude can bruise our fragile egos, says Alua Arthur, author and death doula. “We have no control at all, and that’s very disquieting,” she says. “We think we’re infallible, and death reminds us how small we are, and that’s uncomfortable.”

And the thought of death brings about big feelings that most people would prefer to avoid, says Dr Luyi Kathy Zhang, a hospice and palliative care doctor.

“So many of us are ill-equipped to deal with uncomfortable emotions, and death is probably one of the peak uncomfortable experiences,” she says. “It is easier for us to say that death is an eventuality that we will deal with when it comes rather than to face the feelings now.”

Finally, dying increasingly happens out of sight, says Hone – in hospitals or care homes. But it wasn’t always this way.

“Throughout human history, we had death around us,” Hone says. “We’d care for the sick and dying at home, so we were forced to talk about it and think about it.”

This shift accelerated in the mid-20th century. “In Boston in 1912, about two-thirds of residents died at home,” the New York Times reported in 2019. “By the 1950s, the majority of Americans died in hospitals and by the 1970s, at least two-thirds did.”

Removed from our immediate surroundings, for many death became something more distant and abstract.

Not talking or thinking about death “doesn’t mean that it’s not coming, it just means that you’re going to be ill-prepared when it does come”, says Arthur.

Thinking about and planning for the logistics of death can also make things easier for the people around us. “That way, they’re not in grief and also trying to figure out where your social security card is,” says Arthur.

Planning for how we’d ideally like to spend our last days gives us agency, says Zhang. “You can choose to be involved in it rather than [experience] the overwhelm and stress of being forced to deal with it,” she explains.

There are more immediate benefits too. I spoke to over a dozen experts on death, and they raised the same point again and again: thinking about death helps us live better lives.

“Accepting that we’re going to die allows us to live more purposefully,” says Hone. For her, losing Abi and confronting grief in her work clarified the brevity and fragility of life. Given that, she says, “I need to know who and what matters most to me now and focus my attention on them.”

Reflecting on our mortality can be a good way to keep things in perspective, says Zhang. For example: will this frustrating traffic jam matter to you on your deathbed? And if you are nervous about asking someone out, or applying for a job, ask yourself how you might feel at the end of your life if you didn’t go after what you wanted. “That might be enough of a perspective shift for us to overcome fear or hesitation,” Zhang says.

It can also help us appreciate our life now. “If we ask ourselves, ‘What if this is the last time I get to have dinner with my family?’ that is a very different way of experiencing something that feels ordinary and mundane,” Zhang says.

Often, familiarity with death is something we don’t have much of a say about – the loss of a friend, family member or even beloved pet forces us to confront it, whether we’re ready or not.

But experts say there are certain practices that can help one begin to “tolerate” the thought of death, as Hone puts it. “I’m not at peace with the fact that I’m going to die and all the people I love are going to die,” she admits. “But I can tolerate it, because I can tolerate difficult things.”

Don’t feel ashamed of your fear. Fear of death is natural, and often a big part of what keeps us alive, says Arthur. “It’s the thing that tells you to stop walking when you get to the edge of that cliff, and to drink water when you’re in the desert,” she says. The goal, Arthur argues, is not to completely eliminate the fear of death, but to understand where and why it might be holding us back.

Start planning. Whether it’s writing your will or an advance directive – a document outlining who you want making your financial and medical decisions for you if you can’t – thinking about the practicalities of death can be a helpful, less emotionally fraught way to approach it, Arthur says.

Ask yourself some big questions. Questions like, “What will I regret not doing in 10 or 15 years?” and “Will I care about this on my deathbed?” help put the current moment and emotions into perspective, says Zhang.

Think about someone you know who died. Even if it’s just for five minutes, Hone says, reflect on what you learned from that person, and how you might want to live differently because of what they taught you. “That’s quite a nice, constructive way to think about death,” she says.

Think about your relationships. Reflect on the important people in your life and whether you’re holding anything back from them, Arthur says. “Who do you need to say sorry to? Who do you need to say thank you to? Who do you need to forgive?” she asks.

Learn how to balance the present and the future. As important as it is to be present in our lives, we cannot only live in the moment, says May. “We need to keep our engagement in activities with a future,” he says. But because we could die at any moment, “living solely for the future sacrifices the riches of our present”. The aim is to exist in a balance of both, May says, which is “difficult, but perhaps achievable to some degree.”
