Stop worrying about my AI, says multibillionaire Sam Altman. So we bear the risks and he keeps the money

The Guardian Tue, 06 Oct 2026 15:30:17 GMT

OpenAI’s CEO seems to want to privatise his company’s huge financial gains while making all of us pay for any negative consequences

Tech bros’ messianic streaks can show up in subtle ways. But one of Sam Altman’s flaws is that he often lacks that subtlety. “We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology,” said the OpenAI chief executive in an interview with Politico last weekend.

That’s easy for Altman to say. But it’s pretty galling to hear for the rest of us. Lest we forget, we didn’t ask for OpenAI to unleash AI agents that went rogue and weaselled their way into government IT systems and private businesses around the world. Nobody voted for ChatGPT to be released, but the company put it out into the world as a test product that happened to catch the zeitgeist. That kickstarted an arms race among AI companies to push the frontier of the technology ever further and faster, resulting in the mess we now find ourselves in.

OpenAI’s competitors, including Anthropic, have started to step back from the brink – as has OpenAI itself, deciding not to release its latest model because it’s purportedly too dangerous. Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, has talked about needing to “pace the frontier”: tech-bro jargon for pumping the brakes to bring down the speed at which the runaway vehicle is skidding out of control.

Yet we’re expected to take these incidents – and the harm they cause – as the natural consequences of OpenAI’s continued march towards an IPO that would bring its investors millions. It’s hard to escape the idea that Altman wants to privatise his company’s gains while socialising the risks of untrammelled AI development.

Every useful technology – and AI is a useful technology, despite the holdouts and occasional users’ carping – carries risk. Cars can and do crash, while medicines that save us often have harmful side effects. Very rarely, aircraft fall from the sky. But we accept those risks because the benefits are substantial, and we build rules to limit the harm. We also make companies liable. And most importantly, we get some say in deciding what level of risk is and isn’t acceptable.

Altman seems to suggest that his company’s messes are our problem to sort out – or worse, that the consequences of his tech are ours to tolerate. But Altman would do well to think about this differently. OpenAI gets to decide how fast it develops its technology and when it releases it. Its investors benefit financially if those bets pay off. But it feels as if he’s suggesting that when the tech creates problems outside OpenAI’s own walls, the costs of cleaning up are ours to bear, not his company’s.

The idea that private companies profit while we’re left to deal with the consequences becomes even harder to defend as AI stops being something we opt into using as a chatbot, and becomes something that acts on and changes the world around us. If I ask ChatGPT something and it gives me a bad answer, I chose to expose myself to that risk, so should share that burden. But the same isn’t true for a government department that suddenly finds an OpenAI agent lurking in its files and rooting around. It didn’t opt in; it became an unwilling participant in someones experiment.

That’s why Altman’s argument sounds so disingenuous. OpenAI shouldn’t be able to decide for all of us what is and isn’t an acceptable level of failure, then ask everyone to live with the result. The burden ought to be on it to prove its technology can be trusted – and to pick up the bill if it can’t.

It’s no wonder that OpenAI wants to travel quickly. The company is seeking $30bn in new funding, and a valuation of $1.4tn ahead of a public listing likely next year. There’s money to be made – never mind at whose expense.

To his credit, Altman also acknowledged in the Politico interview that there will need to be a liability framework for companies offering models such as OpenAI’s, and that the company will have to take responsibility for at least some of what goes wrong during training. But that “some” is doing a lot of work.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

If Altman believes some bad things are an acceptable price for AI’s progress, OpenAI can dig into its deep pockets to pay that price itself – for instance if its agents go rogue and do damage to government or private company systems, or compromise user data. It can’t, and shouldn’t, get the financial upside when everything goes right, then ask the rest of us to accept the consequences when things go wrong. That’s especially the case when we never agreed to the unregulated experiment in the first place.

Chris Stokel-Walker is the author of TikTok Boom: The Inside Story of the World’s Favourite App

The Register that shatters the myth of Britain’s role in profiting from enslavement

The Guardian Tue, 06 Oct 2026 15:10:46 GMT

In this month’s newsletter: for Caribbean scholars, the evidence of how deeply slavery shaped Britain’s wealth has never been in doubt. Plus, heritage walks in Manchester

Don’t get Cotton Capital delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

Welcome to this month’s Cotton Capital newsletter. I’m Ahmed Reid, coming to you from Jamaica, where I am programme manager for the Guardian’s Legacies of Enslavement team.

The recently published Register of British Slave-Traders, reported exclusively in the Guardian, lists 13,000 men and women who invested in and profited from the trafficking of more than three million enslaved Africans between 1563 and 1807.

The Register captures a broad range of investors, from ordinary men and women in provincial towns to the monarchy. Queen Elizabeth I and many in her court invested in John Hawkins’s 1563 and subsequent missions. They provided Hawkins with money and ships, including the royal ship Jesus of Lübeck, which trafficked 359 Africans to the Americas in 1568. Elizabeth I’s successors – including James I, Charles I, Charles II, James II, William III, Queen Anne, George I, and George II – were major investors, shareholders, and directors in the state-sponsored Company of Royal Adventurers Trading in Africa, the Royal African Company, and the South Sea Company.

Other investors included famed philosopher John Locke (who ironically championed the concept of natural rights) and Tobias Rustat a University of Cambridge benefactor whose bust is still displayed in the Chapel at Jesus College despite the college’s attempts to seek permission from an ecclesiastical court to remove it). Forty-five vicars from the Church of England and 24 directors and governors of the Bank of England were also investors. As the project’s lead researcher, William Pettigrew, has stated, slavery was not a footnote in British history – it helped shape the country.

Some have expressed surprise at the extent of the involvement. The question worth asking is this: why, 193 years after emancipation, is the true scale of Britain’s role in chattel slavery still not fully understood in Britain?

Pre-existing evidence

The findings are not surprising to scholars in the Caribbean and the wider diaspora. Eighty-two years ago, Eric Williams, the Trinidadian scholar who later became prime minister, argued in Capitalism and Slavery that profits from chattel enslavement “financed the Industrial Revolution” in Britain. Williams, showed how manufacturing towns and industries, including banking, shipbuilding, insurance and warehousing, were integrated into colonial trade, as were some families.

The Nigerian scholar Joseph Inikori, in Africans and the Industrial Revolution in England, has shown that these linkages provided the scaffolding for Britain’s industrial advancement. During the 2007 Commons debate marking the Bicentenary of the Abolition of the Slave Trade, William Hague pointedly stated that: “William Pitt, when he was prime minister, said 80% of British overseas income was derived from our West Indian colonies.” Pitt should know.

Caribbean scholars, among them Williams, Sir Arthur Lewis, CLR James, Walter Rodney, Elsa Goveia, Kamau Brathwaite, Hilary Beckles, Orlando Patterson, George Beckford and Verene Shepherd, have spent their professional careers exposing the magnitude of Britain’s involvement in the trafficking of enslaved Africans and its impact across the Caribbean archipelago. Plantation ledgers, deeds, wills and probate inventories, whether in repositories in the Caribbean, Britain, or across Europe, show the accumulation and transfer of mind-numbing wealth to Britain.

Ship records document the names of ship captains and owners as well as the sadistic violence inflicted on enslaved men, women and children. Those of us who have worked in these archives have spent our careers seeing the names of these monarchs, merchants, vicars, bankers, absentee owners and institutions written alongside the names of the enslaved men, women, and children they owned as “property”. The evidence is not new.

Wall of silence

The reception of the Register reveals much about British attitudes towards chattel slavery and how it is taught in schools (pdf) as well as raising questions about why Britain’s role in chattel slavery has not been fully realised.

The reason, Catherine Hall has argued, is the conscious effort to occlude the archives. Hall argued that forgetting a nation’s violent past is an active process, not an accident, and Britain’s began as soon as the trafficking in enslaved people was outlawed in 1807.

Thomas Clarkson’s history of the abolition campaign celebrated white humanitarian men and omitted Black and women abolitionists and the horrors of trafficking in enslaved people. Abolition of the trafficking in 1807 and emancipation of chattel slavery in 1833 were recast as proof of British liberty and virtue. At the same time, the newly freed people were forced into an unpaid “apprenticeship” while the government paid £20m – or 40% of Britain’s public expenditure – in compensation to the owners of enslaved people. What emerged was an amalgamation of institutions and social and cultural forces to create a wall of silence around the period of chattel enslavement, colonialism and its harmful legacies.

The reaction to the Register shows that what Hall described 13 years ago remains true today. The real strength of the Register is that it will help break the wall of silence around Britain’s trafficking in enslaved Africans and “undo the forgetting”.

Nearly 4m records of enslaved people searchable online | Aamna Mohdin

Monarchs, MPs and merchants: the register laying bare Britain’s slave trading past | David Conn

Caribbean nations draft action plan to push UK to redress reparations over slavery | Natricia Duncan

Giving voice to a lost history: retracing the steps of the Black lives that shaped Manchester | Chris Osuh

King Charles III to acknowledge ‘darkest days’ of Britain’s colonial rule during Caribbean tour

Manchester | Did you know that 7 October is World Cotton Day? Created in 2019 by representatives from Benin, Burkina Faso, Chad and Mali, it aims to address the issues facing the cotton industry today while acknowledging its history. This year, the Legacies programme is co-hosting an event at the Science and History Museum including talks, workshops and live textile demonstrations.

Starting with the Guardian’s own history, Guardian journalists explore the legacies of enslavement and reparative justice around the world

after newsletter promotion

In the evening there will be a panel discussion featuring Duncan Ivison, the vice-chancellor of University of Manchester, Cleo Lake, the first black female lord mayor of Bristol, Adeola Adelakun, the co-founder of Black Creative Trailblazers, and artist Liam Hopkins, to discuss how World Cotton Day can help us work together to reflect on Manchester’s interwoven history. You can book free tickets for the evening event here. Across the city there will also be heritage trails looking at how Manchester’s history is woven into the streets. Keisha Thompson, Legacies of Enslavement programme manager

Sea Islands | October is Gullah Geechee Cultural Heritage Awareness Month, a time to honour the culture and history of the descendants of enslaved West Africans in the south-east US who retained their unique heritage. Started in 2014, the heritage month includes conferences, festivals, workshops, and film showings in the four states that encompass the Gullah Geechee Cultural Heritage Corridor: Georgia, Florida, North and South Carolina. Visitors come from all over the world to attend celebrations throughout the month.

The events kicked off with the Lowcountry Fish and Grits music festival on Hilton Head Island on 3 October with performers including Latrese Bush, a Gullah Geechee woman from Bluffton, who sung the jazz, soul and gospel music that defined her upbringing. The Georgia-based Gullah Geechee Ring Shouters also displayed the ring shout, a traditional ritual rooted in West African culture and Christianity. While moving counterclockwise in a circle, the performers stomp their feet, clap their hands and sing in call and response. The month will culminate with Charleston’s Grand Gullah-Geechee Hoodoo Ball in Mount Pleasant, South Carolina, on 31 October, where guests will be treated to Gullah Geechee cuisine, live music, spirituality and dance performances. Melissa Hellmann, US race and equity senior reporter

Jamaica | The global reparations movement has been gaining phenomenal pace, shifting from the fringes of international debate to the centre of diplomatic discussions. Caribbean governments have managed to push reparations on to the agendas of the Commonwealth, the UN, and in the parliaments and public domains of countries in the region, as well in the UK.

But within this broader push, one of the often overlooked elements is the call for repatriation – the right of people of African descent to return to the continent from which their ancestors were taken. For decades, repatriation was dismissed as symbolic or utopian. But African governments including Ghana, Sierra Leone and Liberia are now developing concrete pathways to residency and citizenship for diaspora Africans.

As the Commonwealth leaders summit approaches in November, repatriation is likely to become a prominent part of the conversation about what meaningful repair should look like, and how the Caribbean envisions its relationship with Africa. Natricia Duncan, Caribbean correspondent

I really enjoyed reading Dominoes by London-based actor, playwright and novelist Phoebe McIntosh. It’s a smart and witty romance that offers a powerful reflection on the legacies of enslavement. The story follows Layla as she prepares to marry her sweetheart Andy, with whom she happens to share the same surname. Thanks to some sleuthing from Layla’s best friend, it emerges the couple also share a complex, unsettling history – threatening to derail their upcoming nuptials. Angela Foster, assistant editor

Manchester will host Barack Obama as part of Black History Month celebrations. The former US president will appear at Co-op Live on 15 October for an eagerly anticipated evening of conversation.

Meanwhile, the Booker prize-winning author Bernardine Evaristo will join acclaimed screenwriter Russell T Davies on 11 October at Manchester Literature Festival. Chris Osuh, community affairs correspondent

Pedro Sánchez is a master of the political comeback. But calling a snap election in Spain may be a gamble too far

The Guardian Tue, 06 Oct 2026 14:57:19 GMT

A thriving economy, a model green transition, social advances – Spain’s PM shouldn’t be in trouble. Yet he is, and it’s a lesson for progressives everywhere

To progressives across the west, Spain has been a rare glimmer of hope in a world where far-right parties are increasingly entering government. Under Pedro Sánchez, who became prime minister in 2018, the country has combined a post-Covid economic boom with a bold green energy transition programme, and a pro-immigration stance with a principled opposition to the war agenda of Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu. Yet, at the end of next month, this rare beacon of democratic progress could fall.

On Monday Sánchez called a snap general election, set for 29 November, after two decrees to address the country’s housing crisis were voted down in the lower chamber by politicians from rightwing parties. Speaking from the staircase of the Moncloa palace, Sánchez admitted that his government had not achieved all it had set out to do. “Many injustices remain to be corrected … particularly regarding inequality in public services and access to housing,” he said, adding: “To do more, we need to renew and expand public support.”

Sánchez attempted to pass the legislation after tens of thousands took to the streets to protest against the housing crisis, setting up camps reminiscent of the country’s 15-M anti-austerity movement and the global Occupy movement of 2011. But this explosion of popular anger has been long in the making. According to Spain’s national public opinion research institute Centro de Investigaciones Sociológicas (CIS), housing has been the country’s top preoccupation since the end of 2024, as a growing number of people struggle to pay rent.

In the latest gamble of his long career as master of the political comeback, Sánchez hopes to ride the wave of popular mobilisation to turn public attention away from the Ceuta immigration crisis of July, which rightwing opponents exploited as a demonstration of the government’s failures, and focus attention on the housing crisis, an issue where the left holds stronger political ground.

But this time it will be hard to convince Spaniards that with a new lease of life, the progressive coalition government will solve an issue it had promised to address a long time ago.

Sánchez’s troubles provide useful lessons for progressives all over the world about the difficulties of translating policy achievements into a solid base of political support. They are also a reminder that – as championed by New York’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani – addressing the affordability crisis rather than promising abstract economic growth is of more significance to voters.

In the US midterm election campaign, Republicans are struggling because of rising prices at the gas pump, while in Brazil, rightwing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro just rode to an impressive result in the first round of the presidential elections partly due to discontent with living conditions and household pressures. In Spain, Sánchez’s government is facing similar concerns about affordability, which are obfuscating an otherwise impressive macro-economic performance.

Indeed, seen from the outside, Sánchez’s Spain may appear to be a dazzling political success. The country, which in the 2010s was derided as part of the European Piigs – a term coined to mock Portugal, Ireland, Italy, Greece and Spain as the eurozone’s weakest economies – has become an economic powerhouse. In the years after the Covid pandemic, Spain’s GDP grew at a rate of around 3%, while France, Germany, the UK and Italy grew at a miserly 1% or less.

Spain is also held up as a model of successful green transition, with renewables now generating close to 60% of the country’s power, which has also kept energy bills low and helped insulate the country from the energy shocks caused by international crises. Spain, enabled by significant Chinese investment, is also surprisingly becoming the leading European hub for electric car production, to the dismay of some of the country’s traditional allies.

To these economic and environmental achievements add the significant social improvements achieved under Sánchez, exemplified by the rise in the minimum wage from €736 to €1,184 per month since 2018.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Yet despite these measurable successes, Sánchez’s centre-left coalition is now trailing the right by about 7 percentage points in national polling. That’s partly because while minimum wages have increased, median wages have remained relatively stagnant. But it is real estate that Sánchez’s government has been judged as failing to deliver: during its eight years in power, house prices have risen by an estimated 50%, with rents rising by over 40%.

As climbing the housing ladder becomes prohibitive, a growing number of young people in Spain are forced to pay extortionate rents. This is acutely felt in large urban areas, where the presence of tourists and digital nomads further increases rents, forcing out local residents; this is enabled by private equity firms, who purchase entire blocks to expel local inhabitants in order to create Airbnbs. Sánchez’s government has repeatedly promised to take action on these issues, but its measures have been thwarted by political gridlock or otherwise proven indecisive, partly due to fear of alienating homeowners and antagonising international finance.

If Spain’s centre-left coalition falls, the country could be left with an alliance of the mainstream conservative Partido Popular and the far-right party Vox. It would be the most rightwing Spanish government since Francisco Franco’s dictatorship. The lesson for progressives everywhere is clear: economic growth and ambitious reform will count for little unless working people feel the benefits in their daily lives.

Paolo Gerbaudo is a senior researcher at the faculty of political science and sociology of Complutense University in Madrid and a lead researcher at the Alameda Institute

Reform MP raises concerns about second homes – then buys one for £800,000

The Guardian Tue, 06 Oct 2026 14:41:17 GMT

Sarah Pochin bought Anglesey property two days after writing to minister about impact of second home ownership on rural communities

A Reform UK MP bought an £800,000 second home on a picturesque Welsh island two days after raising concerns in parliament about the impact of second homes on rural communities.

Sarah Pochin completed the purchase of a Grade-II listed property on the southern coast of Anglesey (Ynys Môn).

The MP for Runcorn and Helsby in Cheshire bought the property two days after she submitted a written question on 15 June to the housing minister Matthew Pennycook, according to the Will Hayward newsletter.

Pochin asked Pennycook “what assessment he has made of the potential impact of second home ownership on housing availability in coastal and rural communities”.

Pennycook replied: “Excessive concentrations of short-term lets and second homes impact on the availability and affordability of homes for local residents to buy and rent, as well as local services.”

According to the Land Registry, the purchase was made jointly with Pochin’s husband, Jonathan. The couple, who have submitted plans at Anglesey county council for changes to the property, retain ownership of another home in Cheshire.

Anglesey, famous for its coastline and ancient Celtic and Roman history, has become a hotspot for second home ownership in recent years. The island had the largest increase in holiday home users among local authorities from 2011 to 2021, according to the Office for National Statistics.

As of March 2026, Cyngor Sir Ynys Môn (Anglesey county council) recorded 2,635 furnished homes that were not an individual’s sole or main residence.

The local authority introduced a council tax premium on second homes in 2016. Initially set at 25% on top of the standard rate, it has since risen incrementally to the current 100% premium, to address local housing affordability.

Critics have argued that second homes and short-term holiday rentals can adversely affect local communities by reducing housing supply, inflating property prices and putting a strain on infrastructure.

Robin Wyn Williams, the deputy leader of Cyngor Sir Ynys Môn, said: “It has a longer-term impact on things like the provision of schools and other local services. That community spirit gets killed off. We’ve seen it in the likes of Rhosneigr, where it appears to have lost its identity because it is very much a village of second homes in the main these days.

“It tends to be more middle-aged and older people, and that then can bring with it pressures on our adult services. Obviously then that has an impact on the situation whereby families are being displaced from certain parts of the island. And then you just end up in a situation where you have fewer children in the community and that has an impact on schools.”

Pochin became Reform UK’s first female MP after winning the Runcorn and Helsby byelection in May 2025. She previously served as a Conservative mayor and a local councillor on Cheshire East council, latterly as an independent, before joining Nigel Farage’s party.

Reform did not respond to a request for comment.

‘My poetry won me asylum’: Cecilia Vicuña on exile life in ‘sad’ Britain after Pinochet’s coup

The Guardian Tue, 06 Oct 2026 14:28:38 GMT

Five decades after convincing judges she’d be killed if she returned to Chile, the artist is back with a politically charged retrospective in the country she grew to love

Cecilia Vicuña was 24 when she first arrived in London. She had come from Santiago on a British Council scholarship to study at the Slade School of Art, and her stay was supposed to be so brief that she didn’t even unpack her suitcase.

Then, in September 1973, General Augusto Pinochet’s military coup overthrew Chile’s democratically elected president, Salvador Allende. Vicuña was one of a handful of Chilean students in London immediately expelled from their universities and expected to leave Britain. At a Home Office hearing, her pro-bono lawyers argued that she would be killed if she returned to Chile, and showed the judges her recently published art and poetry book, Saborami, which documented the aftermath of the coup. The judges granted her asylum.

“It’s really one of the main stories of my life,” Vicuña says now. “How my poetry came to protect my wellbeing.”

We meet on Zoom, with Vicuña in her apartment in New York, where she has lived since 1980. Wearing a knitted hat, she speaks softly and sagely, like a shaman offering advice – small and fragile, but with big, existential ideas about life and art.

More than half a century since her arrival in London, Vicuña, now 78 and one of Latin America’s most renowned artists, poets and feminist activists, is returning – specifically to Stepney Green, where she lived as a young artist – for her first major UK exhibition, at the Whitechapel Gallery. She has mixed feelings. “In a way, I’m going back to relieve my original experience,” she says.

The London Vicuña encountered in the 1970s was very different from the image of “swinging London” exported around the world. “When you walked down the streets, people were extremely poor,” she says. “People had to put a penny to heat their little apartments. There was a feeling of sadness, of not being able to realise one’s full potential.”

But she began meeting exiles from failed revolutions across Africa, the Middle East, Greece and Latin America, found a thriving art community, and published her first book in London after it had been censored in Chile. “I grew to love it,” she says. “But I also understood that true creative energy was on the other side of the continent.”

The new exhibition, Living Threads, brings together six decades of Vicuña’s work across painting, textile, photography, installation and film. It also returns to her political life as a young artist speaking at trade union gatherings on the top floor of English pubs. A room is dedicated to Artists for Democracy, which Vicuña co-founded in 1974 with Guy Brett, David Medalla and John Dugger in solidarity with Chile and other liberation struggles worldwide, bringing together never-before-seen documents, photographs and printed materials.

“There have been a few attempts to tell this story without my presence,” she says. “The story has been told as if I was a visitor to the organisation.”

Her involvement began after artist Conrad Atkinson invited her to an ICA discussion about artists’ rights and sales. Shocked that people were discussing money while artists were being killed in Chile, Vicuña stood up to speak. Brett, Medalla and Dugger, sitting at the back, sent her a note afterwards. “I proposed that we should found an organisation for democracy,” she says.

“England was the first country to acknowledge Pinochet as the new leader of Chile,” she adds. “This violent overthrow of democratic government was celebrated by Britain.” Yet the same country had granted her the legal protection to stay: “The place where the defence of the law was powerful enough to grant me that.”

The exhibition also brings back a painful part of that period: the work Vicuña lost. During her exile, she left pieces with friends in London, Chile and Bogotá; one trunk contained 400 sculptures, eventually thrown away.

“I was so devalued as a person, as an artist,” she says. “To be a dark little South American woman, even in Latin America, is to be in a position of pain, disrespect and inappreciation.” Some have since been recreated from memory and photographs – not reconstruction, she says, but something closer to reincarnation. “It’s the stories and images that want to live again.”

That idea of disappearance runs through the two forms Vicuña is best known for. She began making what she calls precarios in the 1960s from sticks, feathers, leaves, stones, bones and debris – deliberately fragile, impermanent works, a response to standing as a 17-year-old on a Chilean beach, in the shadow of an oil refinery built over an ancestral burial ground, suddenly aware of the relationship between sea, wind and objects. The only surviving precario from her London years is in the show.

“To preserve and disappear are not opposite things,” she says. “Awareness of disappearance is what needs to be preserved. It’s the belief that life itself is poetry, and poetry is life. Disappearance is regeneration.”

Her quipus, meanwhile, are made from knotted and unspun fibre, drawing on an ancient Andean system of recording and communication. Vicuña has spent decades reimagining the form, including in Quipu Menstrual, a towering installation in deep red that will be shown at Whitechapel.

Her work has increasingly turned towards ecology. She has worked with water for more than 50 years, and she describes the current situation in Chile as both devastating and potentially transformative.

“Latin America is the most destroyed of all continents: 95% of its biodiversity has been destroyed already, because people continue to vote for leaders who open the gates to this violent extraction. They call them resources, but it’s not resources. It’s life.” But she points to hope: “Reports show that young Chileans see their future as professional defenders of the land. That, to me, is the most beautiful sign that this shift is still possible.”

The current shift to the right in Chile, she argues, doesn’t simply repeat 1973. Back then, she says, those seeking justice, democracy and freedom of expression were the majority and were “violently crushed by foreign intervention. Now, people are willingly choosing to be aligned with the forces that deny global warming and deny people’s rights, women’s rights, the rights of nature.”

I ask her if democracy has become more fragile. “I think, in truth, democracy was never really practised in the west.” She points to Allende’s Chile as one example of participatory democracy, and argues that many indigenous societies offered earlier models that were destroyed by colonisation.

The internet, she adds, was another squandered chance: a tool for universal access to knowledge that became a place of surveillance and misinformation. “Each chance that the people of this planet have had to open up to the potential of democracy a destructive force comes in to stop it.”

She sees artificial intelligence through a similar lens. Her concern is that AI is controlled by private companies for profit, while governments have failed to regulate what she sees as an existential threat.

“Now AI has been trained to train itself, and as soon as that happens, it started to behave in a destructive way. Powerful people are saying the existential threat to humanity is a hoax. I have the feeling most people in the world don’t feel it’s a hoax at all. So where is the democratic will of this planet? Is it crushed or prevented?”

Vicuña spent decades operating relatively under the radar before a burst of institutional recognition began with her inclusion in Documenta in 2017, aged 69 – she was the youngest artist in a group that included women in their 80s and 90s. “It was the event that changed my life,” she says. “My work was acknowledged for the first time as a work that had meaning and importance.” The museum told her visitors came looking for “the red thing” – her quipu. Since then she has won the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement at the Venice Biennale, received a Guggenheim survey, and completed a Tate Modern Turbine Hall commission.

That 2022 work, Brain Forest Quipu, featured huge mobiles of fraying wool, knotted rope and debris mudlarked from the Thames, an elegy to lost language and wilful destruction; the Guardian’s five-star review called it the most moving Turbine Hall commission in years.

She sees the greater visibility of women, and of Latin American, Asian and African artists, in major museums as a genuine shift – but remains cautious. “Will that translate to women being valued as equals? We will see.”

For now, she is returning to the neighbourhood where the young artist she once was became an exile and activist. The Whitechapel exhibition brings together works that survived, works that disappeared, and works that have been remade. “I do hope it will be healing,” she says.

Cecilia Vicuña: Living Threads is at the Whitechapel Gallery, London, from 7 October until 14 February

South Africa in running to stage Africa’s first Olympics as 2036 race hots up

The Guardian Tue, 06 Oct 2026 14:05:41 GMT

Qatar frontrunners of bidders, with India and Hungary

Turkey, Germany and Korea to present to IOC next month

South Africa is in the hunt to stage Africa’s first Olympics after it was named as one of seven countries that will formally present its case to host the 2036 Games in November.

However its bid, which would probably be spread across Cape Town, Johannesburg and Durban, is seen as a distinct outsider, with Qatar widely regarded as the frontrunner ahead of India and Hungary.

Turkey, Germany and South Korea make up the remaining countries that have been asked to present to the International Olympic Committee’s future bid committee next month, marking the first stage of a process that will end with a vote in 2029.

Qatar’s position at the top of the pecking order is partly down to the perceived strength of the bid and the fact that Asia will not have hosted a Games since Tokyo 2020. However a Doha Olympics would have to be moved from the Games’ traditional July-August slot due to the heat.

India is seen as the closest challenger, although its bid to host in Ahmedabad is seen to have slipped back during the past 18 months.

As the Guardian reported last year, the Indian bid was given a wake-up call when it visited Lausanne in the summer of 2025, with concerns raised about mismanagement and governance issues at the Indian Olympic Association, the lack of detail in the bid and the country’s dismal performance in the Paris Games.

If there is to be another strong challenger to Qatar, it could come from Hungary. Its bid, which is said to include not only Budapest but the Austrian capital, Vienna, and the Slovakian capital, Bratislava, is very well regarded. However it is unclear whether the new government in ­Hungary cares as much about hosting the Olympics as the previous prime minister, Viktor Orban.

At this stage most of the other bids are being seen as placeholders for the 2040 Olympics. That includes Germany, given the ­potentially tricky optics surrounding a centenary Games.

In a handbook published on Tuesday, the IOC said the bids would be based on a number of technical factors – including the venues and athlete experience, political and public support, and the ability to deliver a great Games and a long-term legacy – as well as their vision for the Olympics.

“I was fortunate to compete at five Olympic Games, across four continents. Each had their own character,” said the IOC president, Kirsty Coventry. “Each host brought something unique through its people, its culture and the way it chose to stage the Games. But wherever the Games take place, one thing must never change: athletes have to be at the heart of everything we do.

“As an athlete, you spend years working to make your Olympic dream come true. The experience you have when you finally reach the Olympic Games stays with you for the rest of your life. That is why, for every future host, delivering the best possible experience for the athletes must always be the starting point.”

Other countries interested in bidding for 2036 have until the end of October to confirm their intention before nominations close. The IOC said it would conduct feasibility assessments by March 2027 and in December 2028 its executive board would open a “targeted dialogue with a select number of preferred hosts”. In the summer of 2029, a vote will then be taken to select who will stage the 2036 Games.

How I Shop with Jonathan Van Ness: ‘The price you pay for impulsivity is years later’

The Guardian Tue, 06 Oct 2026 14:00:16 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Always wondered what everyday stuff celebrities buy, where they shop for food and the basics they scrimp on? The Queer Eye legend talks handmade gifts, secondhand shopping and bag obsessions with the Filter

Don’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

Jonathan Van Ness rose to fame as the beauty and hair care expert on the multi-award-winning show Queer Eye. Their eight-year tenure as one of the “Fab Five” presenters ended when the show’s final season aired in January 2026. A hairstylist by trade, they have their own cruelty-free, vegan haircare brand, JVN Hair.

Beyond TV and beauty work, Van Ness has continued a career as a comedian, writer and podcast presenter. They have written five books, including the New York Times bestselling memoir Over the Top and their latest young adult novel, which they wrote alongside Julie Murphy, Let Them Stare. Van Ness continues to be an advocate for the LGBTQIA+ community, working on campaigns with The Trevor Project and Planned Parenthood.

A spray tan at Sugared + Bronzed.

The farmers’ market. I live two blocks away from it in New York and go there all the time.

This obnoxiously hard-to-find twilly [narrow silk scarf] also from Hermès. The queen of my heart, my very best girl[friend], wanted one so bad that I went to 15 Hermès stores in like 15 cities and finally got it; it was the best Christmas present ever.

My mum made this stunning throw blanket with the nicest, thickest yarn, but I don’t want to use it because I have five cats who would slice it with their claws. I begged her to make me a duplicate, but she made me the world’s skinniest one – not as nice. I was like: “Mom, that’s not as big and chic as the first one.” She’s like: “Use the one I made you! I’m not knitting you another!” She’s a really crafty, fierce artist.

EBay. I think resale is really interesting; I’m particularly obsessed with bags. It’s a little bit nerve-racking because who authenticated it? But I do like the prices, and I’ve seen so many gorgeous pieces on there that do check out.

In England, I’ve got to say Space NK – I love to buy Skin Rocks by Caroline Hirons products there, especially the eye cream.

Skin Rocks the eye cream, 15ml

My Mophie portable phone charger.

Mophie PowerStation 5K

A house in Texas. I was in this era where I was like, “I must have more space”, but then it was way too much space – I bought at the top of the market, and then real estate in Austin tanked. It taught me that sometimes the price you pay for impulsivity is years later.

A grocery delivery service called Gopuff, for non-farmers’ market staples like Cinnamon Toast Crunch, milk, and kitty litter.

I am obsessed with Hanro. It’s stupidly expensive, like $50 (about £38) for a pair of underwear, but those bitches hold up. I think I’ve had some of them for like five, six years, and they are very well made.

Hanro cotton essentials pants, two-pack

JVN Hair notwithstanding, what I do like that’s under £20 is CeraVe body moisturiser. I suffer from psoriasis and, in a really bad flare, it is gentle, so nurturing and doesn’t sting.

CeraVe moisturising cream, 454g

after newsletter promotion

For £200, fragrance from D’Orsay. Oh. My. God. One I would choose right now is Vanilla Affair.

D’Orsay Vanilla Affair extrait de parfum, 90ml

My husband wants a 50cm Hermès Kelly Relax bag the soccer guys were carrying during the World Cup. He says he wants one that looks as if he filled it up with rocks and then threw it down the stairs, a bit [beaten up], but that’s kind of hard to find.

Protein Pop-Tarts. I’m so addicted to them, I can’t keep a box in my house for more than two days. (Though it says “protein” in huge letters, it’s just 5g per tart – or 10g per suggested serving of two tarts – instead of the regular 2g).

Protein Pop-Tarts Slammin’ Strawberry, box of eight

Also, the fizzy tail Percy Pigs. Target just started carrying them, so now my husband isn’t hiding them from me. Before, I would be like: “Why are there 40 packages of Percy Pigs in the back of my sock drawer?”

Percy Pig Phizzy Pigtails, 170g

In a Breville (marketed under the Sage brand in the UK) coffee machine – an americano with a splash of cold milk.

Sage Oracle Jet automatic bean-to-cup coffee machine

Bags. Being socialised as a boy growing up, purses were for girls, so my mum let me carry around one of her bags in secret when my dad wasn’t around.

Alongside Hermès, I love bags by the Row, and also Ikea shopping bags. Do I quit my life and start a bag resale business, where I just find people’s dream bags?

Taxis: I ride my bike [instead], or use public transport. In London, I’m up on that tube or on Lime bikes. I was spending so much money on taxis, I was like, girl, I don’t need to do all that. I love to bike; I’ll just get a helmet.

My birthday present to myself this year. I found a black lizard Hermès Kelly Sellier from 1987, the year I was born, which has its original hardware, at Sotheby’s. It’s [so pristine] I think someone bought it in ’87, wore it twice, put it back in the box and thought: “I don’t like that thing.” In order for me to convince my business manager that this is OK, I had to sell however many bags it takes – which was seven – so it was not coming out of my income. I told myself the famous lie when I’m buying something too expensive: “This can be my everyday bag. I’m just gonna beat it up, it’s gonna be totally worth it.” But then I get it home, and I’m like: “I could never!”

Who owns ‘brain rot’?: inside the international legal drama over a beloved meme

The Guardian Tue, 06 Oct 2026 14:00:16 GMT

Copyright law in the US only applies to human-made creations, but AI characters like Tung Tung Tung Sahur are challenging that

One of the most beloved characters in an absurdist genre of online video content has become the center of an international legal battle that could determine where human creativity ends and artificial intelligence begins.

Tung Tung Tung Sahur, also known as Triple T, was created in 2025 by an Indonesian teen who goes by the username Noxa, using OpenAI’s image-generation tool. Based on a kentongan – a type of drum used to wake south-east Asian Muslims for their pre-dawn meal during Ramadan – the character is an anthropomorphized version of the instrument with a broad smile and a vacant stare. He sits under the umbrella of “Italian brain rot” internet videos.

Since his creation, Triple T has become a global sensation: YouTube and TikTok host dozens of videos with hundreds of millions of views starring the character. People dress like Triple T at cosplay conventions and lovingly create fan art and animations of the stick-like creature, and his likeness appears on plushies, perfume and stickers.

The character has generated a great deal of money and stands to create much more – he will soon be joining Fortnite as a skin. But who should benefit from this virality?

That question is at the heart of a lawsuit filed in the US district court’s northern district of California, where a games company is suing the French creative agency Mementum, which represents Noxa, over the right to use Triple T as a character in a popular Roblox game.

Eben Jeda, co-founder of Mementum Lab, said he started the agency with the goal of modernizing economic infrastructure around internet-native works, the creators of which are often completely cut out of any resulting profit.

“Brain rot is one of the first highly visible manifestations of a much larger transformation: internet native creativity can now become global almost instantly, while the people who originate it can remain economically invisible,” he said.

Opponents argue no one person should own a meme whose ultimate value has been amplified by the online collective. Fabian Mosele, a self-described “Italian brain rot expert” who has made several Tung Tung Tung Sahur videos, said they see brain rot as collectively owned.

“There are a ton of creators who made these characters come to life,” Mosele said. “Before, they were really just images. Having been part of making the virality of these characters, to gatekeep it to the original prompter of this character doesn’t seem right.”

Tung Tung Tung Sahur is one of many characters that have emerged as part of the Italian brain rot genre of meme – a universe of strange, AI-generated characters beloved by generation Alpha and younger members of gen Z. These include the likes of Ballerina Cappuccina (a ballet dancer with a coffee cup for a head), Tralalero Tralala (a shark wearing sneakers), and a variety of other intentionally bizarre creations.

Capitalizing on the virality of these mascot-esque characters, video game company Do Big Studios released a game populated by recognizable personae in May 2025 called “Steal a Brainrot”, which quickly became one of the most-played games within Roblox, where users can create minigames.

But in September 2025, Spyder Games LLC and Speedy Simulator Gaming LLC – the owners of Do Big – received a cease and desist letter from Mementum regarding the use of Tung Tung Tung Sahur in the game. Do Big initially pulled the character and attempted to negotiate a resolution with Mementum, but ultimately Spyder and Speedy sued the company instead, stating in a complaint: “Mementum’s claimed rights do not exist. Under established law, copyright protection requires human authorship, and AI-generated material does not qualify.”

Copyright law in the United States applies only to human-made creations – but AI is challenging the interpretation of that rule. A 2025 report from the United States Copyright Office declared that copyright protects “original expression” in work created “by a human author” even if the work also includes AI-generated material, but that it “does not extend to purely AI-generated material, or material where there is insufficient human control over the expressive elements”.

The copyright office’s report does not offer a clear standard for ownership of creations that involve AI: “Whether human contributions to AI-generated outputs are sufficient to constitute authorship must be analyzed on a case-by-case basis.”

Do Big argues that, in the case of Tung Tung Tung Sahur, the level of human intervention in the character’s creation is not sufficient to claim ownership. Court documents filed by Mementum in a separate trademark-related dispute in France show that Tung Tung Tung Sahur was created over the course of 15 minutes using seven prompts before he achieved his final form. The prompts included basic instructions like, “draw a pentungan sahur with a face and legs”, then “human face”, and “no hands, legs like a human, and a human face”.

“We are not claiming in this case that AI-assisted work can never be owned by anybody,” said Aaron Moss, a copyright lawyer representing Do Big through the firm Mitchell Silberberg & Knupp LLP. “In a case where somebody makes real creative choices, there is human authorship that is subject to protection. But it’s our position that sparse prompts – typing in a few words and picking [the image] you like – does not constitute human authorship.”

after newsletter promotion

The blurry nature of authorship in the age of AI is not the only complicating factor in the case – the global reach of online content also makes enforcement difficult. An Italian brain rot character that was created by a TikTok user in Indonesia and largely popularized in Latin America is being claimed by a French company in a California courthouse. Jeda said that as a French company, Mementum does not “view this question exclusively through an American legal lens”.

Case in point: Mementum issued a takedown request under the EU’s Digital Services Act, requesting the removal of Tung Tung Tung Sahur from Do Big’s Steal a Brainrot game, which was successful. Mementum then countersued in the United States for trademark infringement. The company does not yet hold a trademark for Triple T in the United States, but in some cases trademark infringement can be argued before registration.

“Our client is pursuing a global strategy on all of this,” said Steven Stein, a partner at Greenberg Glusker, the US law firm representing Mementum Lab. “It is less about approaching it from a copyright law standpoint, and more about approaching it from the standpoint of – in this new wild west, where works are created with the involvement of AI, what can you do to make it so they are protectable under intellectual property law?”

How the lawsuit plays out will come down to a complicated, international web of legal dealings surrounding intellectual property laws – one that could have major implications moving forward, said James Grimmelmann, a professor at Cornell Tech and Cornell law school.

“This is the kind of case that could do one of two things: we could get a court decision that tells us, in a concrete setting, what is copyrightable and what isn’t when AI is involved,” he said. “It could also start establishing best practices and widespread norms on how people use AI.”

Such best practices could include better documenting creation processes, including what prompts are used to create characters. The prompt used to create Tung Tung Tung Sahur is at the center of this story – both in the legal case, where documentation of the process was revealed in pre-trial discovery – and online, where speculation over how Triple T was created has repeatedly gone viral.

Adam Aleksic, a content creator who has made multiple videos on the topic, said the frenzy over trying to back-solve the origin of the character reflects the mythological status and quasi-religiosity of brain rot characters.

“There’s this idea of origination when it comes to Tung Tung Tung Sahur – somehow out of the void, some memes are able to emerge into the cultural forefront, into our collective mainstream discourse,” he said.

The collective creation of such characters, which made brain rot popular in the first place, is exactly what makes it difficult to claim an origin for Tung Tung Tung Sahur, legally and culturally. When it comes to Tung Tung Tung Sahur, even speaking the name of the character has now come to inherently reference the absurdity central to brain rot, similar to how “skibidi toilet” became shorthand for “being really online”.

It is perhaps fitting, then, that of all of the Italian brain rot characters, the hero who has most come to represent virality itself has become a lightning rod for this kind of copyright battle.

“That’s the thing about archetypes – they are empty vehicles for you to project your expectations, desires, or narratives on to,” Aleksic said. “Triple T is a tool for you to tell your narrative, broadly, across the entire internet. That’s what memes do – they are a way for us to create our own stories in a time when it feels like our stories are meaningless.”

F1 drivers face ‘unhealthy’ Singapore air as ‘super’ El Niño fuels wildfire haze

The Guardian Tue, 06 Oct 2026 13:57:24 GMT

F1 circus greeted by smoky skies before this Sunday’s GP

Pollution affects reaction times like ‘alcoholic beverage’

Singapore’s Formula One night race is an annual opportunity for the city-state to showcase its dazzling, illuminated skyline. But this year the lights of the country’s many skyscrapers will shine a little less brightly.

The south-east Asian nation is shrouded in a thick haze that has drifted from huge wildfires in neighbouring Indonesia, with Singapore now among the world’s most polluted cities.

Haze is a recurring problem in Singapore during Indonesia’s dry season, but conditions have worsened this year as a “super” El Niño exacerbates fires across parts of Sumatra and Kalimantan.

“Rainfall across the region has been about 80% below normal since June, fuelling the most intense fire season in over a decade,” said Wang Jingyu, an assistant professor at Singapore’s National Institute of Education at Nanyang Technological University.

Air quality levels in Singapore were classified as “unhealthy” on Tuesday by the country’s National Environment Agency and F1’s travelling circus will be greeted by smoky skies when it arrives from Kuala Lumpur following Sunday’s eventful race at Sepang.

The polluted conditions are not expected to cause any disruption to the racing schedule this weekend, but an FIA spokesperson said that “there is a contingency in place” if the haze worsens and there “may be some restrictions on outdoor activity”, although those are unlikely to apply to members of the paddock and would instead focus on “entertainment activities”.

The organisers of the Singapore night race said they will ensure the availability of N95 masks on site if required and will “work closely with the relevant agencies” to make any decisions regarding the race weekend if the haze causes “visibility, public health or operational issues”.

The polluted air will add another challenge for drivers racing around the Marina Bay Street Circuit, already regarded as one of the toughest events on the F1 calendar because of its high humidity and tight, twisting track.

Chris Carlsten, a professor of medicine at the University of British Columbia and an expert in the effects of air pollution on physiology, said prolonged exposure to the haze during the race could affect drivers’ cognitive performance.

In one study, participants spent two hours in conditions with high levels of air pollution before completing a series of cognitive tests, including assessments of their reaction times. “Our findings show that the pollution effect is similar to that of an alcoholic beverage,” Carlsten said.

The haze could also affect the drivers’ pre-race preparations, said Chris Tyler, a reader in environmental physiology at the University of Roehampton who has worked with F1 drivers including Oscar Piastri and Carlos Sainz. Drivers often exercise outdoors to acclimatise to the Singapore heat in the run-up to the race, but Tyler warned that “these are the sorts of environments where prolonged exposure to the pollution over a number of days could be somewhat detrimental”.

Lewis Hamilton received similar advice in 2019, when the Singapore Grand Prix was last held in hazy conditions. The seven-time world champion said he had been advised not to go running outside in the days leading up to the race. Carlsten said he would advise all drivers to wear masks if the air quality remains poor, allowing them to “keep their lungs clean” before the race.

after newsletter promotion

While the murky air is currently shrouding Singapore’s striking skyline, it should not obscure the drivers’ view as they weave their way through the illuminated city streets this weekend. The FIA said it has “no concerns” about visibility. A Formula One spokesperson said: “There is absolutely no risk to the event and the conditions where the event is taking place are not at any level of concern.”

George Russell’s dwindling championship hopes have been dealt a further blow as he is set to start this week’s Singapore Grand Prix from the rear of the grid.

Russell’s heartbreaking power-unit failure in the closing stages of Sunday’s Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia left him a whopping 84 points adrift of team-mate Kimi Antonelli with seven rounds left to run. It is now understood that the 28-year-old Russell will need to take a new power unit this weekend which means he will exceed the limit on several components and the penalties are likely to leave him starting from the rear of the grid around the streets of Singapore. Antonelli won the Italian Grand Prix last month having taken a similar penalty and Russell will need something similarly miraculous. Press Association

There is also little indication that the teams are worried, with several saying they have made no changes to their plans. Audi, competing in their first Singapore Grand Prix, said their drivers are trained to cope with a range of conditions, including “varying levels of air quality”.

For the hundreds of thousands of spectators expected to pack the circuit, however, the health implications are less straightforward. Unlike the drivers, who will spend only a relatively short period on track, fans could be exposed to the polluted air for several hours, particularly those attending the concerts and other events around the race.

Wang said short-term exposure to haze will generally cause only mild irritation in healthy people, probably in the form of a dry or sore throat, coughing or sneezing, but vulnerable groups, including elderly people, pregnant women and children, face a higher risk, with haze potentially aggravating pre-existing conditions such as asthma or triggering acute bronchitis.

Rain could offer some respite from the smoky conditions, with thundery showers forecast for Singapore on Friday and Saturday afternoon.

Is this the end of the British school photo?

The Guardian Tue, 06 Oct 2026 13:54:57 GMT

For generations, professional photographers have captured the country’s pupils in all their awkward glory. But an increasing number of parents are using AI to avoid paying them

Name: School photos.

Age: Around since Victorian times.

Future: Uncertain.

Surely not. The school photo is a grand British tradition, and one that shall not be given up without a fight. Yes, but have you seen the price of them recently?

No. My kids just had theirs done. It’s £20 for one photo, but if you want extras – for the shot to be turned into a magnet, keyring or snow globe, say – then prices can run up to about £100.

Changed my mind. No fighting. Let it end. Well, you could let it end, or you could just do what some parents have been doing.

Which is what? Getting the low-res preview shots from the photographer’s website, then using AI to upscale them and remove all the watermarks, as the Times reports.

Are people actually doing that? Oh yes, and apparently in such numbers that the photographers are starting to notice.

Or could it be that photos are so expensive that parents just aren’t buying them any more? Possibly, but the AI hack is everywhere too.

Those poor photographers. Well, yes and no. The average spend on these things is £25. A big primary school with two classes of 30 kids a year group could pull in £10,500, which does sound like a fortune. But once you knock off expenses such as printing, mounting, shipping, the cost of cameras and lights – and the school’s commission, don’t forget – the net take will be a lot less. And that’s before you get to wages …

And isn’t it immoral to take something without paying? That too. And besides, the school photograph is an important document of your youth. Where else are you going to keep a record of all your bad haircuts and adolescent skin complaints?

I dunno. Selfies? Yes, but they don’t have the hallmarks of a school photo. There’s no self-consciousness with a selfie, no sense of being trapped within an oppressive institution.

So we’re agreed that using AI is bad. Of course we’re agreed. Using AI for anything is bad, especially making posters for restaurants. Nobody wants to look at unconvincingly rendered AI images of plasticky-looking sausages. It isn’t appetising. When will people learn?

You’ve strayed from the subject a little. Fine. But the same goes for school photos. Using AI to remove watermarks is bad and will put people out of work, but next you’ll be using it to make your child’s teeth whiter and their hair shinier, and soon you’ll have a row of pictures of grinning deathless mannequins on your mantelpiece. Avoid it altogether, I say.

Do say: “Watch the birdie.”

Don’t say: “Say ‘ChatGPT’.”

Djokovic ends title drought with China Open triumph while Alcaraz claims glory in Japan

The Guardian Tue, 06 Oct 2026 13:35:03 GMT

Serb victorious after De Minaur retires injured

Alcaraz beats Lehecka for first title since February

Novak Djokovic capped an outstanding week at the China Open with his first title for nearly a year. The 39-year-old profited from the retirement of his final opponent, Alex de Minaur, after only one game of the second set to win a seventh title in Beijing and maintain his record of never having lost at the tournament.

The 7-6, 0-1 victory means Djokovic has won at least one title in each of the past 21 years, while he now has 102 tour level trophies overall. Both men reached the final without having to complete their matches on Monday – Djokovic thanks to the much-publicised disqualification of Daniil Medvedev, while De Minaur’s opponent Hubert Hurkacz pulled the plug because of injury.

Djokovic edged a very tight first set on a tie-break before the two men each took a medical timeout, but it came as a big surprise when De Minaur abruptly shook hands after winning the opening game of the second set. The Australian, who returned to court with strapping on his left thigh, said in his on-court interview: “I want to say sorry to all the amazing fans that came to watch this match. I didn’t want to finish like this.”

When Djokovic lost in the opening round of the US Open amid ongoing physical struggles, the sporting obituaries were being prepared, but the Serb has shown once again that writing him off would be premature.

Djokovic, who also defeated the top seed, Alexander Zverev, during his run, said: “It’s been 11 years since I played here last. I always have high expectations for myself and always want to visualise myself with the trophy, but particularly here in Beijing, the place where I’ve never lost.

“I was also quite aware that reality’s a little bit different these days. This year has been quite challenging for me, lots of ups and downs and physical and health issues, so I was just trying to find a good feeling on the court.

“I know that when I’m feeling well and striking the ball well I can still compete at the highest level. This week has been an evidence to that. I’m very proud. This trophy means much more than one trophy, one tournament.”

Earlier, Carlos Alcaraz defeated Jiri Lehecka in the final of the Japan Open to win his first individual title since February. Playing only his third tournament since returning from four and a-half months out with a wrist injury, Alcaraz recovered from a shaky start to defeat the Czech Lehecka 7-6, 6-4.

It is a second title in a row in the Japanese capital for Alcaraz, who showed patchy form at times but finished strongly. The Spaniard told Sky Sports: “I’m really happy to be able to lift a trophy again. It’s been a while and obviously it’s extra special after my injury.

“It was a tough week that I didn’t find my best tennis, my best level, but I did find the good solutions and I think that’s what matters in the end. I would say today was the best match of the week, or at least more consistent the level that I played, so I’m just really, really happy.”

Meanwhile, Jannik Sinner confirmed on Tuesday that he will be out for the rest of the year due to an injured knee.

“On ‌the advice of his ‌medical team, Jannik Sinner will follow a course of treatment for inflammation in his knee,” his ‌team said in a statement. “The decision has been ​made to have the treatment now to give Jannik the necessary ⁠time to recover before beginning ​preparations ​for 2027. As ​a result, Jannik ​will ‌be unable ​to ​compete again during the 2026 season.”

The west has a blinkered view of African music – and it’s hurting the whole continent’s culture

The Guardian Tue, 06 Oct 2026 13:07:37 GMT

The term Afrobeats is applied to all sorts of genres, flattening them into one. Artists, media and the music industry must do better at showing off the richness of African pop

In 2024, South African pop star Tyla won the best Afrobeats award at the MTV VMAs. Beaming in a yellow dress, she began her acceptance speech in a celebratory tone. “This is such a big moment for African music. The global impact of Water,” – her hit single – “proves that African music can be pop music.” But as the audience’s cheers swelled, she became more sombre, describing the moment as bittersweet. “There’s a tendency to group all African music as Afrobeats,” she continued. “Even though Afrobeats has opened so many doors for us, African music is so diverse. I come from South Africa, I represent amapiano”, referring to the country’s rolling, sensual dance subgenre. Her passionate entreaty notwithstanding, months later she’d reprise her win in the Afrobeats category of the American Music Awards.

Tyla is hardly the only African artist to rail against the Afrobeats tag. Tems has spurned the term, describing her music as a cocktail of “Afro, R&B, soul and alternative elements”. Likewise, Burna Boy prefers to call his music Afrofusion, a fitting characterisation of the smorgasbord of sounds that converge in his music. Wizkid, Ckay, King Promise and Davido have also chafed at the term Afrobeats, yet it persists and holds back African music.

The term emerged in the early 2010s as an umbrella label used to categorise contemporary dance music from west Africa, such as D’Banj’s Oliver Twist, spreading across European cities. London-based DJ Abrantee – per reporting in the Guardian – appended an “s” to Fela Kuti’s Afrobeat, creating a catch-all to market these sounds on radio and a burgeoning streaming marketplace. In recent years, however, as African music has exploded globally – underscored by hits like Water as well as Rema’s Calm Down or Moliy’s Shake It to the Max – Afrobeats has become the de facto label for all African pop, dance, rap, R&B, gospel, highlife and a sizeable amount of the continent’s alternative music scenes.

This might come across as a minor quibble to be slugged out by music buffs, and “Afrobeats” has undoubtedly been successful as a brute marketing strategy – when the UK Official Charts Company introduced a chart for African pop in 2020, it was named Afrobeats. But what happens when a western description becomes the dominant way a culture understands itself? Grammy award-winning Nigerian producer and singer Bloody Civilian, who heads out on tour with Tyla in October, says the label is “deeply limiting” and finds it “confusing that westerners continue to box the numerous ways Africans experiment with sound”.

Western popular music is allowed to exist across a wide spectrum of genres, while the music of an entire continent is routinely shoehorned into this single category. This does more than obscure its diversity; it flattens the nuances of distinct musical traditions and, in doing so, disconnects artists from those traditions. West African music, which has the biggest range of artists dubbed as Afrobeats, has also disproportionately felt the effects of the term: artists and producers from the region continue to synthesise new genres but these innovations are often treated as fodder for the larger Afrobeats machine, sustaining hype until they are discarded for the next shiny thing.

Consider Mr Eazi’s “banku music”, a sound synthesised from Nigerian pop and Ghanaian highlife. Mr Eazi, a Nigerian who had attended university in neighbouring Ghana, vaulted to continental fame in 2015. It is difficult to overstate how much his languid, yearning music riveted west Africa, and banku music had many of the characteristics of a genre in its own right: its laid-back tempo and distinctive four-stroke kick-drum pattern engendered a vibrant culture around the sound. Artists such as Runtown and Tekno adopted its sonic vocabulary and put their own spins on it, while university students across the region embraced Mr Eazi’s distinctive style of dress: a straw hat and dashiki.

In another world, banku music, like South Africa’s amapiano (which emerged around the same time), blossoms into a cultural force and perhaps spawns other genres. Instead, it wasn’t marketed to the west or contextualised locally as a distinct sound, so it faded into obscurity rather than developing into a culturally specific musical form. Countless other genres and styles have faced a similar fate: azonto, zanku, cruise, afropiano. Culture journalist Tiléwa Kazeem explains that international publications often find these nascent genres and styles to be “esoteric”. Afrobeats, he argues, “has not just obscured other genres but also affected their documentation”.

The west seems increasingly unwilling to engage with the richness of African music: the Afrobeats category was dropped from the MTV VMAs this year, but not on the grounds that the term was limiting, and now there is no African music category at all. But Kazeem adds that west African publications, used to the Afrobeats label, also hesitate to substantially document new genres and styles, similarly viewing them as esoteric.

New styles continue to emerge, ranging from the spiritually minded afro adura to mara, an explosive fusion of street pop and electronic music. But for them to take hold in the way, say, grunge or hyperpop have done in the west, “there has to be enough documentation, enough lore, enough intentionality around them,” says Dolapo Amusat, founder of Nigerian music and creative network WeTalkSound. “Mara is a good example of what that can look like when people who genuinely care about the sound start building substantial identities so these sounds can stand on their own.”

That responsibility falls on those marketing this music in the west, but also on the artists, and those in the African music and media industries. “There’s a tension between culture and commerce,” culture writer Dennis Ade Peter says. “Afrobeats artists and stakeholders routinely rail against the term, but still market their music as Afrobeats and validate awards and events where their music is described as such; it’s paradoxical.” As bell hooks noted in her essay collection Art on My Mind, Black people “must be held accountable when we do not make needed critical interventions” required to correct insular views around Black art.

Just as stalwarts like Kuti and King Sunny Adé were allowed to float new genres that continue to define contemporary African culture today, a new generation – who have proved themselves just as charismatic and musically adept – must be given the same opportunity.

Jailed Lego collector’s insurance scam highlights UK’s £1.3bn fraud problem

The Guardian Tue, 06 Oct 2026 13:07:23 GMT

Industry leaders say bogus claims rose 14% last year, pushing up premiums for all customers

An insurance fraudster who pocketed more than £14,000 for the supposed theft of Lego sets, fishing gear and gaming consoles was behind one of last year’s most high-profile bogus claims.

Investigators uncovered £1.34bn of fraud in 2025, a 14% increase on the year before, according to the Association of British Insurers (ABI).

The Lego fraudster, Matthew Johnson, was sentenced to 28 months in prison last December after an investigation by the City of London police’s insurance fraud enforcement department.

Johnson, of Misterton in Nottinghamshire, submitted false claims to Axa Insurance between May 2021 and January 2022, relating to alleged burglaries at properties in Shetland and Goole, East Yorkshire.

He claimed that high-value items had been stolen, including MacBooks, televisions, gaming consoles, fishing equipment and large quantities of collectible Lego sets. Johnson received more than £14,000 in insurance payouts across four claims. He was ordered by Nottingham crown court to repay the money.

Axa raised concerns after inconsistencies were identified in the documentation provided by Johnson, including repeated use of the same receipts across different claims and invoices that appeared to have been altered to match the policy address.

The ABI and police warned that insurance fraud pushed up the cost of premiums for all customers.

Mark Allen, head of fraud and financial crime at the association, said: “Anyone considering committing insurance fraud should be under no illusion – it’s a serious crime with serious consequences, including a criminal conviction and imprisonment.”

While the number of detected fraudulent claims fell by 2.7% to 93,900 cases last year, the value of scams rose sharply. The ABI said this was a sign of its growing scale and sophistication.

The average value of a fraudulent claim reached £14,300 last year – the second-highest figure on record, just below the peak of £14,600 in 2022.

Motor insurance was again the area with the most fraud, accounting for 55% of all cases. With 51,900 fraudulent motor claims worth £625m uncovered last year, the figures point to fewer but more costly cases. The average value rose to £12,000, the second-highest figure since 2015.

A fraudster who staged motor collisions using women he met online was sentenced for the “crash for cash” scheme designed to generate fraudulent insurance claims, the ABI said.

Aviva discovered bogus insurance claims worth £233m last year, it said in June. Scammers tried new tricks including using artificial intelligence to fake car accident scenes and documents.

Simon Klust, who heads the City of London police fraud team, said more than 250 bogus claims were detected each day but this was “likely to be just the tip of the iceberg”.

The travel sector had the sharpest rise in the number of bogus claims. Investigators uncovered a £300,000 insurance scam that used multiple fake identities, fabricated medical documents and bogus websites to support false medical emergency claims.

Exaggerated loss remains the most common type of fraud, with 26,900 cases identified. This is when someone deliberately increases the cost of a claim beyond its true value.

Ursula Jallow of the Insurance Fraud Bureau, which is funded by insurers, said: “Insurance fraud is devastating. It costs honest consumers when times are already tough.”
