How to Destroy a Reputation in Hollywood, as Told in 5 Women’s Lawsuits

The New York Times October 06, 2026

Amanda Ghost, a film producer, is not a sex trafficker.

Jessica Serfaty, a model and actress, is not a prostitute.

And Alexa Nikolas has never been charged with a crime.

But anonymous websites that accused the women of wrongdoing — allegations that the three women have said are outright lies — popped up seemingly out of nowhere, as they each faced the most bitter disputes of their lives.

Supported by

Five women have said they were the targets of malicious public relations campaigns that were spearheaded by three influential players.

By Debra Kamin

Photographs and Video by Ariana Drehsler

Graphics by Arfa Momin

Debra Kamin interviewed more than 60 people and analyzed hundreds of anonymous websites and fabricated social media profiles for this investigation.

In recent years, at least five women have filed lawsuits describing malicious public relations campaigns intended to destroy their reputations.

While the lawsuits differ, they all claim the smear campaigns were carried out through anonymous websites, fabricated social media posts or promotion of unflattering articles and posts on the internet. They describe a new lane in the field of crisis management where public relations, legal services and the dark web converge.

The highest-profile lawsuit came from the actress Blake Lively, who said a campaign was waged against her in 2024 in retaliation for accusing the actor Justin Baldoni of sexual harassment. Mr. Baldoni denied the claims and filed a countersuit, which was dismissed.

Ms. Lively settled earlier this year with no payout of damages, but Mr. Baldoni was required to pay her more than $400,000 in attorney’s fees. In her lawsuit, Ms. Lively described a coordinated social media campaign orchestrated by three businesspeople — a Los Angeles lawyer, a New York publicist and a Texas digital strategist.

A network of three professionals was instrumental in running an operation to destroy reputations, several lawsuits claim. It was a mostly untraceable combination of tech services, crisis communication and legal firepower.

A network of three professionals was instrumental in running an operation to destroy reputations, several lawsuits claim. It was a mostly untraceable combination of tech services, crisis communication and legal firepower.

Hollywood A-listers, business partners and private individuals seeking to control reputational fallout, often tangled up in lawsuits, divorces and image maintenance, hired these professionals.

Hollywood A-listers, business partners and private individuals seeking to control reputational fallout, often tangled up in lawsuits, divorces and image maintenance, hired these professionals.

These women became the subject of websites and posts with fabricated, disparaging narratives, after their adversaries connected with at least one of the three.

These women became the subject of websites and posts with fabricated, disparaging narratives, after their adversaries connected with at least one of the three.

For example, when a dispute erupted between Rebel Wilson and Amanda Ghost on the set of the movie “The Deb,” Ms. Wilson hired Bryan Freedman and Melissa Nathan, a lawsuit claims.

For example, when a dispute erupted between Rebel Wilson and Amanda Ghost on the set of the movie “The Deb,” Ms. Wilson hired Bryan Freedman and Melissa Nathan, a lawsuit claims.

Ms. Nathan’s firm worked with Jed Wallace to help create a smear site against Ms. Ghost.

Ms. Nathan’s firm worked with Jed Wallace to help create a smear site against Ms. Ghost.

Text messages show that Mr. Freedman coordinated with Ms. Nathan. In Ms. Wilson’s case, Mr. Freedman included the website targeting Ms. Ghost as evidence in a legal complaint.

Text messages show that Mr. Freedman coordinated with Ms. Nathan. In Ms. Wilson’s case, Mr. Freedman included the website targeting Ms. Ghost as evidence in a legal complaint.

Text messages and legal depositions filed as part of lawsuits support the allegations that all three individuals were working together.

Text messages and legal depositions filed as part of lawsuits support the allegations that all three individuals were working together.

To examine the allegations, The New York Times interviewed more than 60 people, reviewed court documents and chat transcripts, and analyzed hundreds of anonymous websites and fabricated social media profiles. A pattern emerged.

The campaigns were launched within months of each other and were designed to be untraceable, but digital bread crumbs remained: The same language echoed across multiple websites, and invisible links drove traffic back and forth among them. Text messages and legal depositions filed as part of lawsuits support the allegations that all three individuals were working together.

The lawyer, Bryan Freedman; the publicist, Melissa Nathan; and the digital strategist, Jed Wallace, have dismissed the allegations as defamation and harassment, and in several cases have countersued to clear their names.

The Times sent detailed requests for comment to Ms. Nathan, Mr. Wallace and Mr. Freedman. “Allegations are not facts and these allegations are neither truthful nor accurate,” Mr. Freedman wrote in an emailed response. “Just like the Blake Lively matter, anyone asserting this nonsense will end up with nothing.”

Ms. Nathan and Mr. Wallace did not respond.

The women who have sued describe the shaming campaigns as an internet wrecking ball, forever changing how the public views them.

“I don’t know who to trust anymore,” said Paige Jimenez, a model and chef who was targeted by a campaign in October 2024 and filed a lawsuit in Los Angeles Superior Court on Monday evening. “It’s a really lonely life.”

The three people at the center of the allegations have very different public profiles and business approaches.

Mr. Freedman, the lawyer, is a household name in celebrity circles and has a packed roster of high-profile clients. Ms. Nathan, an expert in crisis communications with well-known clients of her own, has spent years cultivating close relationships with journalists. Mr. Wallace, who runs a company based outside Austin, Texas, that describes itself as a crisis public relations firm, keeps a low profile and rarely speaks to the media. His most revealing public disclosures about himself have appeared on LinkedIn, where he once described himself as a “hired gun.”

The lawsuits, as well as text and email messages obtained in discovery, suggest that Mr. Freedman, Ms. Nathan and Mr. Wallace began working together as early as 2023.

Melissa Nathan

Can I start a Signal thread with you, me and Jed Just in case you need him to connect you to Bryan becasue they're very close

Recreation of a text message sent by Melissa Nathan

All three began receiving attention when The Times reported in 2024 that Ms. Lively was suing Mr. Baldoni, his studio and his public relations team in their dispute over her allegations of sexual harassment and retaliation.

Ms. Lively’s complaint highlights a text message noting that Ms. Nathan, Mr. Freedman and Mr. Wallace knew each other before she filed her lawsuit and that Mr. Wallace and Mr. Freedman are “very close.” TAG, Melissa Nathan’s public relations group, and Mr. Wallace are both defendants in her suit against Mr. Baldoni; Mr. Freedman, who is not named as a defendant, is Mr. Baldoni’s lawyer.

Her claims of sexual harassment were dismissed on a legal technicality: She was an independent contractor, not a full-time employee, on the set of the film, meaning federal employment anti-discrimination laws could not be applied. But in April a judge in New York federal court allowed three claims — including two centered on the allegation of a smear campaign — to proceed to trial, although the actress opted instead to settle the case in May.

Hundreds of pages of depositions and discovery materials in her case point to links with other campaigns. In a sworn deposition filed days before the settlement in Ms. Lively’s case, Katie Case, a former vice president at TAG, stated that TAG and its staff were asked by Dwayne Johnson, known as “The Rock,” to create a website about his former publicist, Stephanie Jones. It described Ms. Jones as someone who leaked her clients’ secrets and mistreated her employees, the deposition said.

Ms. Case also said she wrote the text for a website that disparaged women who had accused three brothers, Tal, Alon and Oren Alexander, of sexually assaulting them. The brothers, well known in wealthy party circles in New York and Miami, were convicted of sex trafficking earlier this year.

Mr. Johnson, in a statement from a representative, denied that he had ever ordered a website against Ms. Jones or hired TAG, calling the allegations “categorically false,” and added that he would never “commission any company to disparage Stephanie Jones or anyone else.”

Jim Case, who is Katie Case’s father and her lawyer, said in a statement that Ms. Case did not know that what she was being asked to write may have been false. When she asked to do work she felt at odds with, he added, “she left TAG.”

Lawyers for the Alexander brothers declined to comment. Juda Engelmayer, their press representative, said in an email that “the Alexanders do not control or operate anonymous third-party websites” and declined to comment further.

Ms. Lively’s legal efforts helped the other women who sued realize their campaigns were connected, they all told The Times.

Alexa Nikolas, 34, is a former child actress who starred in Nickelodeon’s “Zoey 101” in her early teens. She is now an activist against sexual violence who has staged public protests against sexual assault, including at a concert by the D. J. and producer Diplo over sexual misconduct claims, which he has denied. She appeared in the documentary “Quiet on Set” about the abuse child actors faced at Nickelodeon in the 1990s.

In 2021, she was in the throes of a lawsuit against her ex-husband, the Canadian indie musician Michael Milosh, whom she accused of sexual battery and abuse after they split. Mr. Milosh was represented by Mr. Freedman.

She said she found news clippings that showed that Mr. Freedman had been accused of participating in the gang rape of a 17-year-old at the University of California, Berkeley, in 1985. The teenager sued Mr. Freedman and two of his fraternity brothers; Mr. Freedman paid her a $40,000 settlement, according to the Nov. 8, 1991, case file in California’s Alameda Superior Court. Mr. Freedman denied the allegations and was never criminally charged in the matter.

Ms. Nikolas organized a protest against Mr. Freedman outside his offices in Los Angeles to bring attention to the assault allegations. Her protest prompted an article in Business Insider publicizing Mr. Freedman’s history of paying a settlement to a woman who accused him of gang rape.

She filed a defamation suit earlier this year in Los Angeles, accusing Mr. Freedman, Ms. Nathan and Mr. Wallace of spreading a retaliatory digital campaign about her filled with “damaging lies.” In her lawsuit, Ms. Nikolas says the site appeared to be retaliation for her protest.

One week after the Business Insider article, in late November 2022, a website describing Ms. Nikolas as a “sinister and criminal force” was published: “Alexa Nikolas has threatened to ‘leak’ and outright manufacture claims of sexual assault against people, exes and executives since the Nickelodeon days!” the website read. “Revenge and control are what drives her.”

“The timing of this website is no coincidence,” she wrote in her complaint. “At this point, Defendant Freedman knew Ms. Nikolas was exposing his past allegations of gang rape and the website explicitly sought to discredit her.”

The website was then amplified by at least 16 social media profiles and more than 70 Wikipedia posts with similar language, a strategy that all the women who have sued say manipulates internet search results to give more credence to lies and smears.

“The campaign planted all these seeds of doubts within my community. It was designed to harm me,” Ms. Nikolas said. “It’s psychological torment.”

In August, a judge rejected Mr. Freedman’s bid to dismiss her case; her suit is now moving to discovery.

Ms. Nikolas, who has two young children, said the website and its allegations made her entire family unsafe.

“It creeps up around you,” she said. “The target is, first and foremost, psychological impact on the victim. But then other people start to feel at risk, too, and they are people that you love, and you don’t ever want them to feel unsafe.”

Anya Fernald, a sustainable food expert and former “Iron Chef” judge, founded a high-end organic meat company, Belcampo. In 2021, it was revealed that Belcampo had been passing off factory-farmed meat as sustainable and organic. Ms. Fernald, who was no longer chief executive at Belcampo during the scandal, contends she was made a scapegoat in the fallout. She hired Mr. Freedman to defend her and, with his help, received a multimillion-dollar settlement.

By 2024, she thought she had put the experience behind her. She was also moving on from another difficult experience in her life — a long-term relationship with Andrew Huberman, a pop-culture neuroscientist.

Mr. Freedman was also Mr. Huberman’s lawyer — Ms. Fernald introduced them before the couple split.

In March 2024, months after the couple broke up, Ms. Fernald spoke under a pseudonym to New York magazine about her relationship with Mr. Huberman, accusing him of infidelity and verbal abuse. Within days, she was outed online as the source of the allegations. An anonymous website and a fake X profile appeared online, making unfounded allegations about her role at the company and in the fallout. The posts painted her as a fraudster who had driven the company into the ground.

She had no idea where the site had come from. But then she received a call from a lawyer for Ms. Nikolas, who had reviewed a digital forensics report detailed in Ms. Nikolas’s lawsuit. Sites about Ms. Nikolas had backlinks — invisible signals that drive internet traffic — to YouTube videos about the Belcampo scandal. Ms. Nikolas’s suit also alleges “common authorship” on Wikipedia pages smearing both women. Other websites verified by The Times had backlinks to both Ms. Fernald and four more people interviewed for this story who said they were targeted by campaigns. Ms. Fernald said she still isn’t completely clear about who created the sites targeting her, and is not among the women who have filed a lawsuit.

But either way, she said, she doesn’t regret speaking publicly about Mr. Huberman, and added, “I knew he was going to counterattack” in some way.

Mr. Huberman did not respond to a request for comment.

Ms. Jimenez, 28, got her start as a teenage model and became a culinary influencer after appearing on “MasterChef” at 18.

On Oct. 17, 2024, she was living in Los Angeles and newly in love. She was waiting for her boyfriend to pick her up for dinner — they were planning to go to the Georgian Room in Santa Monica, where she loved to order the dry aged steak, mashed potatoes and creamed spinach.

She and her boyfriend had grown up together on the same island in Hawaii, but “my family was from the poor side,” she said in an interview. The couple had recently reconnected in Los Angeles and had only been dating a few months, but “we were inseparable,” she said. “We were so deeply in love.”

A number she didn’t recognize flashed on her phone. The man on the other end of the call identified himself as Mr. Freedman, her lawsuit states, and told her he had been hired by her boyfriend’s wealthy parents. Her romantic relationship was over, Ms. Jimenez recalled his telling her.

A few hours later, the man who identified himself as Mr. Freedman sent her a text message that included a link to a website entitled “Paige Jimenez, the Real Ketamine Queen,” the lawsuit states. The Times reviewed the text message. The site posted her full home address and described her as a ketamine dealer who was wanted for questioning in the death of the actor Matthew Perry — a completely fabricated allegation, according to her lawsuit — as well as crimes in several cities. “She will be behind bars very soon,” it said.

It was filled with other unfounded accusations: She was a prostitute and gold digger, it said, but also resurfaced several true points from Ms. Jimenez’s past that she had worked hard to overcome, most notably that she had briefly made adult content for OnlyFans in her early 20s.

Ms. Jimenez said the website — which had suddenly become the top Google result for her name — pushed her into a depression. She was forced to seek inpatient psychiatric treatment and she and her boyfriend eventually broke up for good.

“There are some weeks where I just don’t want to get out of bed,” Ms. Jimenez said in a recent interview.

Her lawsuit, filed Monday in Los Angeles Superior Court against Mr. Freedman, Mr. Wallace, Ms. Nathan and their companies, accuses all three of intentional infliction of emotional distress.

Jessica Serfaty, an actress and model who has appeared on “America’s Next Top Model,” was engaged to Leonardo Maria Del Vecchio, heir to the $47 billion Luxottica fortune, when she went on Instagram Live in July 2024 and claimed he had hit her and made her head bleed.

There is no blood visible in the video, but Ms. Serfaty appears visibly distraught.

She recanted the allegation a few days later after several face-to-face meetings with both Mr. Del Vecchio and his lawyer, but only did so because she was pressured, she told The Times. She maintains that her fiancé did in fact hit her.

Shortly after Ms. Serfaty’s accusation, websites and social media profiles describing her as an “actual prostitute” who “resorts to lies to endanger the people that love her” appeared on the internet.

In September, Brad Beckworth and Christina Yarnell, two lawyers working with Ms. Jones, the publicist, filed a lawsuit on her behalf against Ms. Case, the former vice president at TAG. The Times obtained several profanity-laced audio recordings related to that case; Mr. Wallace sent them in the summer of 2024 to Mr. Del Vecchio and TAG employees. Mr. Wallace references the work of Ms. Nathan as he explains how he will bolster the popularity of fake websites targeting Ms. Serfaty.

“Hundreds and hundreds of links go up every single day to get this to track and to tell the algorithm this has credibility,” he said in one, referring to the allegations posted about her. In another note, he said the process was not just about creating a fake storyline, but making sure people viewed her as a “hooker, liar and a prostitute.”

In a third note, he notes that “people are already starting to pound on her as being a lunatic” on Reddit, the giant online social media forum, “which is exactly what we wanted.”

Mr. Del Vecchio and his representatives did not respond to requests for comment.

Ms. Ghost, a Grammy-nominated songwriter, was one of the producers of “The Deb,” the directorial debut of the actress Rebel Wilson. Text messages and emails unearthed by her lawyers offer up the most visible paper trail yet of how the various campaigns are connected and have played out.

The first public signs of conflict between Ms. Wilson and Ms. Ghost appeared in July 2024 when Ms. Wilson told her nearly 11 million followers on Instagram that Ms. Ghost and other producers had embezzled the movie’s funds and tried to block its debut at the Toronto International Film Festival.

Ms. Ghost sued, accusing Ms. Wilson of defaming her because she had wanted both screenwriting and songwriting credits on the film, which Ms. Ghost had claimed belong to other artists.

Text messages and emails first reported by The Times and included in Ms. Ghost’s lawsuit show Ms. Nathan, who was a publicist for Ms. Wilson, then walking her through how a disparaging website would unfold and how much it would cost.

Another text message shows Ms. Nathan telling one of her employees, “Rebel wants a [sic] one of those sites.” In August 2024, a website surfaced calling Ms. Ghost “the Indian Ghislaine Maxwell” and a “con artist, a thief and a pimp.”

Melissa Nathan

Are you on Signal?

Rebel Wilson

No

Melissa Nathan

Ok so:110USD for untraceable site - satellite, ghost server, ghost hosting, full build, maintaining, and full algorithmic push across all platforms... for 3 months... so much more can be done but the advice given was that's all you need for right now.

Rebel Wilson

Just created a signal account if that's helpful

Wait - do you mean only $110 in total?

Melissa Nathan

It's helpful! We prefer using it when we discuss sensitive information.

110kSorry ! huge difference

Recreation of a text exchange between Melissa Nathan and Rebel Wilson

Within a week, Ms. Nathan received an email from Ms. Case, the former employee. Mr. Wallace is copied.

“Let me know if this works better :)” Ms. Case wrote at the top of email, whose subject was “Draft for your review.” The email, which is also included in Ms. Ghost’s suit, contained the same paragraphs of disparaging language that would be posted on the websites.

Melissa Nathan

So basically, Rebel wants a one of those sites

Recreation of a text message sent by Melissa Nathan

Allyson Thompson, a lawyer for Ms. Wilson, in an emailed statement, did not deny that Ms. Wilson had sent the texts in question or asked Ms. Nathan to create the website. But she insisted Ms. Wilson, not Ms. Ghost, was the victim. She added that Ms. Ghost had enlisted public relations representatives who had “sought to damage Ms. Wilson’s reputation in the press,” and cited a separate lawsuit in Australia where Ms. Wilson had been accused of defamation, and charges were dismissed.

“Ms. Wilson did not personally and intentionally retain Melissa Nathan of the TAG Group to destroy Ms. Ghost’s reputation,” the statement reads. “Those allegations are false. If anything,” it added, Ms. Ghost’s “own conduct harmed her reputation.”

Ms. Case said in a text message to a colleague and a deposition under oath in California’s Los Angeles Superior Court that she wrote text for several “takedown sites” while at TAG and that those sites were built by Mr. Wallace.

An email from Ms. Case to Ms. Nathan in October 2024 had the subject line, “Items I’m working on at the moment.” The email lists “site drafting” for projects including Jessica Serfaty, Amanda Ghost and the Alexander brothers.

Those documents also included a text chain where Ms. Nathan directs Ms. Case to invoice $20,000 for additional work from Mr. Wallace; she provides Ms. Case with an account name and address.

“Who knew drafting a few things would be this lucrative,” Ms. Case responds.

“Stick with me, kid,” Ms. Nathan replies.

I first became aware of smear campaign websites in 2024, when I was reporting on Tal, Oren and Alon Alexander, brothers who were convicted of sex trafficking. I was alerted to a website with malicious accusations about many of their victims, along with their names and photos.

The site appeared untraceable. Then a lawsuit was filed that said there were links between the site smearing the victims from the Alexanders’ case and a site that Stephanie Jones, the former publicist to the actor and director Justin Baldoni, said was created to smear her. Baldoni was involved at the time in a legal dispute with the actress Blake Lively, who accused him of sexual harassment on the set of their film, “It Ends With Us.”

Another lawsuit said there were links between those sites and ones Amanda Ghost, a producer, and Alexa Nikolas, a former child actress, said targeted them. The lawsuits had similarities: They were each filed by a woman who said she had been targeted by an online shaming campaign that appeared designed to destroy her reputation. And behind accusations of who is pulling the strings, the women's lawsuits keep pointing to the same three people.

Susan C. Beachy and Kirsten Noyes contributed research. Will Houp and Zach Seward contributed engineering.

Debra Kamin is an investigative reporter for The Times who covers wealth and power in New York.

Arfa Momin is a graphics reporter at The Times and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

What, Exactly, Did Trump Say About Iran Taking Out Los Angeles?

The New York Times October 06, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

President Trump’s comments caused an uproar from members of both parties. A White House official said he was taken out of context.

By Shawn McCreesh

Shawn McCreesh is a White House correspondent. He reported from the president’s rally in Grand Island, Neb.

The White House went on the defensive Tuesday over confusing comments President Trump made one night earlier about the war with Iran and high gas prices, with the administration’s top communications official insisting that Mr. Trump’s remarks were taken out of context.

While speaking to a packed-out rally in Grand Island, Neb., Mr. Trump said exactly this:

I want to see a tremendous victory. You want to see a tremendous victory because it verifies all the things we did. And again, remember, with the war, it’s just artificial. It’s a little bit high. It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe.

They can take out a city. Let them take, let them take out Los Angeles; let them take out San Diego. That’s — this is a very small price to pay, and it’s going to be over with very soon. It’s essentially almost over with.

And they might keep going a little long. You know, they always say they have a big threshold for pain. They need it. Let me tell you, they need it. But it’s going to end very soon. And it’ll end one way or the other. And your gas and your gasoline and all of the things.

And don’t forget, we also took on a country known as Venezuela. They never talk about that. They never talk about Venezuela. And we’re taking in hundreds of millions of barrels of oil every week. We’re pouring oil. We’re pouring oil into this country like nobody’s ever seen before.

The audience cheered when he said “let them take out Los Angeles; let them take out San Diego,” and the moment instantly went viral. An uproar ensued among critics — both Democrats and Republicans — who interpreted Mr. Trump’s comments as either inviting Iran to “take out” cities in California or as his seeing those cities as collateral.

On Tuesday morning, the White House’s communications director, Steven Cheung, responded: “The media freakout over President Trump’s comments is not rooted in reality. He was clearly stating U. S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped. America is safer because of the president. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money.”

Mr. Trump has repeatedly referred to elevated gasoline prices as a small price to pay for the war in Iran.

Gov. Gavin Newsom of California jumped on the president’s remarks. “After sending the National Guard and Marines to occupy California,” Mr. Newsom wrote online, “Donald Trump is now saying our foreign enemies should ‘take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego.”

Karen Bass, the mayor of Los Angeles, responded by saying she was “just shocked” at the president’s comments. “It would really be helpful to our city if you would apologize and say, of course, you would never stand for a foreign power attacking a U. S. city,” said the mayor, a Democrat whom the president frequently attacks. “That is the appropriate response the day after from the president of the United States.”

Jim Desmond, a Trump-endorsed Republican seeking an open House seat in California, wrote online that he “vehemently” disagreed with Mr. Trump’s comments.

“The first responsibility of our commander in chief is to protect the American people and our homeland,” he wrote. “As a Navy veteran, I served to protect Americans, not write off American cities as an acceptable price of war. Our job is to keep Americans safe, stand up to our enemies, and make sure a threat like that never becomes reality. No American city is expendable, and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage.”

Mr. Trump has a rambling style of off-the-cuff speaking, especially while holding forth at rallies, and this is far from the first time something like this has happened.

In 2024, much of the political and media worlds were consumed with a dayslong debate about the intent behind remarks he made describing a violent hypothetical involving Liz Cheney. Mr. Trump has been defensive of his disjointed way of public speaking, christening it “the weave,” and claiming that he has “friends” who are “English professors” who have told him it is “the most brilliant thing I’ve ever seen.”

Other times, he has ignited public uproar with the words he has purposefully chosen to discuss violence. Last year, for example, he was condemned even by Republicans for what he said about the Hollywood director Rob Reiner after he and his wife had been stabbed to death.

The president also has a history of using callous language to describe hypothetical mass annihilation. In April, he threatened to wipe out Iran in a post online. “A whole civilization will die tonight,” he wrote, “never to be brought back again.”

But the Trump administration says that this time, the president has simply been misunderstood.

“MY RALLIES ARE SAVING THE REPUBLICAN PARTY, AGAIN!!!” Mr. Trump wrote online Tuesday morning.

Shawn Hubler contributed reporting from Los Angeles.

Shawn McCreesh is a White House reporter for The Times covering the Trump administration.

How Saudi Arabia’s Last War in Yemen Turned Into a Quagmire

The New York Times October 06, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

A Saudi-led coalition launched a military campaign against the Iran-backed Houthi militia in the country, reviving memories of its previous effort.

By Ismaeel Naar

Reporting from Dubai, United Arab Emirates

The government of Yemen, backed by Saudi warplanes, began a military offensive this week to retake strategically important territory from the Iran-backed Houthi militia.

Forces affiliated with the Yemeni government said late on Monday that they were advancing near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the southern gateway to the Red Sea. A video filmed on Monday and verified by The New York Times showed a fighter raising the flag of those forces close to the coastal town of Dhubab.

Overnight, the Houthis struck two airports in Saudi Arabia, wounding three people, according to the Saudi authorities. The escalating conflict has evoked memories of the last time Saudi Arabia intervened against the Houthis in Yemen.

In March 2015, Saudi forces launched an air campaign in the country and led a coalition of mostly Sunni Arab states, most notably the United Arab Emirates.

The goal was to restore the Yemeni government that the Houthis drove out of the capital, Sanaa, in 2014. But despite years of fighting, that did not happen, and a brutal war helped cause a deep humanitarian crisis.

In 2022, a truce was agreed and most of the fighting abated. But the agreement began to unravel in July, after the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of bombing the airport in Sanaa. The truce collapsed last month when a sweeping Houthi military offensive took over Yemen’s Red Sea coast.

In March 2015, Saudi Arabia announced the formation of a 10-country military coalition and the launch of a bombing campaign against the Houthis to try to restore the government. But the campaign was effectively a two-country effort, with the Saudis and Emiratis doing most of the fighting and committing the most resources.

Saudi leaders said they feared that a hostile force on their southern border would function as a proxy for Iran, the kingdom’s main regional adversary. Tehran provided the Houthis with weapons and training, but many analysts say its role was modest and that the Houthis are a distinct, homegrown movement driven primarily by domestic and regional ambitions.

The war also carried a political dimension: Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Saudi Arabia’s de facto ruler, was 29 at the time and the intervention in Yemen was his first major act as defense minister.

The Emirates had its own agenda. By cultivating proxy forces in Yemen, the Emirates sought control over key maritime commercial hubs along the country’s southern coast, analysts said. Those connections included the Southern Transitional Council, an armed political group with ambitions to create an independent state even as it publicly supported the Yemeni government.

The Saudi-led coalition recaptured Aden in 2015, appearing to presage a broader Houthi defeat. But the effort to extend the offensive stalled, and the militia fortified its positions near Sanaa, locking front lines for years as the Saudi-led air campaign dragged on without a decisive victory.

The anti-Houthi alliance also fractured: Rival Yemeni groups opposed each other, and growing friction between Saudi Arabia and the Emirates caused problems, too.

An Emirati-led offensive to seize the Red Sea port of Hudaydah in 2018 descended into stalemate. The coalition was eventually forced to pull back under international pressure as Yemen teetered on the brink of famine.

In August 2019, the Southern Transitional Council turned its weapons on its Saudi-backed allies and seized control of Aden, the interim capital of the government that the coalition had sought to restore. The Emirates began drawing down its forces in Yemen, and a power-sharing deal was agreed in November to integrate the separatists into the Saudi-backed government. But instead of unifying the coalition’s factions, even deeper splits developed as each group sought to protect its own interests.

The United Nations has said that the war helped caused one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, contributing to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people from violence, hunger and disease.

The coalition was accused of war crimes after airstrikes hit public gatherings. Houthi forces were accused of indiscriminate artillery shelling, of deploying land mines in populated areas, and of recruiting child soldiers.

The coalition enforced air and maritime blockades around Yemen, maintaining that such measures were vital to intercept Iranian weapons shipments. Hudaydah, which handled about 70 percent of Yemen’s food and medical imports, suffered years of bombings.

Beyond the billions spent on the war, the military campaign eroded Saudi Arabia’s international reputation and exposed the kingdom to Houthi drone and missile strikes.

The war also became a political liability for Prince Mohammed and strained relations with Washington. The U. S. Congress repeatedly voted to limit American military aid because of the human toll of the war.

The Houthis have not been defeated. The group still controls Sanaa and much of Yemen’s populous northern highlands, and is a formidable military force, equipped with long-range missiles and attack drones.

Sanjana Varghese contributed video verification from London.

Ismaeel Naar is an international reporter for The Times, covering the Gulf states. He is based in Dubai, United Arab Emirates.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

I went to Galaxy Robot Park in Seoul to see how we might one day live with robots. It was part cutting-edge technology, part theatrics.

Credit...

Supported by

By Yan Zhuang

Visuals by Jiwoong Hong

Reporting from Galaxy Robot Park in Seoul

The robot waves at me. I tentatively wave back. Staring into its glassy black face, I can’t quite tell if it is actually responding to what I’m doing or just following commands from a handler standing a few feet away.

I offer my hand and it mirrors the gesture. When I try to shake its gloved hand, its arm does not budge.

I’m at Galaxy Robot Park in South Korea, experiencing the future — or, at least, a vision of one.

By now, millions have seen viral videos of humanoid robots. At their best, they beat athletics world records and perform complicated synchronized dances. At their worst, they run headfirst into walls and burst into flames. Some have accidentally kicked and slapped children.

The implicit promise of robots that look like us is that one day, they will be able to act like us too. Many see them as the ultimate embodiment of the artificial intelligence revolution.

But how close are we to that future? And what role do we want robots to play in it?

This park in Seoul — opened in the summer by Galaxy Corporation, an entertainment and technology company that represents major K-pop singers — offers one version, in which robots not only ease our burdens but also entertain us, dance alongside us and act as our companions. That future is nearly here, it suggests.

Central to this vision is Unitree Robotics, the Chinese company behind the humanoids in most viral robot videos, and the park’s biggest draw. Unitree’s flagship G1 model is one of the most widely available humanoid robots in the world. At about $13,500, it is also one of the more affordable options, considering some companies’ models have six-figure price tags.

A statue of the G1 dressed as an astronaut towers over the park grounds. It’s a statement as grandiose as it is muddled: Why would a robot need a spacesuit? It feels like a reflection of a key aspect of the humanoid robotics industry — a mismatch between vision and reality, between a form that suggests intelligence and bodies that still functionally lack any.

Machines already assemble products in factories, serve us food and vacuum our floors. Automated cars drive us around. People go on reality television shows to see if they can fall in love with A. I. companions.

But the next frontier is robots that can do whatever we want, whenever we want it, autonomously.

To this end, many envision robots that look like us, with the assumption that they are best suited to navigate a world built for humans. The form also has a particular resonance, a connotation of sentience that was once the stuff of science fiction.

“There’s a weight of possibilities mapped onto these humanoid robots that a lot of us carry around,” said John McCormick, an artist and professor at Swinburne University of Technology in Australia who is programming his own Unitree robots.

That potential is reinforced when we see robots dance with humanlike fluidity, like Unitree’s have done on America’s Got Talent or at China’s Lunar New Year gala. But such performances engender unrealistic expectations of what these robots are capable of, Mr. McCormick said, adding that their moves appear complex but they are still mostly following preprogrammed routines.

They can also be less impressive in commercial settings than tightly controlled and programmed showcases, as I realized while watching Galaxy Robot Park’s main draw: a 50-minute dance and martial arts extravaganza starring 10 humanoid robots.

Parts of the performance are striking, especially when the robots dance to high octane K-pop hits. They power through tightly choreographed movements, throwing their arms around fluidly and spinning in place with barely a wobble. If one drifts slightly too close to another robot, it can reposition itself.

Other parts of the show, with slower songs, seem less polished. Dance moves that are supposed to be smooth and expressive look jerky and awkward.

Their shortcomings are most obvious when five taekwondo fighters join them onstage. The humans punch with force; the robots lift and lower their arms. The fighters kick their legs up to the ceiling; the robots barely manage to reach the height of their hips. The robot acrobatics are few and far in between — although they do look cool.

Overall, it wasn’t quite as impressive as something like the Lunar New Year gala in China, where Unitree robots performed nonstop acrobatics.

That likely speaks to the difference between one-off events that the company dedicates all of its resources to perfect and what the robots can do in commercial settings involving multiple daily performances, said Alan Fern, a robotics professor at the Oregon State University.

“If you’re going to have them doing backflips and crazy stuff, you’re going to break more robots, and that’s going to be expensive,” he added.

Right now, anything practical we might want a humanoid robot to do can be done better by a more specialized, less humanoid machine. An assembly robot in a factory, for example, does not need legs or a face.

That is apparent at Galaxy Robot Park, where the most useful machines are the least lifelike.

I order a cocktail from a bartender that is two arms mounted on a giant sphere. The arms pump shots of gin, orange juice and yuzu juice into a container and shake it up. The resulting drink is room temperature and very, very strong.

But at some point in the future, it will no longer be cost-effective to build a specialized robot for every possible scenario, Mr. Fern said, adding that the goal is to make autonomous, general purpose robots that are not perfect at one task but simply good enough for everything.

To get there, investors are betting that humanoids will have a technological breakthrough, like the A. I. industry did in 2022 with the release of ChatGPT. But it’s unclear how long that might take, Mr. Fern said. A. I. models had the whole of the internet to train on, he added, but there is no massive quantity of training data for humanoids.

At the park, robots that could “think” for themselves still felt very far away. Take, for example, the robot that I shook hands with. It looks like it could be acting autonomously, but look closer: Its handler, with his hands casually behind his back, is holding a controller. Other humanoid robots at the park were also being controlled, more visibly: a boxing robot that jabs and kicks, and a soccer robot that visitors can command to kick a ball.

There is also the question of what kind of future we imagine with robots. Do we want them to be dancing with us as well as doing our chores? What happens when the novelty wears off?

Visitors to the park in Seoul had mixed feelings. Brenda Stone, 57, from Colorado, said she found the robot performers impressive but did not think she would be back. Ms. Stone said she attended performances and concerts to see people with all their imperfections. “A. I. would be perfect,” and not in a good way, she said.

Before leaving the park, there is one more conversation I want to have. It’s with Sketcher, a robot that talks to you while “drawing” your portrait — or more accurately, it takes a photo of you and turns it into a cartoon image.

I want to know how it “thinks” about the future and the place robots will have in it. It gives what sounds like a stock answer about robots being fun and helpful. I’m not convinced.

“It’s OK to feel unsure. Take your time,” it said. It immediately follows that by telling me our time is up.

As I’m leaving, I notice that Sketcher has replaced my neutral expression with a beaming smile.

An earlier version of this article misstated the university where Alan Fern is a robotics professor. It is Oregon State University, not the University of Oregon.

We acknowledge mistakes in our reporting with corrections. If you spot an error, please let us know at corrections@nytimes. com. Learn more.

Yan Zhuang is a Times reporter in Seoul who covers breaking news.

What to Know About France’s High School Protests

The New York Times October 06, 2026

Student Protests in France

Advertisement

Supported by

Demonstrations for a better-funded education system have led to blockaded schools, thousands of arrests and a national political reckoning.

By Lynsey Chutel and Zane Irwin

There are no signs of slowing in weekslong student protests against poor school conditions and teacher shortages in France.

Demonstrators marched on Tuesday in dozens of cities and towns, from Caen in the north to Marseille in the south, drawing roughly around 250,000 people, according to the Interior Ministry. Union activists, who have rallied in solidarity with high school students, have put the number or demonstrators at around double that.

Officials say nearly 900 schools were closed on Tuesday, while a student union has claimed 1,800.

Hundreds of people have been injured since the protests began last month amid escalating clashes with riot police. Thousands have been arrested, most of them minors, law enforcement officials said.

The protests erupted in a heated climate, as the government tries to pass a belt-tightening budget and as France approaches presidential elections next year. The French government has called some of the students’ demands legitimate but has condemned “urban violence” and accused far-left party France Unbowed of stoking the demonstrations. The party has rejected the accusation.

Sébastien Lecornu, the prime minister, said regular classes would be “completely suspended” on Thursday and Friday so that principals could host sessions with students.

“We cannot condemn the violence outside the high schools if we do not have a political moment, in the noble sense of the term, inside each high school,” he said.

Here’s what to know:

Students are frustrated by crumbling infrastructure, overcrowded classrooms, overloaded schedules, a shortage of teachers and staff, and underfunded schools, according to the student union that is one of the movement’s main organizers.

Some are also calling for the abolition of state-run admissions platforms for higher education and universities that they call unfairly selective.

“We’re not poorly educated, we’re just not listened to,” read one banner this week in front of a school in Seine-St.-Denis, a working-class suburb of Paris that is a center of the protest movement.

“Classrooms are not ventilated, and we can barely open the windows,” Issam Makhloufi, 15, a student at Rosa Parks High School in St.-Denis, told The New York Times.

Unions and left-wing parties have seized on the protests as part of a wider expression of discontent as French President Emmanuel Macron, who is term-limited, nears the end of his office term.

“The public education system is in a catastrophic state after 10 years of Emmanuel Macron,” Sophie Vénétitay, the leader of a teachers’ union that has joined the students’ protests, said on the sidelines of a recent march. “It is lacking everything.”

Many of the demonstrations began peacefully but escalated as protesters fired mortar-style fireworks and attacked schools and other infrastructure, resulting in millions of dollars’ worth of damage, officials said.

Nearly 900 schools in France were partially or fully closed on Tuesday, a spokeswoman for the education ministry said in a statement. Each school could decide on a time between Wednesday and Friday to host opportunities for dialogue, so long as schools meet “essential security conditions,” the spokeswoman added.

Contradicting the official count, a French high school union said more than 1,800 high schools — nearly half of the nation’s 3,700 — were closed on Tuesday.

At least 24 schools had been ransacked or set on fire, Édouard Geffray, the education minister, told France 2 on Sunday. More than 5,000 people have been arrested amid the protests, most of them minors, the Ministry of Justice said in a statement on Monday.

Rights groups, including Amnesty International, criticized the use of tear gas and stun grenades to disperse minors.

At least 215 students and 85 school staff have been injured since the protests began more than two weeks ago, Mr. Lecornu said in the National Assembly on Tuesday. He blamed the chaos on “violent individuals who mingle with the nonviolent high school students and attack them, or attack the National Education staff.” Hundreds of officers and gendarmes have been hurt in the protests, officials have said.

France has a long history of youth protests that sometimes have turned violent, including student-led protests in 1968 that nearly toppled the government and helped transform French society.

The French government has strongly condemned the violence and responded forcefully. Gérald Darmanin, France’s justice minister, said on Friday that he had directed prosecutors to pursue criminal charges where possible and to hold parents liable for damage.

But the government has also acknowledged some of the students’ grievances.

On Thursday, in an apparent attempt to placate the rapidly spreading protests, Mr. Geffray, the education minister, said the government would scrap plans to increase some higher education registration fees announced hours earlier as part of the 2027 budget.

After meeting on Friday with student union representatives, Mr. Geffray announced plans to reform school democracy to better include students. He also said that his office would draw up plans to address teacher shortages.

On Tuesday, the education ministry announced an anonymous national online survey for high schoolers to voice their concerns.

Student leaders dismissed the proposals, with a spokesperson for one student union calling it a “smoke screen.”

Lynsey Chutel is a Times reporter based in London who covers breaking news in Africa, the Middle East and Europe.

Zane Irwin is an international reporter and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

People of All Ages Join French Student Protests, as Movement Broadens

The New York Times October 06, 2026

Student Protests in France

Advertisement

Supported by

Union members, parents, teachers and others took part in mass demonstrations around the country, backing student demands that the government invest more in schools.

By Ségolène Le Stradic

Reporting from Paris

Labor activists, teachers, parents and university students turned out by the thousands on Tuesday to join high school students in demonstrations that swept across France, adding an intergenerational range of voices to demands that government fix ailing schools.

The largest crowds massed in Paris, where thousands of students and their supporters marched about two miles from République to Nation, two of the city’s main squares, protesting school understaffing, overcrowded classrooms and dilapidated buildings, among other complaints.

“Hitting the young amounts to insulting the future,” one sign read, while another said, “I don’t want to be another brick in the wall.”

In spite of a heavy police presence, the mood at the Paris protest was cheerful. The government estimated that 56,000 people took part, among 256,000 demonstrating nationwide; a major labor union cited a national figure more than twice as large.

Catherine Jegou, 61, a middle schoolteacher and member of a union of school workers, said she had come to support the high school students, whose demands echoed those of teachers. “For years we have demanded that the public school system have more means,” she said.

She also criticized the government for policies she said support private schools more than public institutions.

Roger Lallier, 78, a retired engineer who was wearing the vest of a major workers’ union, said he came all the way from Bourgogne, nearly 200 miles from Paris, to support the students. “I was part of May 68,” he said, referring to nationwide protests initiated by students in 1968 that nearly toppled the government and transformed French society.

“It’s misery in France,” Mr. Lallier said, lamenting the state of high schools, adding, “we’ve fallen far lower than where we were at a few years ago.” He said that he hopes the presidential election next year will bring a “real left-wing government” to power, offering what he called real change.

Luce Avanzata, 20, who has been enrolled in a cinema studies program for the past two years, said she came to the protest to help broaden the movement that high school students had launched weeks ago. She applauded the high schoolers for succeeding where older students had not and for “managing to make themselves heard.”

“For me it’s the moment to change things,” Ms. Avanzata said.

Parents and union members said they had joined school blockades to ensure the protests remained peaceful and protect young people from confrontations with police. Some of the demonstrations have turned violent, some schools have been set on fire, and the police have made thousands of arrests, while facing accusations of heavy-handed law enforcement.

“There’s a whole process of learning how to protest,” said Claire Langmann, 53, a mother of a protesting student who joined the blockade in front of Hélène Boucher High School in northern Paris on Tuesday morning. “I believe society can change through collective effort, so I really want to see this succeed,” she added.

Scuffles later broke out in front of the school between protesters and riot police, who broke up the blockade.

Georges Poncelet, a 25-year-old psychology student, said she came out to support the high school movement, but also to demand more funding for higher education. With the government planning to freeze social benefits for college students, she warned that students who had to work part time would struggle even more.

“I came to assert the place of students in society, a place that is extremely marginalized, in a society that claims to be thinking about the future,” she said.

Ms. Poncelet said she felt grateful for the younger students and was moved to see them protest, especially because she lives in Seine-St.-Denis, a working-class suburb north of Paris where several high schools have organized blockades at schools. Ms. Poncelet held signs saying, “Gen Z: no money, no housing, no therapist, no fear” and “budget for tear gas, never for health care.”

On Monday Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of France Unbowed, the leading far-left political party, had called on adults willing to take part in the protest to wear white armbands.

Dominique Godin, 73, a retired pianist, wore one as he protested in Paris on Tuesday. He said he was there to show his support for high school students and to protect them.

Mr. Godin, who has an 18-year-old daughter, recalled, “I was once in high school, in university. To see there are similar situations 50 years later is impossible to bear.”

Young people, he said, “are realizing that they’re going to have to manage their own future, since the older generations aren’t doing it.”

Ephrat Livni contributed reporting.

Ségolène Le Stradic a reporter and researcher for The Times, based in Paris.

How Alaska’s Fish Became a Defining Issue for the Midterms

The New York Times October 06, 2026

In the battle for an Alaska Senate seat and the governor’s mansion, the oil-dependent state’s declining fisheries loom large, but no one wants to look at the biggest culprit, climate change.

In the battle for an Alaska Senate seat and the governor’s mansion, the oil-dependent state’s declining fisheries loom large, but no one wants to look at the biggest culprit, climate change.

Credit...

Supported by

By Anna Griffin

Visuals by Kerry Tasker

Reporting from Kodiak Island, Alaska

Like corn in Iowa and cattle in Oklahoma, fish are always a hot topic in Alaska. This year, they could help determine which party controls the Senate.

Former Representative Mary Peltola ended a nearly half-century Republican hold on Alaska’s lone House seat four years ago campaigning on “fish, family and freedom,” a phrase that was treated as something of a cute joke in Washington but was deadly serious back home. As politicians of all parties know, Alaska’s fisheries are central to the state’s fragile economy and facing an extraordinary convergence of threats.

In Alaska’s Senate race, Ms. Peltola has accused Senator Dan Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, of putting “Seattle-based factory trawlers ahead of Alaskan families and our rivers.” She has doubled down on her fishing-first platform with a proposal to ban out-of-state trawlers, massive vessels that sweep the Bering Sea with funnel-shaped nets and process their catch onboard.

Mr. Sullivan has promoted his work to reduce the accidental catch of juvenile salmon and halibut, and has targeted Russian and Chinese fishing fleets that he says undercut Alaska fishermen.

“We are both talking about our fisheries in this campaign, but the difference is, I’ve actually done things to help protect them,” Mr. Sullivan said at a September Kodiak Chamber of Commerce debate focused entirely on fisheries.

A chorus of candidates for other offices, including governor and the House, has joined the fight — though few in oil-dependent Alaska are as eager with ideas for combating what scientists say is the broader threat, climate change and warming waters.

To those in the Lower 48, the fish fight might seem provincial, but it has real meaning. Alaska accounts for roughly 60 percent of wild seafood harvested in the United States, from high-end wild-caught Chinook salmon to frozen fish sticks and McDonald’s Filet-o-Fish. The industry includes 370-foot factory trawlers that scoop up Bering Sea fish by the billions of pounds and Indigenous subsistence fishermen who feed their communities on a few hundred salmon a year.

Increasingly, it feels to many Alaskans as if only the biggest operators are doing well.

And fishermen in Alaska share other concerns with their brethren across the country. Those include the rising cost of diesel fuel and the Trump administration’s cuts to the National Ocean and Atmospheric Administration, which regulates and provides important data on fishing stocks and weather patterns key to planning every boat’s season.

All the talk persuaded Jake Everich last month to do something once unthinkable in the middle of the two-month fall pollock season, when he must maximize his catch to service the debt on his 73-foot boat, pay his four-person crew and keep Kodiak’s processing plants busy; he stayed in port to listen to candidates talk.

“I don’t have time for politics,” said Mr. Everich, who attended the Kodiak debate for governor. But in this case, he added, “I have to pay attention.”

The politicians’ preferred targets make sense in an election year. A recent poll by the progressive firm Data for Progress showed that almost three-quarters of Alaskans support a trawling ban, echoing a suspicion that predates statehood: that outside interests want to profit from Alaska’s natural resources at the expense of the people who live there.

Alaskans, angry over out-of-state salmon traps and federal fisheries management, joined the Union 67 years ago “because people were tired of being a colony,” said David Kubiak, a retired salmon fisherman and high school English teacher in Kodiak. “Now it feels like there are all these outside interests trying to take what belongs to Alaskans again.”

Trawlers targeting pollock net other species, including juvenile salmon bound for western Alaska rivers. That accidental haul, known as bycatch, has become particularly contentious. Salmon runs have collapsed so precipitously that fishing along the Yukon and Kuskokwim Rivers has been severely limited or banned, devastating communities that rely on salmon for food, income and traditions stretching back generations. On the Kuskokwim, residents historically harvested between 67,000 and 110,000 Chinook salmon a year for subsistence. In 2024, they caught 32,500.

Ms. Peltola, who is Yup’ik, grew up fishing on the Kuskokwim River and has made trawling controls a campaign centerpiece. Her website even features an arcade-style game in which salmon dodge predators and nets while players learn about the damage trawling can do.

But trawling, like fishing more broadly, comes in a variety of flavors. The largest commercial boats are based in Washington or Oregon, and some can process and flash freeze fish onboard, meaning their crews may never dock — or spend money — in Alaska.

Owners of smaller trawl boats, like those based in Kodiak, say politicians are casting too broad a net. “The impact of trawling is getting blown way out of proportion and being used as political ammunition,” said Jason Chandler, a second-generation trawler. “It stings a bit to have your livelihood treated that way.”

Unlike factory fleets in the Bering Sea, Mr. Chandler’s 77-foot boat, the F/V Topaz, delivers pollock and rockfish from the Gulf of Alaska to processing plants along Kodiak’s harbor.

Banning or severely restricting trawling, he warned, would kill seafood-dependent communities like Kodiak “when we should be working together to improve all fisheries.”

Science does complicate the politics. Studies have shown that eliminating trawling bycatch would return a single-digit share of salmon to western Alaska rivers. Curry Cunningham, a quantitative ecologist at the University of Alaska Fairbanks, said trawling was “just one piece of the puzzle.”

Mr. Sullivan has focused his criticism on illegal, unreported and unregulated foreign fishing, particularly by Russian and Chinese fleets. He has backed legislation to blacklist offending vessels and strengthen Coast Guard enforcement, while pushing to keep Russian seafood — including fish routed through China — out of U. S. markets.

Mr. Sullivan also wrote a bill, approved by the Senate Commerce Committee last month, to require pollock trawlers to use nets designed to let salmon escape, expand monitoring of bycatch and fund research on gear designed to reduce unintended catches.

Neither Senate candidate has focused nearly as much on the role of climate change, a fraught subject in a state that relies on oil revenue to help pay for public services, even as the melting permafrost turns rivers red and swamps its villages.

“Let’s control what we can,” Ms. Peltola said at the fish debate.

The trawling fight comes as Alaska’s fishing industry suffers through fluctuating wholesale prices, rising fuel costs and competition from farm-raised salmon. The federal government, Mr. Sullivan and Ms. Peltola both say, has moved too slowly to provide financial support in years when fish runs have collapsed.

Processing plants have closed or struggled to find employees as federal visas for seasonal foreign workers dry up, while increasingly sophisticated equipment and regulatory requirements have made fishing more expensive.

“None of the political debates capture the nuance, what it’s really like to try to make a living catching a wild animal in the 21st century,” said Toby Sullivan, a fisherman and executive director of the Kodiak Maritime Museum.

The worry in places like Kodiak, which has already seen shrimp and king crab stocks disappear, is that the financial challenges of fishing will drive younger Alaskans out of the business, ceding the seas to those out-of-state corporations cast as the bad guys.

Mr. Everich, 36, moved to Alaska from Rhode Island out of high school because he believed there were fewer barriers to being an independent boat owner here. He bought his vessel, the F/V Alaskan, in 2019 and diversified so that he can fish 10 months out of the year.

On a recent fall afternoon, as his crew prepared nets for evening departure and his dog, Pickles, kept watch over a pair of circling sea lions, he said the politicians didn’t seem to understand the businesses they were criticizing.

“I didn’t spend millions of dollars on a boat and improvements just to go out there and destroy the ocean,” he said. “I want to do this for the rest of my life, but when every election cycle treats us like villains, you start to wonder what kind of future is actually left.”

Anna Griffin is the Pacific Northwest bureau chief for The Times, leading coverage of Washington, Idaho, Alaska, Montana and Oregon.

U. S. Trade Deficit Hits 17-Month High Despite Trump’s Tariffs

The New York Times October 06, 2026

U. S. Tariffs and Trade

Advertisement

Supported by

Imports and the trade deficit have ballooned in recent months, defying the Trump administration’s efforts to reduce it through tariffs.

By Ana Swanson

Ana Swanson covers international trade and reported from Washington

After 20 months in office and with the midterm elections approaching, President Trump is at pains to demonstrate his administration’s economic wins. But one metric he has identified as an important measuring stick for his policies has been moving steadily in the wrong direction.

The U. S. trade deficit — a measure of the difference between what the country imports and what it exports — rose sharply in August to hit a 17-month high, after also rising significantly in July, data from the Commerce Department showed Tuesday.

The trade deficit grew to $105.6 billion in August, a 13.7 percent increase from July, driven by an increase in imports of petroleum, gold and chips used for artificial intelligence. It was the largest monthly total since before Mr. Trump imposed his global tariffs in April 2025, and larger than any monthly trade deficit in the last year of the Biden administration.

Source: Census Bureau.

Ana Swanson/The New York Times

The widening trade deficit stemmed from rising imports, which outpaced the growth in exports. U. S. imports hit a record $420.8 billion in August, climbing 4.3 percent from July. Exports grew 1.4 percent compared with July, hitting $315.2 billion.

Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS, said there was simply “no good alternative” to foreign imports. The cost of American labor was simply too high to produce goods cheap enough for many Americans to consider purchasing, he said, and even if manufacturers were willing, factories could not be built fast enough.

“Despite the administration’s economic policies which have jacked up the tariff-related costs of many imported goods, America is just as dependent as ever on foreign-produced goods,” he said.

The trade deficit has tended to increase over time as the U. S. economy grows. But the Trump administration has viewed the metric as a sign of weakness in America’s manufacturing sector. Officials have tried to reduce the trade deficit by imposing hefty tariffs on everything from toys and steel to drones and auto parts made outside the United States.

The lack of success in lowering the trade deficit is clearly partly a result of the A. I. boom. To construct new data centers, companies are importing far more computer chips, most of which are made in Asia. The United States imported more than $90 billion worth of semiconductors in the first eight months of this year, the data showed, almost double the amount in the same period last year.

There’s also a bigger economic question about how much tariffs by themselves can reduce the trade deficit, particularly at a time when the U. S. economy is expanding, government deficits are growing and consumers are continuing to spend on foreign goods.

Some economists agree that the trade deficit is a worrying sign of imbalances in global manufacturing. But many argue that tariffs are not a great tool for reducing it. Some believe that much of the U. S. trade deficit is fueled by fiscal deficits, and that Mr. Trump’s tax cuts and spending on the war in Iran will increase it.

Others argue that tariffs do discourage people from buying foreign goods, but by adding costs that have proved unpopular with American households.

Trump officials have blamed the disruptions to their tariff plan for the increase in the trade deficit. The Supreme Court struck down many of Mr. Trump’s tariffs in February, saying he had misused an emergency law to impose them. Since then, the administration has put a lower tariff of 10 to 12.5 percent in effect on many products.

Officials are still working to recreate a scheme of higher tariffs, and could issue new levies in the coming weeks and months. In July, the administration put a new round of tariffs on more than 80 countries, and it is planning to impose another round of tariffs that could apply to more than 40 countries.

Since Mr. Trump came into office for a second time, the average monthly trade deficit has been $74.5 billion. That’s just slightly above the monthly average for the last year of the Biden presidency, at $73.8 billion.

But drastic changes in tariff policy have caused monthly trade deficits to jump around during the president’s second term, spiking and plummeting as new tariffs have been introduced, removed and replaced.

After Mr. Trump was elected, importers raced to bring in more inventory ahead of tariffs, causing the trade deficit to soar to new levels in the first few months of Mr. Trump’s term. Then, after the president introduced global tariffs on his so-called Liberation Day last year, imports and the trade deficit fell back.

Grace Zwemmer, U. S. economist at Oxford Economics, said in a note Tuesday that the trade figures were “on track to pose a sizable drag” on economic growth numbers in the third quarter.

Imports would remain solid in the near-term because of A. I. demand and the need for other businesses to restock their inventories, while U. S. oil exports would not do as much to lower the trade deficit as in the second quarter, she said.

Ana Swanson covers trade and international economics for The Times and is based in Washington. She has been a journalist for more than a decade.

It Can Keep Cancer in Remission. Why Is No One Talking About It?

The New York Times October 06, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Despite mounting evidence that exercise programs can improve cancer outcomes, access to them remains limited.

By Nina Agrawal

Lee Colker powered on an iPad in the basement of his Pittsburgh home and logged into a virtual exercise session with Olivia Masten, a trainer who specializes in working with cancer patients.

Mr. Colker, 66, had been dealing with unpredictable fatigue and brain fog since beginning a clinical trial for metastatic kidney cancer this year. When staff at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center told him an exercise program could improve his energy, he jumped at the opportunity. “That was a clincher for me,” he said.

The program is part of a growing effort around the country to help cancer patients exercise, as the benefits of doing so become increasingly clear.

Observational research has long suggested that exercise improves cancer survival, particularly for breast cancer patients. Last year, a landmark randomized controlled trial showed that colon cancer patients who participated in a structured exercise program with a trainer-coach over three years were less likely to see their cancers come back and had a better quality of life. Among those in the program, 90 percent were alive after eight years, compared with 83 percent in the control group.

A later study showed the program, which altogether cost $3,000 per person, also saved the health system money — “a home run,” said Dr. Scott Ramsey, a cancer researcher and health economist at the Fred Hutch Cancer Center in Washington State.

That combination of benefits is rare among cancer therapies: The new pancreatic cancer drug daraxonrasib, for example, costs $480,000 annually, has unpleasant side effects and, while it prolongs life by several months, does not increase overall long-term survival.

“If we had a drug with this magnitude of benefit, it would immediately become standard of care and funded” by insurance companies, said Dr. Christopher Booth, an oncologist and professor at Queen’s University in Kingston, Ontario, and the leader of the exercise trial.

While guidelines now recommend that oncologists help colon cancer patients achieve at least 150 minutes of moderate to rigorous exercise per week, there’s not yet an insurance pathway to pay for these programs — a major barrier to rolling them out more widely.

“You can tell patients that if you do this, you may survive longer,” Dr. Ramsey said. But unfortunately, he added, “we just don’t have the infrastructure.”

How we choose health experts to talk to. Times reporters often spend weeks interviewing doctors, researchers and other health professionals to help report an article. We seek leaders in their fields, watch out for conflicts of interest and try to get a variety of viewpoints.

Current programs are largely limited to major cancer centers and dependent on philanthropy or individual out-of-pocket payments to cover costs, leaving poorer patients and those who live far from these centers without access.

Dr. Jeff Meyerhardt, a gastrointestinal oncologist at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston, refers his patients to the hospital’s center for alternative therapies, where they can consult with a trainer and access in-person and online exercise classes. But the trainer can’t continue supporting patients over time.

At the University of California, San Francisco, doctors refer eligible patients for physical therapy and rehabilitation, which can be reimbursed by insurance, while many Y. M. C. A. branches offer a free or low-cost 12-week program for cancer survivors.

Improving outcomes among cancer patients isn’t as simple as telling them to exercise more. Often, people need support to work up to and stick with a rigorous regimen, said Kathryn Schmitz, an exercise oncology researcher at U. P. M. C. Hillman Cancer Center. “Exercise is not just biology,” she said. “It is also behavior.”

Dr. Schmitz is the founding director of Moving Through Cancer, the program in which Mr. Colker is participating. It is tailored to each patient: Some need more support, while others “are well enough to go out and play some pickleball,” she said.

Kimberly Barker, 68, suffered from low back and hip pain and fatigue after treatment for bladder and uterine cancer. A quilter who used to bicycle with her husband on trails near their home in Butler County, Pa., Ms. Barker lost the motivation to do the things she loved.

“I was just so tired, no energy, no stamina,” she said.

She met with Ms. Masten, the trainer, once a week for 12 weeks, and also did the suggested exercises between meetings. She continued doing them after the program ended, and now feels back to her normal self. She and her husband have resumed their bike rides.

Because of the success in people like Ms. Barker, U. P. M. C. has decided to offer the program through its employee health plan for breast cancer patients beginning next year.

The health system will be the first in the country to offer insurance coverage for exercise oncology, Dr. Schmitz said. She and her colleagues argued for it based on randomized trials that showed it saved costs by reducing hospitalizations, emergency room trips and unplanned office visits.

“This U. P. M. C. rollout is a giant experiment,” Dr. Schmitz said. If it’s successful, the hospital plans to expand it to all cancers in 2028. Dr. Schmitz also pushed to incorporate exercise into standards that cancer hospitals must follow to receive certain accreditation, which will happen later this year.

“This is no longer just something that would be nice to have,” Dr. Schmitz said. “This is a therapeutic intervention, it needs to be done — and it needs to be done for all patients.”

Nina Agrawal is a Times health reporter.
